political.title: Region, rivers, names, and method
political.summary: A historical region, not a timeless border Mithila, Vajji, and Anga belong to different kinds of historical geography. Mithila is at once a remembered kingdom, a scholastic-cultural region, and a modern language homeland spanning north Bihar and Nepal's eastern and central Tarai. Vajji names an ancient confederated political formation centred on the north Gangetic plain. Anga was an eastern early-historic polity associated in textual tradition with Champa and the lower middle Ganga corridor. Their boundaries shifted; none maps neatly onto a modern state or district. This book therefore follows networks, rivers, institutions, and remembered centres rather than drawing a single permanent frontier (Singh 2008; Thapar 2002). Water as archive and agent The Himalayan rivers that cross the Tarai and north Bihar deposit silt, abandon channels, flood settlements, and erase or bury archaeological surfaces. The Ganga simultaneously linked Anga and the north-bank regions to long-distance traffic. Rivers were not a static backdrop: they structured cultivation, ferries, markets, pilgrimage, revenue assessment, and disaster. Later chapters show how attempts to stabilize these rivers also redistributed risk. Rules of evidence Archaeological strata establish material sequences, not ethnic labels. Texts disclose categories and memories at the time of composition and transmission; they do not automatically prove every narrated event. Inscriptions are usually firmer chronological anchors but are public acts of power and piety, not neutral chronicles. Gazetteers contain valuable observation together with colonial classification. This layered method is essential in a region where sacred geography, dynastic memory, and political identity remain active. 3 Three spatial scales The narrative moves among three scales that should not be confused. The first is the site or locality: an excavated mound, a river crossing, a settlement cluster, or a named shrine. The second is the historical region, reconstructed from distributions of objects, texts, routes, institutions, and remembered centres. The third is the state, whose administrative reach varied and whose documents often describe claims more readily than everyday practice. Mithila may be meaningful at all three scales, but not in the same way. Vajji is most securely approached as an early political field known through textual and arc

political.title: Archaeology and early food production
political.summary: production Regional evidence and its limits The prehistory of the wider middle Gangetic plain is reconstructed from unevenly investigated sites, ceramics, plant and animal remains, lithic industries, and radiocarbon samples. Chirand, on the north bank of the Ganga in present Saran, is especially important for eastern Indian early farming sequences. Published radiocarbon lists placed several relevant samples broadly within the second millennium BCE, but investigators also warned about disturbed deposits and anomalous determinations. A responsible narrative presents ranges and stratigraphic cautions rather than a single spectacular date. Food production without a single origin story The archaeological record supports changing combinations of cultivation, herding, fishing, hunting, and gathering. Rice appears within a broader subsistence system rather than as proof of an instant agricultural revolution. Bone and antler industries and riverine resources at sites such as Chirand underline adaptation to wetlands and floodplains. The evidence does not justify projecting the later names Mithila, Vajji, or Anga back onto Neolithic communities. From objects to social history Pottery types and tool assemblages help establish sequence and exchange, but social hierarchy, language, and political identity require independent evidence. Even when a material horizon is widespread, it need not represent one people. The most defensible conclusion is that diverse communities in the Gangetic and Himalayan piedmont zones developed increasingly settled and productive lifeways on different timetables. 21 How archaeological deposits are made An archaeological layer is the outcome of occupation, rebuilding, refuse disposal, erosion, flooding, burrowing, cultivation, and later construction. In an active alluvial landscape, objects can be redeposited far from the activity that first produced them. A radiocarbon determination dates the sampled organic material, not automatically an entire cultural phase; the relationship between sample and layer must be demonstrated. These elementary cautions are crucial in the middle Gangetic plain, where dramatic early dates have sometimes circulated more widely than the qualifications printed with them. The published Chirand evidence is important precisely because it permits discussion of early cultivation and mixed subsistence, while also showing why

political.title: Late prehistoric and early iron-using horizons
political.summary: horizons A long transition Across the middle Gangetic plain, the later second and first millennia BCE saw changes in settlement density, ceramics, metal use, and cultivation. These did not occur everywhere at once. Iron objects are part of the sequence, but older models that made iron technology a single cause of forest clearance, surplus, cities, and states now require qualification. Political centralization depended on labour, exchange, agrarian relations, ritual authority, and ecological opportunity as well as tools (Singh 2008; Thapar 2002). Ceramic labels are chronological tools Black-and-red ware, northern black polished ware, and other ceramic categories are archaeological classifications. They cannot by themselves identify Vedic, Vajji, or Anga populations. Northern black polished ware is associated with the early- historic urban horizon in many Gangetic sites, but local sequences and dates differ. The proper question is how settlements participated in larger circuits, not which text-name can be attached to every sherd. Protohistory and restraint The threshold between prehistory and history is uneven because writing, recoverable inscriptions, and datable textual references appear gradually. Literary works preserved orally may remember older settings while taking form over long periods. This volume therefore stops short of constructing dynastic lists for times unsupported by contemporary records. Iron within a larger technological system Iron mattered because it expanded the range of durable edges, points, fittings, and implements available to communities, but its effects depended on access to ore, fuel, specialist 37 knowledge, exchange, repair, and labour. The presence of an iron object in a layer does not show that iron tools were common in every household, nor that they immediately transformed cultivation. Bronze, copper, stone, bone, wood, and clay continued to be used alongside iron. Technological change is therefore best reconstructed as a changing assemblage rather than a sudden replacement of one age by another. Settlement growth and political concentration Larger settlements and denser site distributions can indicate demographic growth, intensified production, exchange, and administrative concentration. political.title: Environment, mobility, and settlement
political.summary: settlement Floodplains and piedmonts North Bihar and the Nepal Tarai combine Himalayan piedmont, alluvial fans, active channels, wetlands, and older floodplain surfaces. Settlement opportunity and archaeological visibility are both conditioned by this geomorphology. A mound may preserve repeated occupation while nearby low surfaces are scoured or buried. The absence of exposed remains is therefore not equivalent to absence of past population. Mobility alongside village life Fishing, herding, seasonal movement, woodland use, and river transport continued alongside settled cultivation. Later administrative sources often treated mobility as disorder because it complicated taxation and surveillance. Prehistoric reconstruction should avoid the same bias: mobility can be a rational adaptation to variable water, pasture, and labour demand. The environmental caution Neither flood nor drought is purely 'natural' in its historical effects. Exposure is shaped by embankments, land tenure, settlement policy, transport, and unequal access to relief. This principle, documented clearly for the Kosi in the colonial and modern periods, also guides interpretation of earlier settlement without pretending that later institutions existed in prehistory. A connected river system The northern tributaries of the Ganga descend rapidly from Himalayan catchments, cross the piedmont, and spread across low-gradient plains. Their channels carry water and sediment while shifting through time. The result is a mosaic of active channels, levees, backswamps, abandoned courses, and older surfaces. Communities could benefit from fertile deposits, 53 fisheries, transport, and moisture while remaining exposed to erosion, avulsion, waterlogging, and crop loss. The historical importance of the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati, Kamla, and related rivers lies not in a single unchanging course but in the opportunities and hazards created by a mobile system. Seasonality and the organization of work Monsoon rainfall and river regimes shaped calendars of sowing, harvesting, fishing, grazing, building, and movement. Labour demand could vary sharply across the year, encouraging households to combine cultivation with craft, transport, forest use, or seasonal migration. Archaeology rarely preserves this calendar directly, yet botanical remains, animal assemblages, storage, house rebuilding, and site location can provide

political.title: Videha in Vedic and Upanishadic textual worlds
political.summary: textual worlds Sources, recensions, and the limits of a textual chronology Chapter 5 rests principally on two related but differently transmitted Vedic corpora: the Satapatha Brahmana of the White Yajurveda and the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad that forms the concluding portion of the Satapatha in both its Madhyandina and Kanva recensions. Julius Eggeling's nineteenth-century translation follows the Madhyandina school. Patrick Olivelle's modern annotated edition of the early Upanishads follows the Kanva recension for the Brihadaranyaka while recording important Madhyandina variants and providing a concordance between the two arrangements (Eggeling 1882; Olivelle 1998). This textual plurality is historically significant. It warns against treating a single printed sequence as a verbatim transcript of one event or one court archive. The absolute dating of the relevant layers remains debated. Linguistic stratification, school geography, intertextual relations, and comparison with archaeological and political change can establish relative sequences more securely than exact calendar years. Terms such as 'later Vedic' and 'early Upanishadic' are therefore used here as broad scholarly periods. Where a precise date would depend on a contested reconstruction, the prose states the uncertainty instead of converting a relative chronology into a false regnal year (Witzel 1997; Olivelle 1998). Videgha Mathava and the east Satapatha Brahmana 1.4.1 narrates an eastward movement in which Videgha Mathava and the priest Gotama Rahugana follow Agni Vaisvanara from the region of the Sarasvati toward the Sadanira. The narrative explains how the sacrificial fire 'tastes' or burns through lands and rivers until it reaches a river it does not cross. The text later associates the Sadanira with a boundary between Kosala and Videha. Historians have long recognized the 69 passage as important evidence for the eastward extension of Brahmanical ritual geography. Its value is greatest when it is read as a ritual-political representation of incorporation, not as an eyewitness migration diary with a secure year-by-year route (Eggeling 1882; Witzel 1997). The name Videgha in this passage is related to Videha in later textual geography, but the narrative does not authorize a simple map from the Sarasvati to a modern district boundary. political.title: Janaka, Sita, and the discipline of reading tradition
political.summary: reading tradition Epic geography and living memory The Ramayana associates Sita with Janaka and Mithila, and Janakpur became a major centre of pilgrimage and regional identity. The epic is indispensable for the history of ideas, devotion, performance, art, and sacred geography. It is not, by itself, contemporary proof for the reign dates, administrative institutions, or precise borders of an early kingdom. Multiple textual lives The Ramayana developed through a long history of composition, transmission, commentary, vernacular retelling, and performance. Jain, Buddhist, Sanskrit, Maithili, Nepali, and other traditions reworked its characters and moral problems. Historical method asks when and where a particular version was produced and how it was used, rather than searching for one layer that validates every later claim. Why the distinction matters Separating devotion from event-history does not diminish cultural importance. It allows Janakpur, marriage circuits, festivals, painting, song, and gendered readings of Sita to be studied as historical phenomena in their own right. The region's attachment to Sita is securely real as social history even where ancient chronology remains unverified. Epic time and historical time Epic narrative arranges persons, kingdoms, journeys, and moral choices within a meaningful story world. Historical reconstruction asks different questions: when a passage took shape, what earlier and later layers it contains, how manuscripts differ, and which institutions are independently attested. A place named in an epic may preserve old geographical knowledge, later editorial knowledge, or both. It 86 cannot by itself provide a precise regnal list or archaeological date. The distinction between epic time and historical time should therefore be maintained even when a narrative has shaped regional identity for centuries (Thapar 2002; Richman 1991). Figure 1. political.title: Vajji, the Licchavis, and Vaishali
political.summary: A confederated political field The Vajjis enter early Buddhist political narrative as a powerful corporate formation north of the Ganga, with the Licchavis of Vesali or Vaishali among its most visible constituents. Digha Nikaya 16 does not describe a territorial state in modern administrative terms. Instead it presents a political collective whose resilience depends on repeated meetings, concord, inherited rules, respect for elders, limits on coercion against women, maintenance of shrines, and protection of accomplished renunciants. These features support the historical importance of corporate institutions without supplying a complete constitution or census of political participants (Walshe 1995; Vajira and Story 1998; Thapar 1991). The archive and its asymmetries The political history of Vajji is reconstructed from sources written for purposes other than constitutional description. Buddhist canonical texts frame political conduct within moral and monastic concerns; Jain narratives place Mahavira within a sacred and kinship geography; archaeology recovers deposits, fortifications, objects, and religious monuments rather than the minutes of assemblies. Later pilgrims, colonial excavators, modern tourism, and regional memory add further layers. No one archive can therefore stand for the whole society. The strongest reconstruction is cumulative: identify what a source actually records, establish its date and genre as far as possible, compare independent evidence, and leave unresolved gaps visible rather than filling them with a seamless republican story (Singh 2008; Thapar 2002). Vajji, Licchavi, Videha: names and constituencies Vajji or Vriji, Licchavi, and Videha should not be used as interchangeable labels. Textual classifications vary in the number and names of groups associated with the Vajjian 106 political field, and different traditions foreground different constituencies. The Licchavis are especially prominent in Buddhist accounts of Vesali; Videha had its own older textual and regional history. Later scholarship sometimes organizes these names into fixed lists of clans, but the surviving traditions do not justify treating one list as an uncontested federal constitution. A safer formulation is that Vajji denoted a corporate political formation involving more than one elite group, with Licchavi power particularly visible at Vesali (Thapar 1991; Singh 20

political.title: Anga, Champa, and the Magadhan horizon
political.summary: horizon Anga as a historical problem Anga is one of the clearest examples of why political geography must be reconstructed from several different kinds of evidence. Buddhist lists place Anga among the major polities of northern India, usually beside Magadha; Jain texts also preserve Anga within an eastern political and religious horizon. Later Brahmanical and epic traditions give the region additional genealogies and heroes, while archaeology at Champa documents a long-lived fortified settlement whose material sequence cannot be equated automatically with any one literary story. The historical task is therefore not to choose one archive and make all others conform to it. It is to identify what each source can securely establish and where the categories of kingdom, city, sacred place, and remembered homeland diverge (Singh 2008; Thapar 2002). Mahajanapada lists and political scale In the Anguttara Nikaya, Anga appears in the conventional list of sixteen major countries or mahajanapadas. The list is important because it places Anga in a remembered system of large-scale political units, but the form is schematic rather than cartographic. The names are not accompanied by surveyed borders, population totals, or a constitutional description. Different Buddhist and Jain texts transmit partly different lists, which shows that the number and sequence served classificatory as well as geographical purposes. Anga's appearance is therefore strong evidence for political prominence in the eastern Gangetic world, not a warrant for drawing a fixed frontier around modern districts (Singh 2008; Thapar 2002). 127 Early Brahmanical references and the danger of ethnic reading Anga is also named in early Brahmanical textual traditions, including the Atharvavedic corpus, where eastern peoples can be represented through the cultural judgments of authors located elsewhere. Such references are evidence for the existence of names and for perceptions of distance or difference; they should not be turned into timeless ethnic descriptions. A stigmatizing or exoticizing passage tells us about the classificatory world of the text as well as about the people named. The emergence of Anga in several textual traditions is historically significant, but linguistic labels, ritual status, political membership, and archaeological culture must remain separate unless independent evidence connects them

political.title: Buddhism, Jainism, and eastern Gangetic religious change
political.summary: Gangetic religious change Shared landscape, distinct traditions The eastern Gangetic plain was not the birthplace of one undifferentiated 'heterodox' movement. Buddhist, Jain, Ajivika, Brahmanical, and other renunciant or ritual communities shared roads, cities, courts, markets, languages, and arguments while maintaining distinct disciplines and claims to authority. Vaishali, Rajagriha, Champa, Mithila, and the wider Magadhan sphere appear repeatedly because political power, urban concentration, merchant wealth, and itinerant teaching converged there. Similar geography is therefore evidence of interaction, not doctrinal identity. A responsible history reconstructs specific institutions and debates before using broad categories such as sramana or Greater Magadha (Bronkhorst 2007; Gombrich 2006; Dundas 2002). Chronology: founders, texts, and transmitted memory The lives of the Buddha and Mahavira are commonly placed in the middle of the first millennium BCE, but exact dates remain debated. The canonical texts that narrate their lives and teachings were transmitted, organized, and redacted over time. This does not make them historically useless; it changes the kinds of claims that can safely be made. Named places, institutional vocabulary, social categories, and repeated narrative relationships can illuminate the world remembered by early communities, while speeches and event sequences require genre criticism. Absolute dates should be anchored in independently datable inscriptions or archaeology wherever possible rather than assigned merely because a canonical biography supplies a sequence (Gombrich 2006; Dundas 2002; Singh 2008). 140 The sramana field without a single origin story Renunciation, wandering, fasting, meditation, debate, and critiques of household or sacrificial life formed a broader religious field in which Buddhism and Jainism developed. Some practices may have had older precedents, and different groups explained karma, rebirth, liberation, selfhood, and ascetic effort in sharply different ways. It is therefore misleading to narrate one movement as simply copying another or to make all non- Vedic traditions expressions of a single anti-Brahmanical programme. political.title: Empires, inscriptions, and pilgrim itineraries
political.summary: itineraries Empire as a claim with uneven reach The appearance of the Mauryas, Guptas, and later supra- regional powers changes the scale at which the history of Mithila, Vajji, Anga, and the Nepal-facing corridor must be written. Empire did not erase local institutions or turn every settlement into an equally administered unit. Royal inscriptions, coins, pillars, seals, roads, tax relations, ritual patronage, and military claims each register different degrees of incorporation. A proclamation at a pillar is strong evidence that a ruler chose that place for public communication; it is not proof that every village nearby experienced identical administration. The historical problem is therefore to map imperial acts and networks without filling the spaces between them with an assumed uniform state (Thapar 2012; Lahiri 2015). Mauryan north Bihar: monument and text must be separated North Bihar preserves an unusually important group of monolithic pillars associated with Ashoka. Yet the pillars do not all carry the same evidence. Lauriya-Areraj and Lauriya- Nandangarh bear the first six Major Pillar Edicts, and at Rampurva one of the two known pillars is inscribed while its companion is uninscribed. The lion-capital pillar at Kolhua/Vaishali is conventionally accepted as Ashokan but carries no Ashokan inscription. This distinction matters. An inscribed pillar combines monument, royal language, script, and place; an uninscribed pillar establishes monumental intervention but requires other evidence for its purpose and date. A chapter on empire must never silently transfer an edict from one pillar to another (Hultzsch 1925; Falk 2006; Archaeological Survey of India, Patna Circle). 162 Stone, quarry, transport, and state capacity The polished sandstone pillars are also evidence for technologies and labour systems. Quarrying a large monolith, shaping and polishing it, transporting it over long distances, preparing a foundation, raising the shaft, and fitting a capital required skilled stoneworkers, transport crews, supervisors, and substantial logistical coordination. Those operations demonstrate state-supported capacity even when the surviving pillar is uninscribed. They do not tell us whether labour was paid, corvee, hereditary, or organized through contractors in any one locality. political.title: Licchavi Nepal and the problem of continuity
political.summary: continuity What “Licchavi Nepal” can securely mean For this chapter, “Licchavi Nepal” is first of all an inscriptional historical category. The securely dated record in the Kathmandu Valley begins with Mānadeva’s Changu Narayan pillar inscription, whose saṃvat 386 is conventionally converted to 464 CE. From the fifth century onward a substantial Sanskrit epigraphic corpus names rulers, relatives, officials, settlements, taxes, land, religious beneficiaries and acts of donation. That archive justifies speaking of a Licchavi royal lineage and political order in the Valley. It does not by itself establish when the family first entered Nepal, whether all persons called Licchavi shared one biological ancestry, or whether the dynasty was an unchanged continuation of the Licchavis remembered at Vaishali roughly a millennium earlier. The chronological asymmetry must remain visible: political memory of Licchavis in the middle Gangetic plain is early; dated Licchavi rule in the Kathmandu Valley is much later (Riccardi 1989; Vajracharya 1973; Sharma 1983; Whelpton 2005). The epigraphic threshold and the silence before it Mānadeva’s pillar is often called the beginning of “historical” Nepal because it creates a firm dated anchor, not because nothing existed before it. The inscription itself names earlier rulers, and later genealogical traditions push the lineage farther back. Archaeological and art-historical evidence likewise shows that the Valley had complex communities before 464. The methodological point is narrower: before the fifth-century inscriptions, the political sequence is much harder to control with contemporary, internally dated documentation. Chronicles composed centuries later are valuable for cultural memory, but their regnal lists cannot simply be given the same evidentiary weight as a dated stone inscription. The expansion therefore 183 uses 464 as an epigraphic threshold rather than an invented foundation date for settlement, kingship or culture in the Valley (Riccardi 1989; Slusser 1982; Whelpton 2005). Changu Narayan as a dated political act The Changu Narayan pillar is a monument, a religious object and a royal text at once. Its opening date formula, royal genealogy and praise of Viṣṇu place Mānadeva within a Sanskritic idiom shared across much of South Asia. Its political passages celebrate military capability and royal duty; its family narrative

political.title: Tirabhukti and the early-medieval regional order
political.summary: regional order From Videha to Tirabhukti: a change of scale Tīrabhukti, later Tirhut, became a durable administrative and regional name for north Bihar, but it should not be treated as a timeless replacement for Videha or Mithila. The terms belong to different archives and scales. Videha is prominent in Vedic, Upanishadic, Buddhist, Jain, and epic traditions; Tīrabhukti becomes especially visible in Gupta and early-medieval administrative records; Mithila grows in importance as a literary, scholastic, and regional name whose later reach cannot simply be projected backward. The safest history therefore asks when each name is actually attested, what kind of source uses it, and whether the source is naming a province, a city-centred administrative unit, a cultural region, or a remembered homeland. A later equivalence between Tirhut and Mithila is historically real without proving that every early-medieval document used the two words as exact synonyms (Sircar 1971; Salomon 1998; Thakur 1988). The Basarh seals and the first firm administrative archive The excavations at Basarh, identified with ancient Vaiśālī, recovered a remarkable group of clay seals and sealings that makes Gupta-period Tīrabhukti unusually visible. The material includes the seal of Mahādevī Dhruvasvāminī, wife of Chandragupta II and mother of Govindagupta, along with official sealings connected with the establishment of the yuvarāja or crown prince. Read together, these finds show that Vaiśālī was not only a place of ancient republican and Buddhist memory; in the Gupta period it also functioned as a centre of provincial administration. Sealings are not narrative chronicles. Their strength lies in naming offices, establishments, persons, and institutional relationships in a securely archaeological 206 urban context (Bloch 1906; Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, vol. III, revised ed. 1981). Vaiśālī as headquarters: strong inference, bounded claim The Basarh record has often been summarized by saying that Vaiśālī was the capital of Tīrabhukti. That is a reasonable description of the administrative concentration revealed by the seals, but the word capital can imply more than the evidence establishes. What the sealings directly support is the presence of provincial and crown-prince establishments at the site, including offices whose jurisdiction related to Tīrabhukti. political.title: The Karnatas and Simraongarh
political.summary: A border-crossing kingdom The Karnata polity is best understood as a kingdom whose political geography crossed the modern India–Nepal boundary rather than as a dynasty confined to one present-day national space. Its best-known capital, Simraongarh (Simraungadh), lies in the Nepal Tarai, while its agrarian, religious, intellectual and military field extended southward into the plains of Tirabhukti or Tirhut. The modern frontier therefore cuts through a historical landscape that was connected by roads, river crossings, marriage alliances, landholding networks, pilgrimage, commerce and the movement of scholars. The kingdom’s history belongs simultaneously to the histories of Mithila, north Bihar, Madhesh/Tarai and the Kathmandu Valley, but connection must not be inflated into uniform territorial control over all of those regions. The familiar dynastic sequence beginning with Nānyadeva and ending with Harisiṃhadeva is a scholarly reconstruction assembled from inscriptions, literary works, Nepalese chronicles and genealogical traditions, archaeological evidence and later regional histories. These categories of evidence do not all speak with the same chronological precision. The task is consequently not to make them sound artificially unanimous, but to show where they intersect and where uncertainty remains. This is especially important for the opening date of the dynasty, the rebuilding of Simraongarh’s defences, and the final conquest horizon in the fourteenth century (Sinha 1979; Petech 1984; Salomon 1998). The 1097 horizon and what an inscription can establish The year 1097 CE has long functioned as the conventional beginning of Nānyadeva’s rule. It is useful as a chronological horizon, but it should not be described as though an extant Nānyadeva inscription bears that Gregorian date in an unambiguous modern form. Luciano Petech, reviewing the early 228 chronology in relation to Nepal, noted the traditional chronogram that converts to 18 July 1097 while also observing that the surviving inscription associated with Nānyadeva’s reign and his minister Śrīdhara is undated. The distinction matters: a conventional date can organize discussion without acquiring an evidentiary status it does not possess. political.title: Oiniwar rule, Sultanate power, and political transition
political.summary: political transition Reconstituted authority after 1324–25 The Oiniwar period should not be introduced as the automatic restoration of a sovereign Mithila kingdom immediately after the fall of the Karnatas. The Tughluq conquest horizon around 1324–25 changed the political scale on which regional authority operated. Local chiefs, learned families, landed intermediaries and religious institutions remained, but they now negotiated in a field that could include Delhi, provincial governors, Jaunpur, Bengal and neighbouring Nepal. The Oiniwar rulers emerged from this field. Their authority could be substantial in local jurisdiction and patronage while still being exposed to tribute, military intervention, recognition by a superior power or rivalry among branches of the ruling family. Older histories often provide a smooth accession list beginning with Kāmeśvara Ṭhākura. Modern source criticism is less confident. Vijayakanta Mishra’s classic chronology study and D. C. Sircar’s numismatic discussion both emphasize that the chronology is difficult, not least because the epoch and application of Lakṣmaṇasena-era dates have been debated and because simultaneous or joint authority may have existed. The dynasty is consequently better reconstructed around evidence clusters—literary, manuscript, epigraphic and numismatic— than around a single unbroken list of exact reigns (Mishra 1953; Sircar 1957–58). The problem of the dynastic beginning Kāmeśvara is remembered as the progenitor of the Oiniwar line, with Oini and Sugauna appearing in later historical geography associated with the family. Some regional accounts place his rise close to the immediate aftermath of the Karnata collapse; other reconstructions connect his recognition more 253 closely with the reign of Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq in the mid- fourteenth century. The evidence does not justify pretending that these alternatives are identical. ‘Foundation’ may itself compress a process in which a locally influential lineage acquired wider fiscal and political responsibilities under changing Sultanate conditions. That process fits a broader pattern of regional state formation in late medieval north India. A lineage could hold land, mobilize armed followers, patronize scholarship and exercise jurisdiction while also seeking confirmation or protection from a more powerful court. political.title: Two Vidyapatis: Maithili, Sanskrit learning, and law
political.summary: learning, and law Governing distinction: two Vidyāpatis This history adopts a two-Vidyāpati reconstruction as a governing rule of attribution. Mahākavi Vidyāpati is treated as the earlier, pre-Jyotirīśvara poet of the Maithili Padāvalī tradition. Vidyāpati Ṭhakkura is treated as the later Oiniwar- period intellectual associated with Sanskrit and Avahaṭṭa works, including Kīrtilatā, Kīrtipatākā, Puruṣaparīkṣā and Likhanāvalī. The distinction is applied throughout the book to chronology, language, patronage, caste claims, legends, bibliography, glossary and index. A work or anecdote is not moved from one figure to the other merely because later tradition uses the same name. This is an explicit historiographical position of the present book rather than a claim that all modern scholarship already agrees. The mainstream one-author model remains influential: Ramanath Jha’s Sahitya Akademi monograph and Pankaj Jha’s study of the fifteenth century both organize major corpora under one Vidyāpati. Yet Ramanath Jha also warns that Vidyāpati was a common name, that several authors of that name—including more than one Thakur—survive, and that identification from the name alone is hazardous. That warning supplies an important methodological bridge between the conventional model and the sharper separation adopted here. Why the distinction is historically necessary Conflation produces more than a literary inconvenience. If the Padāvalī poet and the later court intellectual are treated as one person, the biography of an Oiniwar scholar is projected onto a vernacular song tradition; the date of one corpus is made to control the other; court patrons become patrons of every song; and later genealogical or caste narratives can be transferred backward without an independent witness. The 275 result is a circular biography in which works authenticate a life that was itself reconstructed from the same works. The two-person model breaks that circle. Each corpus must first be dated and attributed on its own evidence: manuscript colophons, internal royal names, linguistic register, citations, early anthologies, performance history and external references. Only after those controls are established may biography be reconstructed. political.title: Mughal-era Tirhut, Anga, and early-modern institutions
political.summary: modern institutions From Oiniwar collapse to Mughal provincial government The sixteenth century did not replace a bounded medieval kingdom with a uniformly administered Mughal province in a single act. North Bihar, the Ganga corridor, the Munger- Bhagalpur zone, Purnea, and the Himalayan-facing frontier entered Mughal political structures through conquest, appointments, fiscal assessment, military service, and accommodation with entrenched local power-holders. The result was a layered order in which imperial sovereignty coexisted with strong landed intermediaries, village institutions, religious endowments, and ecological constraints. For this chapter, 'Mughal incorporation' therefore means the extension of an imperial language of subah, sarkar, mahal, pargana, jagir, zamindari, assessment and office. It does not imply that every locality was surveyed with equal precision, that every revenue demand was collected in full, or that regional institutions lost their own histories. The distinction is particularly important in Tirhut and eastern Bihar, where floodplains, frontier zones and powerful intermediary houses repeatedly complicated the map drawn at court. The 1580 provincial reorganization and the making of Subah Bihar Akbar's administrative reorganization, conventionally dated to 1580, treated Bihar as one of the empire's major provinces. This institutionalization followed the Mughal defeat of the remaining Afghan power in Bihar and Bengal and created a provincial framework in which subah-level officers coordinated revenue, military and judicial functions. Contemporary and near-contemporary sources nevertheless show that provincial organization remained a process of consolidation, not a 299 completed cadastral fact from its first year (Imtiaz Ahmad 2002; Ansari 2019). Patna became the principal provincial centre, while older strategic nodes such as Munger retained importance. The institutional geography mattered because Tirhut was administered within Subah Bihar, whereas parts of the eastern frontier lay within Bengal's sarkars. The modern boundaries of Bihar, West Bengal and Nepal must therefore not be read backward into Akbar's territorial vocabulary. Source hierarchy for the Mughal period The source base is richer than for the Karnata and Oiniwar centuries, but richer does not mean transparent. political.title: Company rule, Permanent Settlement, and Darbhanga Raj
political.summary: Settlement, and Darbhanga Raj Revenue before representation The East India Company acquired fiscal authority in Bihar before it created representative institutions or a modern public administration. That sequence matters. From the grant of the dīwānī in 1765 onward, the Company's first durable claim on villages, markets and landed houses was a claim to revenue. Courts, policing, survey, registration and bureaucratic classification expanded around that fiscal core. For Tirhut and the eastern districts, colonial rule therefore first appeared less as a sudden replacement of every local institution than as a new sovereign claimant attempting to make inherited rights calculable, enforceable and remittable (British Library, Mss Eur B373; Marshall 1987; Travers 2007). 1765: the dīwānī and a new revenue sovereign The Mughal emperor Shah Alam II's grant of the dīwānī of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company in 1765 supplied a legal-political basis for Company revenue collection. British Library records include Robert Clive's September 1765 correspondence explicitly concerning that grant. The change was fundamental, but it did not create a blank institutional field. Company servants still depended on zamindars, chaudharīs, qānūngōs, bankers, village accountants, revenue farmers and local knowledge. The new regime inherited a vocabulary and personnel that had developed under Mughal and post-Mughal government even as it gradually altered their legal position. 325 The limits of the 'dual government' shorthand The years after 1765 are often summarized as a period of 'dual government', with revenue power and nominal executive responsibility separated. The phrase is useful only if it does not conceal uneven practice. Revenue collection, policing, adjudication and local coercion were already entangled. What changed over the following decade was not simply the abolition of a tidy dual system, but the Company's progressive decision to supervise and standardize functions that it had initially tried to exercise through inherited structures. In north Bihar the pace of this change varied by locality and by the reliability of intermediaries. The famine of 1770 and the fiscal state The great famine of 1770 exposed the vulnerability of a revenue regime whose information, transport and relief capacities were limited. political.title: Agrarian society, markets, caste, and labour
political.summary: and labour Beyond the self-contained village The agrarian history of Mithila, Vajji-country, and Anga cannot be reconstructed from the image of an isolated, self- sufficient village. Periodic markets, fairs, ferries, river ports, roads, railway stations, pilgrimage centres, credit networks, and seasonal migration connected cultivators and labouring households to district towns, Patna, Bengal, Nepal, Assam, and wider commercial circuits. Anand A. Yang's work on Bihar's bazaars is especially important because it treats the market as a social and political institution rather than a mere place where prices were formed (Yang 1998). The village nevertheless remained a crucial arena of production, tenancy, caste power, household reproduction, and local dispute. The methodological point is therefore not to replace 'village' with 'market,' but to reconstruct the traffic between fields, households, estates, courts, haats, transport routes, and migration destinations. The archive is socially uneven Settlement reports, rent cases, estate papers, gazetteers, censuses, agricultural vocabularies, and statutes were produced for different purposes. A cadastral survey sought legally actionable classifications; a gazetteer compressed official knowledge; an estate record followed income and control; Grierson's Bihar Peasant Life catalogued material culture and vocabulary; later social histories read these records against the grain. No one source can be treated as a transparent photograph of rural society (Grierson 1885; Kerr 1926; Yang 1989). The people most visible in durable records were not necessarily the people most numerous in the countryside. Landless workers, women, sharecroppers, artisans, itinerant traders, herders, and people whose claims rested on oral custom 351 often entered the archive mainly when a dispute, survey, debt, crime, tax, or administrative enquiry made them legible. Agrarian zones were not identical North Bihar's alluvial plains, the Kosi belt, the Ganga corridor, Bhagalpur-Munger tracts, and the margins toward Purnea and the Tarai differed in flood risk, soils, transport, crop possibilities, estate structure, and labour demand. A category established in a Darbhanga settlement report cannot automatically be exported unchanged to a Kosi diara or to southern Bihar. This chapter therefore uses comparison without flattening regional difference. Darbhanga

political.title: Rivers, calamity, transport, and the colonial state
political.summary: colonial state A floodplain governed through records Colonial rule in north Bihar and the eastern Ganga plain encountered a landscape in which rivers altered fields, roads, ferries, administrative boundaries, and taxable assets. The state answered with surveys, flood reports, embankment files, railway engineering, remission rules, relief codes, and district statistics. These records make environmental change unusually visible, but they were produced for government purposes and must be read as interventions as well as descriptions. The central question is therefore not whether the colonial state 'controlled' the rivers. It did not. The historical problem is how officials, zamindars, engineers, merchants, cultivators, boatmen, and labourers redistributed risk while trying to protect revenue, communication, settlements, crops, and property. Christopher Hill and Praveen Singh both emphasize that river management became a field of social control and political conflict rather than a purely technical response to nature. Rivers were infrastructure before railways The Ganga, Gandak, Bagmati, Kosi, Mahananda, and their distributaries carried boats, supplied fisheries, watered fields, deposited silt, and created ferries and market points long before the railway age. Seasonal navigation and crossing conditions varied sharply. A river could connect a bazaar to wider exchange in one season and isolate the same locality after channel migration or flood damage. Transport history must therefore begin with water. Railway and road systems were inserted into an already active network of channels, landing places, seasonal tracks, ferries, cattle routes, and pilgrim itineraries. The new infrastructure did not replace this older mobility in a single transition. 373 The Kosi as a moving river system The Kosi occupied a broad alluvial fan and repeatedly shifted among channels across the north Bihar plain. Colonial officers encountered erosion, deposition, waterlogging, sand casting, abandoned channels, and newly formed diara land as recurrent administrative problems. The later image of a single river permanently confined between embankments should not be projected backward onto the nineteenth century. political.title: Education, print, language, reform, and nationalism
political.summary: and nationalism Colonial education and older learning Tols, pathshalas, maktabs, Persianate instruction, household teaching, temple- and monastery-linked learning, occupational apprenticeship, and courtly scholarship all predated the spread of colonial schools. The nineteenth century therefore did not introduce education into an intellectual vacuum. It altered the institutions through which learning could be certified, financed, inspected, and converted into employment. The decisive change was not a clean replacement of one system by another but a redistribution of prestige. English, new vernacular curricula, examinations, printed textbooks, government grants, and university affiliation created credentials that could open some occupations while leaving older Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, ritual, scribal, artisanal, and oral forms of knowledge in continued use (Jha 1972; O'Malley 1907). Education before school statistics Official returns measure schools, pupils, grants, teachers, attendance, and examination results. They are indispensable for institutional history but undercount learning that did not fit a recognized school form. Domestic literacy, recitation, account keeping, manuscript copying, ritual training, craft instruction, song, and inherited professional knowledge often remain outside the statistical frame. A source-controlled history therefore reads educational statistics as records of what the colonial state chose to enumerate and subsidize. Rising enrolment is important evidence, but it cannot by itself demonstrate the total distribution of knowledge within villages or households. 394 Tols and Sanskrit scholastic networks Mithila's Sanskrit scholastic reputation survived the growth of English education. Tols and learned households trained students in grammar, logic, ritual, law, philosophy, astronomy, and related disciplines, often through personal teacher-pupil relationships rather than standardized classrooms. Patronage from landed houses and donors could sustain these institutions even when government schooling expanded. Their persistence also complicates a simple 'traditional versus modern' binary. A Sanskrit scholar might participate in print, correspond with university authorities, advise a court, or support a language association while remaining embedded in a scholastic lineage. Institutional boundaries were porous. Pathshalas, village school

political.title: The Nepal Tarai, Rana rule, and the border to 1951
political.summary: border to 1951 Tarai as frontier and homeland The Nepal Tarai was never merely an empty frontier awaiting settlement from the hills. Forests, grasslands, wetlands, farms, market towns, pilgrimage centres, estates, and older settlements linked the Himalayan foothills to the Gangetic plain. Its history therefore has to begin with inhabited landscapes and competing claims, not with the administrative language of reclamation. State revenue, timber extraction, disease environments, transport, and cross-border trade changed the density and distribution of settlement over time. These processes affected long-established Tharu and other communities as well as Maithili-, Bhojpuri-, Awadhi-, Urdu-, and Nepali-speaking migrants and townspeople. “Tarai” names a changing ecological and administrative zone, not one timeless social population (Gaige 1975; Whelpton 2005). “Tarai” as an ecological and administrative category The word Tarai could describe lowland terrain, a revenue region, a forest belt, or a frontier of particular districts depending on date and document. Such usages overlap but are not identical. A nineteenth-century treaty clause, a Rana revenue order, a census table, and a modern provincial map therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable maps of the same space. This distinction also prevents the cultural geography of Mithila from being equated mechanically with every administrative tract of the Nepalese plains. Maithili cultural and linguistic networks were especially important in the eastern and central Tarai, while the wider Tarai also contained many other language and social fields. 420 Border before border Before the nineteenth-century treaty regime, routes, political influence, forests, estates, pilgrimage, and kinship crossed what later became an international frontier. The modern India–Nepal boundary is therefore indispensable for colonial and contemporary history but anachronistic when projected unchanged into the Karnata, Oiniwar, or early Shah periods. The frontier became progressively more consequential as treaties, surveys, customs posts, courts, land records, and police practices attached different legal effects to each side. Social crossing and formal sovereignty should be reconstructed together rather than forced into a choice between a “real” border and an “imaginary” one. political.title: Land reform, democracy, and changing regional power
political.summary: changing regional power The end of zamindari The Bihar Land Reforms Act of 1950 marked a constitutional break in the agrarian order of north Bihar. It provided for the transfer to the state of the interests of proprietors and tenure- holders, dismantling the legal position of zamindars as revenue- receiving intermediaries. In Mithila the change struck directly at Darbhanga Raj and numerous smaller estates; in Anga and adjoining districts it likewise altered the relation among estate holders, raiyats, subordinate tenants, markets, ferries, forests, fisheries, and other revenue-bearing interests (Bihar Act XXX of 1950). The change was profound but not instantaneous. Vesting of intermediary interests did not mean that every cultivator obtained ownership, that every tenancy dispute disappeared, or that local influence was redistributed in equal measure. Legal abolition and social redistribution therefore have to be studied separately. Constitutional land reform and the early Republic The abolition of zamindari became one of the first major tests of the new constitutional order. Property rights, compensation, legislative competence, and the social purpose of agrarian reform were argued before courts while constitutional amendments protected specified categories of land-reform legislation. Postcolonial agrarian change thus advanced through statutes, notifications, adjudication, and administrative transfer rather than through a single decree. The Supreme Court described the common objective of the Bihar and comparable state statutes as elimination of intermediary proprietary structures and a more direct relationship between cultivators and the state. Constitutional 444 validity, however, was not the same as effective implementation (State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh, 1952). What vesting transferred The Bihar statute defined the interests passing to the state broadly. Estates and tenures carried claims not only over cultivated land but also over forests, fisheries, ferries, hats, bazaars, mines, minerals, and other revenue-yielding rights. Zamindari abolition therefore altered the legal status of commercial and environmental resources embedded in the estate system. At village level, the transfer of superior interests did not erase every lower layer of tenure. political.title: The India-Nepal borderland, migration, and exchange
political.summary: migration, and exchange An open border is still a border The India–Nepal frontier is often described as 'open', but openness is a historically specific regulatory arrangement rather than the absence of a boundary. The two states retain separate sovereignty, citizenship, criminal and civil jurisdiction, taxation, property law, electoral membership, customs systems, and security institutions. What is unusual is the extent to which citizens can move across much of the land frontier without the passport-and-visa regime typical of many international borders (Government of India and Government of Nepal 1950; Kumar 2013). The resulting borderland is best understood as a field in which legal separation and social connection operate simultaneously. A marriage may be locally ordinary yet legally cross-national; a weekly market trip may involve little documentary friction while a land purchase, inheritance, arrest, school certificate, or citizenship application activates national law. Article 7 and the limits of treaty shorthand The 31 July 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship is the central bilateral legal anchor. Article 1 affirms sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence, while Article 7 commits the governments, on a reciprocal basis, to grant nationals of the other country privileges concerning residence, property, trade and commerce, movement, and similar matters. The two clauses should be read together: reciprocal privileges do not abolish the international frontier (Government of India and Government of Nepal 1950). It is therefore inaccurate to say that the treaty created a borderless space. Domestic legislation, administrative interpretation, security practice, land law, and later bilateral 459 agreements determine how particular rights operate. The treaty is a framework, not a complete code for every crossing. Open-border practice before and after 1950 Mobility across the plains long predates 1950. Marriage, pilgrimage, market exchange, seasonal work, military recruitment, rail travel, and movement between estates and towns already linked the Tarai and north Bihar. The treaty gave reciprocal mobility a postcolonial inter-state framework, but it did not create the social infrastructure from nothing. This distinction matters historically. A practice can be older than its present legal basis, and a legal basis can reshape an older practice. Borderland h

political.title: Maithili and Angika: language, literature, and recognition
political.summary: literature, and recognition Recognition is not one event Language recognition in modern South Asia occurs through several institutions that answer different questions. A university may accept a language for examination; a literary academy may recognize it for awards and publication; a census may classify a returned mother tongue under a particular heading; a state may authorize official use for specified purposes; the Constitution may place a language in the Eighth Schedule; and a digital standard may encode a historical script. None of these acts creates the speech community from nothing, and none by itself settles every question of linguistic classification. This chapter therefore separates linguistic description, self- identification, literary standardization, census enumeration, educational use, constitutional status, and cultural policy. That distinction is especially important for Maithili and Angika, whose histories overlap geographically and linguistically but whose modern institutional trajectories are not identical. Names, varieties, and the danger of retrospective certainty The names used for speech varieties change over time. A label found in a twentieth-century linguistic survey cannot automatically be projected into the first millennium, and a modern movement name cannot be assumed to have been the self-designation of all earlier speakers. Conversely, a new public label may become socially real through literature, schooling, organizations, broadcasting, and political mobilization. The source-controlled question is therefore not simply whether a form is a 'language' or a 'dialect.' It is who classified it, by what criteria, in which institution, at what date, and how speakers themselves used or rejected that classification. 478 Grierson and the colonial linguistic survey George A. Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India placed Maithili within the Bihari section of the eastern Indo-Aryan field and described several regional varieties. His survey remains indispensable because it recorded grammar, vocabulary, specimens, and classificatory judgments at the turn of the twentieth century. It must nevertheless be read as a historical survey produced through colonial-era categories and field procedures, not as a permanently binding constitution of language identity (Grierson 1903). political.title: Mithila painting, gender, and the cultural economy
political.summary: cultural economy From domestic surfaces to a modern art field Mithila painting is best understood as a history of linked media rather than as a single object with a single origin date. Wall murals, floor drawings, wedding-room images, paper paintings, textiles, books, public murals, museum acquisitions, and digital reproductions belong to different material and institutional settings. Their connections are real, but the historical record does not justify treating every modern paper painting as an unchanged survival from an ancient age. The decisive modern transformation occurred when domestic visual practices were made portable, collectible, attributable, and saleable. This process changed who could see the work, how an artist could be named, how money moved through a household, and how curators and critics classified the result. It also created new inequalities because the people who supplied paper, selected artists, transported paintings, assigned categories, mounted exhibitions, and negotiated prices could influence which forms became visible. What the evidence can and cannot date Claims that Mithila painting began at the wedding of Sita and Rama belong to sacred and regional tradition, not to a datable documentary archive. Such narratives are historically important because they explain how communities connect painting with Mithila's sacred geography and marriage ritual, but they cannot by themselves establish the age of a particular technique, motif, or social division of artistic labor. A source-controlled history therefore separates three questions: how old particular ritual practices may be; when paintings were actually documented by dated photographs, manuscripts, collections, or written descriptions; and when the modern paper-based art market developed. The answers 500 overlap only partly. This distinction protects the tradition from both skeptical erasure and romantic overdating. The 1919 marriage paintings: an early documentary anchor Carolyn Brown Heinz drew attention to paintings made in 1919 for the marriage of a daughter of Maharaja Rameshwar Singh of Darbhanga. They are important because they provide an unusually early dated documentary reference for the visual culture of a marriage household before the paper market. political.title: The Kosi, floods, infrastructure, and environmental risk
political.summary: environmental risk A river system as a historical actor The Kosi is not a backdrop to the history of Mithila. It has shaped settlement, agrarian opportunity, transport, administrative boundaries, public works, migration, and political expectations. Yet a river is not an intentional political actor. Historical explanation must connect geomorphology and monsoon hydrology with institutions that decide where people may live, which structures are maintained, how warnings move, and whose losses are compensated. This chapter therefore treats environmental risk as produced by an interaction of hazard, exposure, infrastructure, and social capacity. Seasonal high water can be beneficial in one landscape and disastrous in another. A breach can convert a protected tract into a catastrophe zone. An avulsion can move the main channel far more abruptly than ordinary bank erosion. Using one word - flood - for all three processes hides crucial differences. The Sapt Kosi basin: one river assembled from many headwaters In Nepal the river system is commonly understood through the Sapta Kosi, the seven-river network that gathers Himalayan and trans-Himalayan waters before entering the eastern Tarai and then Bihar. The basin includes very high-relief terrain and a large sediment-producing mountain catchment before the river reaches the low-gradient Gangetic plain. This contrast between steep headwaters and a flat depositional foreland is central to Kosi behavior. Political boundaries divide the basin among China, Nepal, and India, while water and sediment do not stop at those boundaries. The most consequential flood-management relationship for the lower basin is bilateral India-Nepal cooperation because the barrage and important embankment 525 reaches lie in Nepal while much of the downstream exposure lies in Bihar. Basin geography and state jurisdiction therefore operate at different scales. From mountain gradient to the Gangetic plain A river leaving a high-energy mountain environment loses gradient and transport capacity as it enters the plains. The Kosi carries water, gravel, sand, silt, and finer material generated across a tectonically active and monsoon-affected catchment. Deposition is therefore not an accidental by-product: it is part of the normal construction of the alluvial landscape. Infrastructure changes the places in which deposition can occur. political.title: Madhesh, representation, and plural citizenship in Nepal
political.summary: plural citizenship in Nepal A modern political category, not an ancient homogeneous people Madhesh is indispensable to the modern political history of Nepal, but it must be handled as a historically changing category. The word has older geographical usages, yet the broad political macro-category 'Madheshi' acquired greatly increased institutional and electoral salience after the restoration of multiparty politics in 1990. David Gellner has accordingly emphasized that the post-1990 period produced new large-scale categories of political classification, even where the words themselves were not wholly new. This distinction prevents a contemporary political identity from being projected unchanged into medieval or ancient Mithila. The category is also internally disputed. Some plains-origin caste groups identify strongly as Madheshi; some Tharu organizations have resisted incorporation into a Madheshi umbrella; Muslim identities may be articulated as Madheshi, Muslim, regional, linguistic, or several of these at once. The chapter therefore treats Madhesh as a field of political identification rather than a single ethnos. Madhesh, Tarai, and Mithila overlap without becoming synonyms Tarai or Terai is primarily a lowland geographical and ecological term, though its administrative meanings have varied. Madhesh is at once geographical, cultural, and political. Mithila is a historical-cultural region whose literary, ritual, and linguistic networks span north Bihar and parts of Nepal. Their maps intersect, but none can simply replace the others. Modern Madhesh Province illustrates the difference. It contains the eight districts from Saptari to Parsa, while the broader Nepal Tarai continues both east and west of the 555 province. Mithila, in turn, has major historical and cultural centres inside Madhesh Province but is not exhausted by its present provincial boundary. The borderland existed before modern citizenship documents For centuries, the plains north and south of the later India- Nepal boundary were connected by pilgrimage, marriage, agrarian tenancy, markets, scholarly circulation, seasonal work, and commercial routes. The emergence of modern territorial sovereignty did not erase these connections, but it changed their legal meaning. political.title: Conclusions: connected histories without false unity
political.summary: without false unity Three names, many scales Mithila, Vajji, and Anga do not form a single continuous state, ethnicity, language zone, or administrative unit. They belong to different historical scales and to different moments of political vocabulary. Their histories intersect through the middle and lower Ganga plain, Himalayan foothills, river systems, religious routes, courts, languages, manuscript cultures, landed institutions, markets, migration, and the modern India–Nepal border. A defensible synthesis therefore begins with relation rather than with presumed identity. The names themselves have histories. Videha and Vajji belong to early textual and political worlds; Anga appears as an eastern polity in several ancient traditions; Tirabhukti and Tirhut have administrative histories; Mithila develops overlapping political, literary, ritual, and regional meanings; Madhesh and the Tarai operate at yet other geographical and political scales. Historical connection is strongest when these terms are allowed to remain specific rather than being made interchangeable. Connected history is not a claim of sameness A connected history asks how places, institutions, and communities became linked, what moved across those links, and what changed because of the movement. It does not require the connected units to have been politically united. Merchants can trade across rival jurisdictions, religious specialists can circulate across borders, literary forms can travel between courts, and river systems can bind landscapes that governments divide. Connection is therefore an empirical question about relations, not a rhetorical device for turning difference into unity. This approach is especially important for north Bihar and the Nepal plains because cultural continuities coexist with durable political distinctions. The same pilgrimage route can be sacred, 589 commercial, and international; the same language can have speakers under two constitutions; the same river can be governed by several agencies. The history becomes clearer when those layers are studied together without collapsing one into another. No single territorial line can contain the whole history The maps appropriate to one period can mislead in another. social.title: The Physical Foundations of Society
social.part: Part I — Land, Environment And The Making Of Human Landscapes
social.summary: The socio-cultural and economic history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga begins with landscape, but not with environmental determinism. Rivers, soils, forests, monsoon rhythms, wetlands, seismicity and routes created changing fields of possibility. They affected where settlement was easy or difficult, which crops could be sustained, how goods moved, where towns acquired strategic advantages, and why households repeatedly had to adapt to flood, erosion, drought, sedimentation and earthquake. None of those environmental conditions, however, produced a single inevitable political or cultural outcome. Human institutions mediated them. This chapter therefore treats physical geography as historical infrastructure: durable enough to shape recurring problems and opportunities, but dynamic enough to prevent the historian from treating any river course, floodplain edge or ecological boundary as timeless. Historical regions do not arrive with permanently surveyed natural borders. “Mithila,” “Videha,” “Vajji,” “Anga,” “Tirhut,” “Madhesh” and “Tarai” belong to different chronological and documentary contexts. Their spatial relationships changed with political authority, settlement, language, pilgrimage, transport and administration. Modern districts are useful for locating archaeological sites, soils and hydrological data, but they cannot simply be projected backward. The physical landscape is therefore used here as a frame for asking where movement, settlement, cultivation and exchange were possible, not as a device for drawing ancient borders from modern rivers. This distinction is especially important in the Gangetic plains because rivers themselves migrate. The Eastern Gangetic Plains are characterized by shallow, aggrading channels, frequent avulsion and extensive flooding, while river systems differ substantially in sediment load and hydrological regime (Sinha et al. 2005). A settlement described in relation to a channel two millennia ago cannot automatically be located by assuming that the channel occupied its present course. Floodplain history is, in part, a history of moving reference points.

social.title: Prehistoric Settlement and Subsistence
social.part: Part I — Land, Environment And The Making Of Human Landscapes
social.summary: Prehistory in the Mithila–Vajji–Anga study region cannot be written as the early chapter of a community whose later name is already known. The archaeological record precedes the historical identities, states, literary languages and social classifications that dominate later periods. Accordingly, this chapter asks a narrower but more defensible set of questions: where are prehistoric occupations actually documented; what kinds of settlement and subsistence can be reconstructed from stratified evidence; what remains uncertain because alluvial processes have buried, eroded or displaced sites; and which wider Middle Ganga or Himalayan comparisons illuminate the problem without becoming substitutes for local evidence. The principal direct anchors used here are the Patu/Rato Khola lithic complex in eastern Nepal, Chechar–Kutubpur in present Vaishali district, and Chirand in north Bihar. Wider sites such as Lahuradewa and Senuwar are used comparatively and are labelled as such. Terms such as Mithila, Videha, Vajji and Anga belong to historical geographies whose documentary visibility is much later than the Stone Age occupations considered here. A lithic scatter in the Siwalik foothills is not evidence of an early ‘Maithil’ population, and a Neolithic settlement in modern Vaishali district is not automatically a settlement of the later Vajjian republic. Modern political borders are equally anachronistic as cultural boundaries for the early Holocene. The historian may use present district and national names to locate evidence, but those labels describe where the site is now, not who prehistoric inhabitants believed themselves to be. This distinction is more than terminological caution. It changes the kinds of conclusions that can responsibly be drawn. Archaeology can reconstruct technologies, diets, settlement forms, seasonality, environmental choices and sometimes exchange or mobility. It is usually much less secure for language, ethnicity, caste, political identity or named religious affiliation in periods without writing. Those later categories will enter this volume only when the evidence capable of supporting them appears.

social.title: CHALCOLITHIC AND EARLY AGRARIAN COMMUNITIES
social.part: Part I — Land, Environment And The Making Of Human Landscapes
social.summary: “Chalcolithic” is used here in its conventional archaeological sense for assemblages in which copper appears alongside stone, bone and other technologies. It does not name an ethnicity, language, polity or biological population. In the Middle Ganga Plain, copper is often scarce, while black-and-red ware, microlithic or ground-stone tools, bone implements, wattle-and-daub architecture and farming evidence continue from earlier contexts. For that reason the term is most useful as a descriptive chronological label, not as a claim that metal transformed every aspect of life at once. The excavated sequences do not support a simple staircase in which a Neolithic village abruptly becomes Chalcolithic after the arrival of copper. At Chirand, Chechar–Kutubpur and comparative sites farther south and west, older technologies persisted. House construction remained largely organic; microliths and bone tools continued; cultivation, fishing and animal use remained central. The significant change is therefore an enlargement and recombination of technological and economic repertoires rather than the instantaneous replacement of one system by another (Singh 2004; Archaeological Survey of India 1962–63, 1968–69). There is no single Chalcolithic date range that can be imposed on the whole Middle Ganga Plain. Site sequences begin and end at different times, radiocarbon programmes are uneven, and older excavations were often dated primarily by ceramic comparison. Recent reassessments of Early Farming and Chalcolithic chronologies in the Ganga Plain emphasize precisely this diversity. Senuwar, for example, provides a well-studied comparative sequence from Early Farming into a developed agrarian/Chalcolithic phase, but its dates cannot simply be copied onto north-Bihar or Bhagalpur sites (Singh 2004; Pokharia and colleagues in Indian Archaeology 1990–91; comparative discussion in recent radiocarbon reassessments).

social.title: ARCHAEOLOGY OF FOOD AND EVERYDAY LIFE
social.part: Part I — Land, Environment And The Making Of Human Landscapes
social.summary: This chapter asks what people cultivated, collected, herded, caught, processed, cooked, stored and discarded in the early agrarian landscapes introduced in Chapters 2 and 3. The archaeological record can answer parts of those questions, but it cannot recover a menu in the modern sense. Carbonised grains identify plants that entered fires or deposits; bones and shells identify animals present in the archaeological assemblage; querns, hearths and vessels reveal processing possibilities. None of these, by itself, establishes the proportion of a food in the diet, a named recipe, a ritual rule, or the social identity of the person who prepared it. The method therefore moves from direct residue to bounded inference. This is particularly important for Mithila, Vajji and Anga, because later textual cuisines and modern regional food identities are rich enough to tempt retrospective projection. They belong to later chapters and must not be used to fill prehistoric silence. Food is among the least evenly preserved categories of material culture. Leaves, milk, oils, soft fruits, cooked gruels and many roots normally leave little macroscopic trace unless they are charred, mineralised, waterlogged or preserved as microremains. Bone survival varies with soil chemistry and burning; fish bones can be lost through coarse excavation screens; tiny seeds may remain invisible unless flotation or fine sieving is used. The result is a strong preservation bias toward durable shells, bones and accidentally charred plant parts. The absence of a species from an excavation report may therefore mean that it was not present, that it decayed, that the relevant area of the settlement was not excavated, or that recovery methods did not capture it. Archaeobotanical and zooarchaeological evidence are strongest when sampling procedures, stratigraphy and identification criteria are published. Figure 15 formalises this filtering problem and is a standing caution for every quantitative-looking food list in this chapter. Figure 12 — The preservation filter: archaeological food remains are a selective sample. Absence from the recovered assemblage is not automatically absence from diet.

social.title: ENVIRONMENT, MOBILITY AND SETTLEMENT
social.part: Part I — Land, Environment And The Making Of Human Landscapes
social.summary: A settlement map is not simply a map of where people preferred to live. In the Himalayan foreland and Middle Ganga plain, the ground itself was repeatedly remade by rivers, sediment, monsoon floods, groundwater, erosion and local tectonic movement. The same processes that threatened houses could renew fields, create fisheries, open transport corridors or bury older occupations. This chapter therefore treats settlement as a negotiation among several changing variables rather than as a one-time choice of a “good” site. The purpose is not to make environment a deterministic cause of culture. Human knowledge, labour, storage, social cooperation, route networks and technology all affected how communities used a given surface. At regional scale north Bihar and the adjoining Nepal Tarai appear extremely flat, but that appearance conceals differences that mattered greatly at household scale. Natural levees stand slightly above adjoining backswamps; abandoned channels become linear depressions; crevasse splays and bars create locally raised sandy ground; older alluvial surfaces may drain differently from younger floodplain deposits; and fan surfaces grade southward from the Himalayan front. Sinha’s work on the Gandak–Kosi interfan and later studies of the Gangetic plains emphasize this geomorphic diversity. A height difference of only a metre or two can change the duration of waterlogging, the accessibility of a well, the suitability of a crop, and the probability that a house floor remains dry during ordinary floods (Sinha 1995, 1996; Sinha et al. 2005). Sinha and Friend classified rivers of the northern Bihar plains by source area—mountain-fed, foothills-fed, plains-fed and mixed-fed—and showed that their hydrology and sediment behaviour differ (Sinha and Friend 1994). A large Himalayan river brings a different combination of discharge, sediment calibre and seasonal variability from a smaller plains-fed stream. This matters for settlement history because “living by a river” could mean living beside a braided trunk channel, an anabranching foothills-fed river, a smaller meandering stream, or an abandoned channel that retained water after the active course moved elsewhere. The economic possibilities and risks were therefore not uniform across the floodplain.
