social.title: THE SECOND URBANISATION
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: The expression “second urbanisation” is commonly used for the growth of towns, cities, states, specialised production and long-distance exchange in northern India during the early first millennium BCE, especially in the Ganga plains. It is useful only if it is not turned into a fixed date or a single-cause event. Archaeological sequences differ from site to site; some settlements grew gradually from earlier agrarian occupations, some acquired fortifications or durable architecture at different times, and some remained rural while participating in increasingly complex exchange networks. This chapter therefore uses “second urbanisation” as a regional process whose components became visible at different rates rather than as a moment when villages suddenly became cities (Allchin 1995; Sawant and Shete 2016). The term contrasts early historic urban growth with the much earlier cities of the Indus or Harappan civilisation. It does not imply direct institutional continuity between those urban traditions and the Middle Ganga cities. The long chronological and geographical gap requires independent explanation. The “second” urbanisation is thus a historiographical label for a renewed and differently organised urban process in the first millennium BCE. Its archaeological signature includes settlement concentration, fortifications, specialised crafts, exchange, coins, increasingly durable construction and the emergence of political and religious institutions, but the exact bundle varies among sites. Chapters 2–5 demonstrated long sequences of hunting, farming, animal keeping, fishing, craft production and riverine mobility before the early historic period. Chirand, Chechar, Panda, Oriup and other sites already show communities capable of managing surplus, mixed subsistence and exchange. Urban growth must therefore be understood as a reorganisation and intensification of existing social landscapes, not as civilisation arriving in an unoccupied forest. This point also corrects older models in which dense forest was imagined as the single barrier that iron axes suddenly removed.

social.title: HOUSEHOLD AND FAMILY IN EARLY HISTORIC SOCIETY
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: A history of family cannot begin by assuming that every person lived in a nuclear family, a “joint family,” or a fixed patrilineage. These are analytical labels, not archaeological finds. A household is first of all a unit of co-residence, provisioning, labour and care; family describes relationships created through birth, marriage, adoption and social recognition; lineage refers to descent remembered across generations; and political clan membership may operate at a still larger scale. Early historic sources use several terms—among them kula, gotta/gotra, ñāti and gahapati—whose meanings overlap only partly and vary by textual setting. This chapter therefore reconstructs social relations by scale rather than treating every kin term as evidence for one timeless Indian family form (Thapar 1999; Chakravarti 1987; Olivelle 2019). Domestic life leaves abundant material traces—cooking vessels, hearths, grinding stones, storage facilities, ornaments, tools and architectural spaces—but these objects rarely identify kinship directly. Texts offer names for relatives, marriage rules, household heads and dependants, yet they are selective: Buddhist texts often foreground donors, renouncers and encounters around monasteries; Brahmanical legal texts prescribe ideals for particular social groups; later narratives may preserve older motifs while reflecting later social assumptions. The correct method is therefore triangulation. Archaeology can show how people lived together; texts can illuminate categories and norms; inscriptions can sometimes identify donors and relationships; none should be forced to answer questions beyond its evidentiary scale.

social.title: SOCIAL DIFFERENTIATION BEFORE FIXED CASTE NARRATIVES
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Early historic society in the Middle Ganga valley was unequal, but inequality should not be reconstructed by placing every person into a later, fully elaborated caste order. Political rank, control of land and labour, ritual prestige, occupation, lineage, gender, wealth, freedom or dependency, and access to institutions could all shape social position. These axes overlapped, yet they did not always coincide. A wealthy merchant might possess substantial economic power without belonging to a ruling lineage; a ritual specialist could claim high prestige without controlling the largest productive resources; an artisan could be indispensable to urban life while occupying a lower social rank in some textual classifications. The task is therefore to reconstruct historically visible forms of differentiation before assuming the later fixity of endogamous jātis. This follows the broader methodological shift from treating caste as a timeless fourfold structure to examining how social formations changed with settlement, production, state formation and ideology (Thapar 1999; Chakravarti 1987; Sharma 1983). No single source provides a complete social census. Brahmanical normative texts organise society through varṇa and rules of ritual eligibility, marriage, inheritance and conduct. Early Buddhist texts frequently identify people instead through terms such as khattiya, brāhmaṇa, gahapati, seṭṭhi, vāṇijja, occupational labels, and categories of dependence such as dāsa and kammakāra. Archaeology reveals differences in house size, access to imported or prestige goods, craft production and consumption, but it rarely supplies the names by which people classified themselves. Later inscriptions make some occupational and donor categories more visible, yet they post-date much of the period considered here. These vocabularies must therefore be compared rather than collapsed. Apparent disagreement between texts may record different institutions, audiences and purposes rather than a simple choice between a “true” and a “false” social order (Fick 1920; Chakravarti 1987; Aktor 2017).

social.title: WOMEN IN EARLY MITHILA–VAJJI–ANGA
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Women in the early historic societies of Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be reconstructed as a single, uniform social category. The surviving evidence is uneven and genre-bound: archaeology reveals households, production, consumption and inequality but seldom identifies gender securely; Buddhist and Jain texts preserve named women and institutional debates but are literary and religious compositions; Brahmanical normative texts prescribe marriage, inheritance and conduct rather than recording every local practice. This chapter therefore asks a narrower historical question: what forms of work, dependence, patronage, kinship, public presence and renunciation can be supported by the evidence, and where must inference stop? Gender shaped access to property, labour, marriage, ritual and public institutions, but it did not erase differences of wealth, age, household position, occupation, dependency or lineage rank. An elite woman connected to a ruling family, a prosperous urban patron, a female household manager, a dependent servant, a gaṇikā, a lay devotee and a renunciant occupied very different social locations. The safest reconstruction therefore treats “women” as an analytical category that intersects with class, kinship, political status and work rather than as a homogeneous group. This also prevents later ideals of the respectable housewife, later caste-specific marriage rules, or later regional customs from being read backward into the first millennium BCE without evidence (Chakravarti 1987; Thapar 1999). Most early sources were produced, transmitted or institutionalised in settings dominated by men. That does not make women invisible, but it affects what is recorded. Normative texts often speak about women when regulating marriage, sexuality, inheritance or household order. Monastic texts speak about women when they become donors, disciples, nuns, relatives of monks, or subjects of disciplinary rules. Narrative texts often select exemplary or exceptional lives. Archaeology usually preserves houses, tools, food residues, ornaments and burials without giving the names or social identities of the people who used them. The result is a record rich in episodes but poor in representative statistics. A responsible social history must therefore distinguish an attested possibility from a typical pattern.

social.title: AGRICULTURE AND THE RURAL ECONOMY
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Agriculture sustained the demographic, urban and institutional transformations discussed in the preceding chapters, but the rural economy cannot be reduced to a single image of the timeless Indian village. In the Middle Ganga plains, cultivation was embedded in floodplain ecology, seasonal rainfall, livestock, household labour, storage, exchange, political extraction and religious patronage. The evidence is uneven. Archaeobotany and excavation can establish crops, food-processing tools and settlement sequences at particular sites; early Buddhist texts illuminate social categories such as gahapati, cultivator and dependent worker; later state and normative texts offer models of land, irrigation and taxation that must not be projected mechanically backward. This chapter therefore reconstructs mechanisms and limits rather than inventing a uniform agrarian system for all of Mithila, Vajji and Anga. The phrase “rural economy” covers more than farming. Fields, grazing, livestock, fishing, gathering, fuel, house-building materials, transport, household processing, local exchange and obligations to political or religious institutions all formed part of village and countryside livelihoods. Nor should the village be imagined as an isolated, self-sufficient unit. Chapter 6 showed that early towns depended upon countryside flows of food, fibres, animals and labour, while rural households obtained tools, salt, ornaments and other goods through exchange. The task is therefore to reconstruct a connected agrarian landscape rather than a sealed village economy (Allchin 1995; Sharma 1983).

social.title: CRAFTS AND TECHNOLOGY
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Craft history asks how knowledge, materials, labour and exchange were combined to make useful and valued objects. The archaeological record of Mithila, Vajji and Anga preserves pottery, metal tools, ornaments, beads, terracottas, bone and ivory objects, bricks and other durable remains, but it preserves wood, fibre, leather and many workshop installations much less reliably. The presence of a finished knife, bead or fine pot therefore cannot automatically be converted into proof of a local workshop. Conversely, the absence of textiles or carpentry debris cannot be treated as proof that spinning, weaving or woodworking were unimportant. This chapter reconstructs craft production by matching each claim to the evidence actually available at Chirand, Vaiśālī, Panda, Champa and related Middle Ganga sites, while using better-preserved comparator sites only to clarify technological possibilities rather than to fill local gaps (Sinha and Roy 1969; Verma 1971; Chakrabarti 2009). A technology is a sequence of learned actions: selecting material, preparing it, controlling heat or force, shaping the object, finishing it, maintaining tools and judging quality. These skills were transmitted through observation, apprenticeship and repeated practice. For early historic society, the most defensible questions are therefore not simply when iron, the potter’s wheel or glass appeared, but who controlled particular techniques, how raw materials reached settlements, whether production occurred in households or specialist settings, and how finished goods circulated. Archaeology can sometimes recover this operational sequence, but only when production debris and installations survive alongside finished artefacts.

social.title: Trade, Merchants and Markets
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Chapter argument. Trade in early Mithila–Vajji–Aṅga is best reconstructed as a set of overlapping local, regional and long-distance exchanges rather than as one integrated “market economy.” Archaeology establishes movement of materials and objects; early Buddhist and Jain texts reveal categories of merchants, journeys and transactions; rivers and roads supplied the spatial infrastructure; and urban centres such as Vaiśālī and Campā concentrated demand, craft production, finance and redistribution. Each source illuminates a different scale, and none by itself proves traffic volume, prices, merchant institutions or political control. Commercial history is unusually vulnerable to overstatement because portable objects travel for many reasons. A bead at Vaiśālī may have arrived through exchange, gift, pilgrimage or personal mobility; a punch-marked coin may indicate monetised transaction, savings, tax payment or later deposition. Conversely, written accounts of merchants do not automatically identify excavated marketplaces. The strongest reconstruction therefore combines artefact provenance, distribution, settlement hierarchy, transport geography and texts. This approach follows the material-context emphasis of Allchin et al. (1995), Chakrabarti (2009) and Chakravarti (2001, 2020). It also prevents literary journeys from being converted into maps of measured trade. In this chapter “trade” is used broadly for repeated exchange beyond immediate household reciprocity, while “market” is reserved for institutionalised or recurrent places and occasions of transaction. The preceding chapters showed that stone, shell, copper, beads and specialised ceramics circulated before the full early historic urban horizon. Urbanisation intensified these flows, but did not create exchange from nothing. Village households exchanged food, labour, livestock, tools and craft products; itinerant traders could link small settlements to larger centres; and urban demand drew surplus and raw materials from rural zones. This layered model is important because the archaeological visibility of a large town should not erase the less visible exchanges that sustained it. Chakravarti’s work on early Indian commerce similarly cautions against reducing trade to luxury goods or distant voyages: everyday agrarian and craft commodities mattered at local and regional scales as well (Chakravarti 2020).

social.title: Vaishali as an Economic and Social Centre
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Chapter argument. Vaiśālī should be understood neither as a literary city of splendour detached from archaeology nor as an excavated mound that can be interpreted without texts. Its historical importance lies in the convergence of a large early historic settlement, political institutions associated with the Licchavis and Vajji, a diversified material economy, regional routes, and unusually rich Buddhist and Jain memories. The evidence does not support a single census-like reconstruction of the city. Instead, it reveals an urban system in which residence, exchange, craft activity, political authority, religious institutions, agricultural provisioning and mobility were interdependent (Sinha and Roy 1969; Mishra 1962; Singh 2008). The strongest reconstruction begins by keeping source types distinct. Excavation establishes structures, fortification phases, ceramics, coins, beads, terracottas, seals and other material remains. Buddhist and Jain texts preserve named people, institutions, journeys and social ideals, but they were transmitted for religious purposes rather than compiled as municipal surveys. Landscape history explains why routes, water, floodplain resources and agricultural hinterlands mattered. Finally, modern excavation reports and historical works are themselves products of particular scholarly moments. Yogendra Mishra’s 1962 synthesis remains valuable for its collection of textual evidence on society, education and commerce, but its claims must be checked against archaeology and against the chronology of the sources it uses (Mishra 1962, 250–255; Sinha and Roy 1969).

social.title: Anga and Champa
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Chapter argument. Aṅga and its capital Campā must be reconstructed through a controlled combination of archaeology, early Buddhist and Jain textual traditions, river geography, and later historical testimony. Campā was not simply a literary “great city” or a modern place-name attached to Bhagalpur. Excavation near Nathnagar–Champanagar documents a fortified and repeatedly rebuilt settlement with Northern Black Polished Ware, ring-wells, coins, sealings, craft objects and structural remains. Texts add evidence for political incorporation, brahmanical endowment, religious debate, merchants, travellers and remembered long-distance exchange. The strongest history keeps these source types separate before asking where they converge. Early Sanskrit, Buddhist and Jain traditions use Aṅga as a regional and political name, but its boundaries shifted and cannot be mapped directly onto a modern district. The core association with the lower middle Ganga around Bhagalpur and Munger is strong, while claims about its maximum extent vary by source and period. For socio-economic history, the safer approach is to begin with securely associated places and routes rather than to draw a single timeless frontier. Campā was the principal urban focus of Aṅga in early historic literature, but the lives of cultivators, fishers, artisans and mobile traders extended beyond any capital’s walls. Modern Anga identity and Angika language history belong to later chapters and should not be projected backward as unchanged institutions. The excavated “Champa mounds” lie near Nathnagar and Champanagar, west of central Bhagalpur. Archaeological Survey reports from 1968–69 onward recorded mud fortification, early pottery and later structural phases in this zone (Indian Archaeology 1968–69: 4; 1970–71: 4–5). The resemblance between ancient and modern place-names is supportive but is not the whole case: the riverine setting, early historic occupation and literary geography strengthen the identification. At the same time, the exact limits of the ancient city remain a research question. A large archaeological landscape cannot be reduced to one mound, one modern neighbourhood, or one sacred enclosure.

social.title: Early money and monetisation
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Chapter argument. Early money in Mithilā, Vajji and Aṅga should be reconstructed as a layered history of measurement, portable value, coin manufacture, circulation, credit and institutional payment rather than as a simple transition from barter to cash. Silver punch-marked and copper coins widened the possibilities of exchange, taxation and saving, but their presence does not prove that all transactions were monetised. This chapter therefore combines numismatic evidence with archaeological context, urban systems, textual vocabulary and fiscal institutions while preserving the limits of each source. A key regional anchor is the Gorho Ghat hoard of fifty-eight silver punch-marked coins from the wider Bhagalpur–Aṅga corridor, set beside the urban monetary evidence of Vaiśālī and Campā. The history of money begins before a society becomes fully or uniformly monetised. Money can function as a unit of account, a means of payment, a medium of exchange and a store of value, and these functions need not develop together. A silver piece accepted by weight may settle a large payment even where daily food exchange remains in kind. A coin may be used for taxes or merchant settlement while wages are partly paid in grain. Chapter 12 therefore treated punch-marked coins as one component of expanding exchange; this chapter asks the narrower and more difficult question of how far monetary practices penetrated the societies of Mithilā, Vajji and Aṅga. The central methodological rule is that coin finds prove the presence of portable monetary objects, not a universal cash economy. Monetisation must be reconstructed from the density, contexts and social uses of monetary evidence rather than declared from the first occurrence of coinage.

social.title: Buddhist and Jain institutional economies
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Chapter argument. Buddhist and Jain communities in the early eastern Ganga plain should be understood as institutions that reorganised material dependence rather than escaped the economy. Renunciants limited private possession and ordinary production, yet their food, robes, lodging, medicine, travel, buildings and teaching required durable support relationships. Vaiśālī and Campā provide regional anchors through canonical gift narratives, rains residence, monastic archaeology, a relic stupa containing portable valuables, and the Campā Vinaya chapter on hospitality and valid Saṅgha procedure. Jain evidence adds the fourfold community and rigorous lay–renunciant reciprocity. Comparative inscriptions are used to illuminate institutional possibilities, not to fill regional gaps by assumption; later landed and endowed monasteries are kept chronologically separate from the earlier support economy. Buddhist and Jain renunciants defined themselves through restraint, non-possession and withdrawal from ordinary household accumulation, yet renunciation did not abolish material needs. Food, clothing, shelter, medicine, water, travel, maintenance and the care of the sick still had to be supplied. An institutional economy begins where those recurring needs are organised through durable relationships between renunciants, lay supporters, settlements and collective rules. The point is therefore not to reduce religion to commerce. It is to ask how a community that rejected ordinary accumulation could persist across seasons and generations. In the middle and eastern Ganga plain, this question is inseparable from urbanisation, merchant activity, political patronage and household surplus. The economic effect of a monastery or mendicant network could be substantial even when its normative ideal opposed private wealth. Conversely, the presence of donors or valuable gifts does not prove that an institution was profit-seeking. This chapter therefore treats economy as the organisation of resources, obligations, labour and exchange around religious communities.

social.title: Education, debate and intellectual communities
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Chapter argument. Education in early Videha, Vajji and Aṅga was not a single “school system” and should not be reconstructed by projecting later universities or medieval scholastic institutions into the first millennium BCE. Knowledge moved through households, teacher–pupil lineages, courts, ritual specialists, renunciant communities, urban audiences and mobile networks. Late Vedic and Upaniṣadic traditions place Videha prominently within a culture of learned patronage and disputation; Buddhist sources make Vaiśālī and Campā part of a wider world of travelling teachers, collective recitation, doctrinal argument and institutional discipline; Jain traditions add another durable network of teachers, mendicants and lay supporters. These sources do not give literacy rates, school enrolments or a census of occupations. Read together and with archaeological control, however, they reveal a plural social infrastructure of learning in which memory, speech, reputation, mobility and patronage were as important as buildings. For the early historic eastern Ganga plain, “education” must be defined broadly enough to include the organised transmission of texts, ritual competence, ethical discipline, argument, craft knowledge and institutional memory. The surviving evidence rarely identifies a structure whose exclusive function was schooling. A teacher’s household, a royal audience, a grove used by wanderers, a monastic residence, an assembly hall or a ritual setting could all become places of instruction. This does not mean that learning was informal in the sense of being casual. Vedic recitation required exact training; renunciant orders regulated admission, seniority and discipline; philosophical dialogues presupposed recognised standards of competence. The institutional form was often personal and networked rather than architectural.

social.title: Health, medicine and the body
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Chapter argument. Health in early Mithilā–Videha, Vajji and Aṅga must be reconstructed from bodily vulnerability, care relationships, urban infrastructure, monastic regulation, specialist healing and the environmental conditions of dense settlement. The chapter does not project classical Āyurveda backward as a fully formed regional system, diagnose ancient populations from modern disease maps, or turn wells and drains into evidence for hospitals. Instead it separates archaeological, Buddhist, Jain, Mauryan inscriptional and later medical-textual evidence, then asks where they genuinely converge. A social history of health in early Mithilā–Videha, Vajji and Aṅga must begin from ordinary bodily vulnerability: hunger, fever, digestive illness, wounds, childbirth, ageing, exhaustion, infection and the environmental burdens of dense settlement. The evidence does not permit a regional catalogue of diagnoses in modern biomedical terms, and it does not justify describing every early treatment as “Ayurveda.” What survives is a patchwork. Archaeology records water installations, drains, food remains, tools and settlement conditions; Buddhist and Jain texts preserve rules about illness, medicine and bodily discipline; narratives celebrate healers; and the Mauryan inscriptions speak of royal provision for treatment and medicinal plants. Classical medical compendia systematise knowledge more fully, but their surviving forms are later and layered. The historical task is therefore to reconstruct practices and institutions at the level the evidence can sustain: who cared for the sick, what resources were mobilised, how illness altered rules and work, how ascetic communities understood the body, and how towns attempted to manage water and waste.

social.title: From Vedic ritual landscapes to regional religious cultures
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Religious change in early Mithilā–Videha, Vajji and Aṅga was cumulative and plural. Vedic ritual traditions were extended eastward and transformed in the courts of Videha; Buddhist, Jain and other śramaṇa communities then became deeply embedded in the urban and political landscapes of Vaiśālī and Campā; and Mauryan and later monumentality made some sacred memories archaeologically durable. The chapter keeps textual, archaeological and inscriptional layers separate, treats “Greater Magadha” as a debated interpretive model rather than a fixed cultural border, and rejects both a timeless regional religion and a simple replacement sequence. The religious history of early Mithilā–Videha, Vajji and Aṅga cannot be reconstructed by projecting later, neatly bounded communities backward into the first millennium BCE. “Vedic,” “Brahmanical,” “Buddhist” and “Jain” are indispensable analytical terms, but each covers internal variation and long chronological development. Households could maintain rites of kinship, fertility, ancestors, protection and seasonal obligation that elite texts barely describe. Kings could patronise sacrificial specialists while also receiving renouncers and teachers. Merchants and urban householders could donate to more than one religious network. Ascetic communities themselves debated discipline, doctrine and acceptable relations with lay society. The chapter therefore treats religion as a changing field of institutions, practices, patronage and ideas. It asks how ritual authority moved eastward, how Videha became a celebrated courtly setting for Vedic and Upaniṣadic discourse, how Vajji and Aṅga became central to śramaṇa itineraries, and how later monuments materialised memories that were not necessarily monumental at the beginning.

19.27 Language and oral transmission allowed religious communities to cross social boundaries
19.28 Religious identities became more durable as institutions acquired places, rules and memories
19.29 Long-term continuity should not be confused with unchanging tradition
19.30 Conclusion: the region became religiously important through interaction, not isolation

social.title: Buddhism in the social history of Vajji and Videha
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Buddhism became socially durable in Vajji and Videha through overlapping networks of mobility, patronage, political encounter, gendered participation, monastic regulation and sacred memory. Vesālī provides the densest combination of discourse, Vinaya and archaeological evidence; MN 91 provides unusually direct textual evidence for the Buddha’s itinerary in Videha and an encounter at Mithilā. The chapter keeps these evidence levels separate, treats council and relic traditions as historically valuable memories rather than automatic transcripts, and avoids projecting later Buddhist monumentality backward into the Buddha’s lifetime. A social history of Buddhism in Vajji and Videha must move beyond an itinerary of famous visits. The important questions concern the people and institutions that made repeated religious interaction possible: ruling lineages, brahmins, householders, women patrons, monks, nuns, servants, cultivators and mobile specialists; the parks and halls in which teaching occurred; the food and property that sustained renouncers; and the political and legal settings in which the Saṅgha negotiated its place. Early Buddhist texts are rich in named encounters, but they are not demographic surveys. They reveal social relations selectively, through narratives shaped by doctrinal and disciplinary purposes. The chapter therefore reconstructs patterns only where several kinds of evidence converge and marks the difference between a textual social scene and an independently verified historical event.

social.title: Jainism and the Vaishali–Videha landscape
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Jainism became socially embedded in the Vaiśālī–Videha landscape through disciplined ascetic mobility, repeated rainy-season residence, lay–monastic reciprocity, women’s and men’s participation, elite interaction and later sacred memory. The evidence is strongest when Jain canonical traditions, Buddhist external references, archaeology and later pilgrimage identifications are kept distinct before synthesis. Jainism belongs centrally to the early religious history of Vaiśālī and Videha, but the evidence is uneven. Mahāvīra is linked by Jain tradition with Kuṇḍagrāma in the Vaiśālī–Videha zone, and later canonical material remembers repeated rainy-season residence in Vaiśālī, Vāṇijagrāma and Mithilā. Buddhist texts independently know Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and followers of the Nigaṇṭhas in Vesālī. These strands make the region important, yet they do not justify colouring every early historic structure or settlement as “Jain.” A landscape history therefore asks where teachers, ascetics, householders and patrons interacted, how routes and seasonal residence shaped those interactions, and which claims belong to early textual memory, later sectarian biography, archaeology or modern pilgrimage identification. The result is a layered social geography rather than a single sacred map. The first stream is Jain canonical and quasi-canonical literature: the older strata of the Ācārāṅga and Sūtrakṛtāṅga, monastic prescriptions, and the biographical and itinerary traditions preserved in the Kalpa Sūtra. The second is external evidence, especially Buddhist references to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and to Nigaṇṭha followers at Vesālī. The third is archaeology, which establishes the density, chronology and material character of the Vaiśālī urban landscape but rarely identifies a structure as Jain in the earliest period. The fourth is later Jain memory—commentaries, expanded biographies, pilgrimage identifications and sectarian traditions. Each stream answers a different question. A later sacred biography can preserve an older place association while also elaborating it; a Buddhist conversion story can attest rivalry while caricaturing its opponent; an urban mound can prove occupation without proving sectarian ownership.

social.title: Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava transformations
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Between the late ancient and early medieval centuries, Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava traditions became increasingly visible in Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga through image installation, temples, ritual specialists, patronage, sacred water and pilgrimage. The transformation was cumulative rather than a single conversion: Buddhist, Jain, Vedic, household and local practices continued within a poly-religious landscape. Regional claims are therefore tied to inscriptions, sculptures, architecture and securely controlled textual comparison rather than inferred from later sectarian prestige. Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava traditions became increasingly visible in the religious landscape of eastern India between the late ancient and early medieval centuries, but the process cannot be described as a single conversion from “Vedic religion” to “Hinduism.” Sacrifice, household ritual, local cults, Buddhist and Jain institutions, image worship, temple patronage and ascetic traditions overlapped. New forms acquired monuments, specialists, texts and donors at different speeds. The historian must therefore ask when a deity, ritual or institution becomes visible in a particular evidence stream, who supported it, and whether the surviving material represents a local community, a travelling object, an elite foundation or a later reuse. The central argument of this chapter is that regional religious change occurred through institutional thickening: images, shrines, endowments, ritual experts and sacred places accumulated around older social landscapes rather than replacing them in a single chronological break.

social.title: Sacred geography
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Sacred geography in Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga was produced cumulatively through remembered narratives, repeated movement, water and route infrastructure, monuments, patronage and later pilgrimage. The chapter separates textual, archaeological, epigraphic and later devotional evidence so that modern holy places are not projected backward as unchanged ancient sites. It then reconstructs how rivers, groves, ponds, hills, cities and monastic complexes became connected into layered and often poly-religious regional landscapes. Sacred geography is the organisation of space through remembered events, ritual acts, institutions, routes and material markers. A river may be physically ancient while its association with a particular deity, teacher or pilgrimage circuit is much later. A hill can acquire several religious meanings in different centuries, and a pond can function simultaneously as water infrastructure, a ritual bathing place and a landmark in narrative memory. The history of Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga therefore requires a layered method. It is not enough to collect modern holy places and project them backward. Nor should later pilgrimage be dismissed as mere legend. Sacred landscapes are historical achievements: communities select places, return to them, invest in them, argue over them, rebuild them and connect them to wider narratives. The central question is not simply which places were sacred, but when, to whom, through what evidence, and with what social consequences.

social.title: Festivals and calendrical culture
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Calendrical culture in Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga developed through the interaction of lunar and solar reckoning, seasonal ecology, monastic discipline, specialist astronomy, household ritual and regional festival practice. The chapter distinguishes durable calendrical structures from the much more difficult question of the antiquity of individual festivals, and treats the ritual year as a social technology that coordinates labour, gendered practice, markets, sacred places and institutional authority. A calendar coordinates people who otherwise live by different rhythms. Farmers watch rain, soil and crop cycles; ritual specialists calculate lunar days and auspicious combinations; monasteries organise communal observances; households schedule fasts, marriages and ancestor rites; rulers and scribes date grants, taxes and public acts. Festivals gather several of these clocks into a shared moment. The history of calendrical culture in Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga must therefore be written as a history of coordination. It is not enough to list holidays. The important questions are how dates were calculated, who possessed calendrical expertise, which activities were permitted or avoided, how seasonal ecology shaped observance, and how different communities could inhabit the same year differently. A ritual year is a social arrangement superimposed on astronomical and environmental cycles, and that arrangement changes over time. Calendrical history draws on evidence that differs greatly in date and purpose. Astral and ritual texts define categories such as tithi, pakṣa, month, season and nakṣatra, but they do not automatically describe village practice in Mithila. Buddhist and Jain disciplinary texts preserve lunar observances and rainy-season residence, yet their normative rules require distinction from local behaviour. Inscriptions and dated manuscripts reveal eras, regnal years and the practical use of calculated dates. Pañcāṅgas and almanacs show specialist calendrical knowledge in later periods. Finally, ethnography and oral traditions document annual rites, women’s observances, household routines and local festival sequences. Hiroshi Ishii’s comparison of Mithila and Nepal is particularly valuable for the recent ritual year, but it cannot by itself prove ancient origins. Historical synthesis begins only after each layer is dated.

social.title: Death, ancestors and life-cycle rites
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Life-cycle rites do not simply preserve an unchanged religious system from antiquity to the present. They convert biological events—conception, birth, maturation, marriage, ageing and death—into socially recognised transitions, and their forms change with household structure, inheritance, gender, ritual authority, religious affiliation and historical period. Mortuary practice is especially revealing because it brings body, kinship, property, memory and sacred geography together. The chapter therefore separates Vedic and domestic ritual texts, Buddhist and Jain traditions, archaeological evidence, and later Mithila practice before asking where continuity, transformation or retrospective invention can actually be demonstrated. Birth and death happen to bodies, but societies decide how those events become publicly intelligible. A newborn may receive a name, food, hair-cutting or initiation at prescribed stages; a marriage reorganises kinship, residence, sexuality and property; death changes a person into a corpse, a remembered ancestor, a relic-bearing saint or an absent legal subject depending on the institution involved. The concept of saṃskāra is useful for tracing Brahmanical life-cycle rites, but it should not be treated as a universal description of every community in Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga. Buddhist, Jain, non-elite and local practices followed different ritual logics, while many household actions never entered normative texts. Social history therefore begins not from a fixed list of rites but from the transitions that households and institutions had to manage.

social.title: Land Grants and Changing Agrarian Society
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: Land grants are among the most informative written records for the social and economic history of early medieval eastern India, but they are also among the easiest to overread. A copper-plate charter can describe a village, its boundaries and resources, the dues attached to it, the exemptions granted to a beneficiary, the officials and residents who were notified, and the religious or scholarly purpose of the donation. It does not, by itself, reveal the acreage actually cultivated, the proportion of households affected, the everyday bargaining power of cultivators, or the long-term success of the grant. This chapter therefore treats land grants as legal and fiscal interventions into agrarian society rather than as transparent photographs of village life. For Mithila–Tirabhukti and the Aṅga–Mudgagiri zone, the surviving charters are especially valuable because they can be located within identifiable administrative landscapes and compared across several centuries. Modern language often compresses a land grant into the statement that a king ‘gave a village’. The charters are more precise and more complicated. What could be transferred included claims to revenue, rights over specified resources, immunities from particular royal demands, authority to receive payments from residents, and in some cases judicial or policing privileges. The physical soil, the cultivators’ labour, the king’s fiscal claims and the beneficiary’s rights were not identical things. Historians therefore need to ask what exactly changed hands in each record. The wording of a grant is also formulaic. Repeated phrases are evidence for chancery practice and legal expectations, but their repetition does not prove that every listed privilege was enforced identically in every locality. The method adopted here is to read formula, geography, recipient, revenue terms and local society separately before asking how they combined.

social.title: Village, Market and Town
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: Settlement history is the study of relationships among people, production, exchange, institutions and movement. Early medieval eastern India cannot be reduced either to a landscape of self-sufficient villages or to an unbroken survival of ancient cities. The evidence instead shows differentiated settlements connected by fiscal orders, markets, rivers, roads, courts and religious institutions. For Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga, the documentary record is strongest for villages and administrative geography, while Mudgagiri/Munger and Antichak/Vikramaśīla provide important non-rural anchors. Comparative evidence from the wider Pāla–Sena world helps identify market and merchant forms without pretending that every feature is locally attested. The chapter therefore reconstructs a controlled village–market–town continuum and keeps the limits of inference visible. The words village, market and town appear deceptively simple because modern administration gives each a relatively familiar meaning. Early medieval evidence is less tidy. A grāma could be a revenue-bearing settlement, a cluster of households, a named territorial unit in a grant, or a community whose fields, groves, pasture and water extended well beyond a compact habitation. A market could be a regular haṭṭa, a point of exchange attached to a road or river crossing, or a commercial function operating within a settlement named by some other term. A town might be recognised through political headquarters, dense construction, specialised production, institutional concentration or long-distance connections, even when an inscription does not label it nagara. This chapter therefore treats settlement categories relationally. The central question is not whether a place fits a modern checklist, but how households, cultivators, traders, institutions and officials moved goods, labour, revenue and information among differently scaled nodes.

social.title: Labour, Service and Occupational Communities
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: Early medieval social history is often reconstructed from landholders, rulers and institutions because they dominate the written record. This chapter reverses the angle of vision. It asks who cultivated fields, carried messages, guarded roads, supervised ferries, made tools, carved images, copied documents, supplied monasteries and performed the countless services that turned rights on copper plates into functioning society. The evidence does not permit a complete occupational census. It does permit a controlled reconstruction of differentiated labour, service and skill—and of the gradual processes through which some livelihoods became more tightly organised as hereditary social groups. Labour is easy to see in the results of production and difficult to see in the surviving texts. Fields were cleared and cultivated, embankments maintained, cattle tended, boats moved, pottery fired, metal repaired, images carved, documents copied and institutions fed. Yet royal charters usually record rights, beneficiaries and officials rather than the names and conditions of the people who performed most of this work. A social history of labour must therefore reconstruct relationships from several kinds of evidence instead of treating a list of occupational labels as a census. For Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga in the early medieval centuries, the best regional controls are Pāla-period charters from Munger and Bhagalpur, the archaeology of Antichak/Vikramaśīla, and material evidence from Mudgagiri. Wider eastern Indian inscriptions help identify possible patterns, but they cannot be imported wholesale into north Bihar.

social.title: Social Classification and Its Historical Formation
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: Social hierarchy in early medieval Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga was real, but its categories were historical rather than timeless. Land, office, ritual authority, occupation, migration, household standing and stigma generated overlapping distinctions. This chapter reconstructs how those distinctions became socially legible and, in some settings, increasingly hereditary. It refuses two opposite shortcuts: treating normative varṇa as a complete census, and projecting later caste lists backward into centuries for which they are not documented. Contemporary charters from Munger and Bhagalpur provide the principal regional anchors; wider eastern Indian evidence supplies comparison; later Maithil genealogy is used only with explicit chronological controls. Every society classifies people, but the categories used by rulers, ritual specialists, households and later ethnographers are not identical. Early medieval Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga were marked by inequalities of landholding, service, ritual prestige, occupation, dependency and political power. Some of these differences were expressed through Sanskrit terms that later became associated with caste. Others were recorded as offices, household ranks, ethnonyms or local status labels. The task is therefore not to ask when a complete modern-style caste system suddenly appeared. It is to reconstruct how social distinctions became more explicit, more hereditary in some settings, and more closely connected with marriage, land, ritual authority and occupational reproduction. This chapter treats classification as a process. It uses contemporary charters as its strongest regional evidence, normative texts as evidence for ideals, and later genealogical or caste records only after applying a strict chronological filter.

social.title: Brahmanical Institutions without Retrospective Caste Projection
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: This chapter reconstructs Brahmanical institutions in medieval Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga through land grants, learned credentials, ritual and juristic expertise, household transmission, migration and patronage. Its governing method is chronological: early-medieval Brahman identities are described in the categories actually attested in their sources, while the later corporate organisation of Maithil Brahmans is reserved for the evidence that documents it. In particular, the Sanskrit qualification śrotriya is not treated as proof of the later Mithila Śrotriya sub-caste. Brahmanical power in medieval Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga cannot be reconstructed by taking a later caste list and moving it backward in time. The early and early-medieval evidence shows institutions: learned households, ritual specialists, teachers, juristic authorities, land grantees, advisers and networks of patronage. These institutions could generate durable status and reproduce privilege across generations, but their documentary form is not identical to the later corporate organisation of Maithil Brahmans. The first task is therefore to identify what an inscription or text actually makes visible. A grant may identify a beneficiary by gotra, pravara, Vedic affiliation and learning; a legal text may define an ideal qualification; a later genealogy may regulate marriage. Each belongs to a different institutional layer. This chapter reconstructs those layers without assuming that they had already fused into the later caste structure.

social.title: The Panji Tradition
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: The Panji tradition transformed genealogy into an institution of social memory, territorial identity and marriage regulation in Mithila. This chapter treats the Panji neither as an timeless survival nor as a single document created once and thereafter unchanged. It reconstructs a layered archive: a fourteenth-century process of formalisation associated with the Tirhut court; genealogical and territorial categories elaborated through repeated copying; professional interpretation by Panjikars; later rank vocabularies and marriage procedures; and modern preservation, digitisation and search. The method is chronological and source-critical. Surviving manuscripts, later copies, ethnographic descriptions and modern digital collections are used together but never collapsed into one evidentiary moment. Genealogy exists in many societies as remembered descent, but the Panji tradition is historically distinctive because descent became a maintained documentary system tied to social decisions. A lineage statement could identify ancestors; a Panji institution could preserve, compare and adjudicate relationships across households. That difference matters. The emergence of a corporate genealogical archive created new forms of expertise, because only persons who knew how to read the record, reconcile variant pedigrees and connect family histories could make the archive socially effective. It also created new forms of dependence on writing. Memory did not disappear, but written pedigrees increasingly structured how memory was verified. The Panji therefore belongs simultaneously to the history of manuscripts, marriage, professional knowledge, territorial identity and social classification.

social.title: Women, Marriage and Property in Medieval Mithila
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: Women’s social and economic history in medieval Mithila cannot be reconstructed by taking a single legal rule and treating it as a transparent description of life. The most articulate surviving materials are juristic: Sanskrit digests that classify marriage, gifts, inheritance, maintenance and household obligations. Those texts are indispensable because they preserve categories and arguments used by learned specialists, yet they are normative and selective. Genealogical records illuminate marriage relationships in the communities they document but usually privilege patrilineal continuity. Agrarian records and material history reveal the economy in which households functioned while often leaving women unnamed. Later colonial courts preserve a history of how “Mithila law” was read, but they belong to a much later evidentiary moment. This chapter therefore reconstructs women, marriage and property through a chronology firewall: every claim is tied to the kind and date of its source. The first difficulty is visibility. Medieval archives were not designed to answer modern questions about women’s work, autonomy or ownership. A jurist asked which rule applied to a dispute; a genealogist recorded descent and marriage eligibility; a grant recorded title, privilege or revenue; a literary text pursued aesthetic, devotional or political purposes. Women appear differently in each genre, and silence has different meanings. An unnamed cultivator’s wife in an agrarian record is not evidence that women did no agricultural work. A detailed rule on a widow’s succession is not evidence that every widow successfully exercised the right contemplated by the jurist. Historical reconstruction must therefore distinguish presence in the archive from presence in society. The chapter uses explicit statements where available and cautious structural inference where direct testimony is absent.

social.title: Karnata and Oiniwar-Period Social Economy
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: The Karnata and Oiniwar centuries are often narrated through rulers, invasions and genealogies, yet their historical significance also lies in the institutions that converted land, labour, knowledge and movement into durable social power. The Karnata kingdom, conventionally dated from Nanyadeva’s establishment of power in 1097 to the Tughluq conquest of 1324, was centred on Simraungadh and linked the middle Gangetic plain to the Himalayan foothills. The Oiniwar order that followed operated through smaller, shifting centres and changing relations with stronger neighbouring powers. A socio-economic history must therefore distinguish political command from the underlying systems that sustained it. Agrarian production remained fundamental; villages, market places, artisans, scribes, religious establishments and learned households connected local resources to courts and regional routes. This chapter reads inscriptions, juristic and literary texts, genealogical materials, archaeology and later historiography together, while refusing to turn prescriptive texts into demographic statistics or later caste labels into medieval facts. Karnata and Oiniwar rule should not be imagined as two self-contained economic systems. A dynasty could change rapidly while fields, irrigation habits, village boundaries, kinship obligations, market routines and craft knowledge continued. Conversely, continuity at village level did not mean political stasis: the destination of revenue, the composition of courts, the scale of fortification and the geography of patronage could alter significantly. The most useful comparison therefore separates layers. At the top were rulers, military retainers, ministers and fiscal claims. Beneath them were landed rights, cultivating households and service relationships. Alongside these stood market exchange, routes toward Nepal and Bengal, religious establishments and scholarly networks. The 1324 conquest is consequently treated below as a major political rupture whose economic effects must be demonstrated sector by sector rather than assumed. This layered method also prevents later Oiniwar institutions from being projected backward into the full Karnata period.

social.title: Islam, Migration and New Social Worlds
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: Islam entered the social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga through more than conquest. From the thirteenth century onward, the region stood inside a widening field of movement linking Delhi and the middle Ganga plain, Lakhnauti and Bengal, Jaunpur, Bihar, Anga and the routes toward Nepal. Armies and governors mattered, but so did merchants, transporters, scribes, scholars, Sufis, artisans, soldiers seeking employment, refugees and households that moved with patrons or opportunity. Their presence created new institutions and new forms of language, consumption and association without making every locality identical. The history of these encounters therefore has to be reconstructed as a history of mobility and settlement rather than as a simple sequence of invasions. The chapter also keeps four processes analytically distinct: conquest, migration, durable settlement and religious change. A victorious army does not by itself prove large-scale migration; a migrant population does not by itself prove conversion among older inhabitants; and later demographic patterns cannot be projected backward without evidence. Persian chronicles, Arabic and Persian inscriptions, Sufi letters and discourses, Sanskrit and Avahaṭṭa literature, archaeology, genealogy and later regional histories each preserve different slices of this past. Read together and critically, they reveal a medieval society in which religious difference existed alongside political bargaining, service, exchange, shared routes and multilingual communication.

social.title: Persianate Culture and Mithila–Anga
social.part: Part Iv — Early Medieval And Medieval Social Transformation
social.summary: Persianate culture reached Mithila and Anga through administration, courts, Sufi networks, inscriptions, books, routes and material practices rather than through one uniform process. This chapter reconstructs that field without treating “Persianate” as an ethnic identity, without equating it with Islam as a whole, and without assuming that elite documentary change automatically transformed village speech or social life. “Persianate” is most useful here as a historical category for a transregional field of language, literary canons, bureaucratic technique, courtly ethics, political imagery, Sufi writing, architecture and social distinction that circulated far beyond Iran. It does not mean that the people participating in that field were ethnically Persian, nor that Persianate culture was identical with Islam. Turkic, Afghan, Indian, Iranian and other elites could share Persian political and literary forms; non-Muslim scribes and scholars could also learn them; and communities using Persianate administrative forms could continue to speak Maithili, eastern Indo-Aryan vernaculars, Sanskrit, Arabic or other languages in different settings. The category therefore describes circulation and prestige rather than biological descent or a single religious community. The evidence is strongest where institutions left durable traces: inscriptions, coins, dated buildings, Persian chronicles, Sufi letters, Sanskrit and Avahaṭṭa works, manuals of writing, and later manuscript traditions. Each source illuminates a different social scale. A Persian inscription on a mosque securely dates a patron and a building, but it does not measure the language of surrounding villages. A court text may reveal etiquette and political ideals without representing household practice. A Sufi letter can show an intellectual network but not the demographic size of its audience. This chapter therefore distinguishes documented participation in Persianate forms from claims of wholesale cultural replacement.

social.title: Languages Before Modern Standardisation
social.part: Part V — Language, Literature And Knowledge As Social History
social.summary: Before grammars, censuses, school systems, print institutions and modern language movements imposed sharper names and norms, the Mithila–Vajji–Anga region was multilingual in a more fluid sense. People spoke local vernaculars, learned Sanskrit for specific intellectual and ritual purposes, encountered Prakrit, Apabhraṃśa and Avahaṭṭa as literary categories and inherited registers, and later moved through political worlds in which Persian and Arabic also mattered. The task is therefore not to search for a single moment when one modern language suddenly “began,” but to reconstruct how speech, writing, genre, script, mobility and institutional prestige interacted across centuries. Modern maps encourage the eye to imagine languages as territories separated by lines. That model is useful for administration and contemporary language policy, but it is hazardous when projected into the medieval past. Speech normally changed by degree across neighbouring villages and market zones. A traveller moving from western Vajji country through central Mithila toward Anga could encounter shifts in pronunciation, vocabulary and morphology without crossing a point where one complete linguistic system ended and another began. Written culture added a second layer: the language of a manuscript could differ sharply from the speech of its patron, scribe or audience. A source-critical history therefore treats “Maithili,” “Bajjika,” “Angika,” “Sanskrit,” “Avahaṭṭa” and “Persian” as historically situated labels and registers rather than timeless boxes. The question is not which modern community possessed a medieval district, but which linguistic resources were available to particular speakers, writers and institutions at particular times.

social.title: Formation of Literary Maithili
social.part: Part V — Language, Literature And Knowledge As Social History
social.summary: Literary Maithili did not emerge at one instant when an anonymous spoken dialect suddenly became a written language. It formed through a long interaction among regional speech, oral performance, Sanskrit learning, Prakrit–Apabhraṃśa–Avahaṭṭa inheritances, courts, scribal households, manuscript technologies and cross-border circulation. The surviving archive is uneven: some genres are visible because manuscripts survived, others because later editors collected them, and still others lived primarily in performance. This chapter therefore reconstructs a process of vernacularisation rather than a mythical birth date. It also follows the volume’s adopted two-Vidyāpati framework: the pre-Jyotiriśvara Mahākavi Vidyāpati of the Maithili padāvalī tradition is kept distinct from the later fifteenth-century Vidyāpati Ṭhakkura associated with the Oiniwar court and Sanskrit/Avahaṭṭa works. A spoken language can exist for centuries without leaving an archive that modern literary historians can readily see. “Formation of literary Maithili” therefore means the growth of repeatable conventions for composition, performance, copying, attribution and reception in a regional vernacular. It requires more than isolated vernacular words in Sanskrit documents. A literary language becomes historically visible when extended texts use it deliberately, audiences recognise recurring genres, scribes can reproduce it, and later writers treat earlier compositions as models. None of these developments needs to happen simultaneously. Prose may become writable before a stable dramatic convention; song may circulate orally before manuscripts record it; courtly prestige may rise after popular performance has already flourished. The historical problem is thus to identify converging evidence. Literary Maithili emerged through accumulation: vernacular grammar supplied the medium, oral culture supplied memorable forms, learned traditions supplied techniques of classification and poetics, and social institutions supplied occasions for preservation.

social.title: The Two Vidyāpatis and Two Historical Contexts
social.part: Part V — Language, Literature And Knowledge As Social History
social.summary: The name Vidyāpati stands at the centre of Maithili literary memory, but a name is not a chronology. This chapter follows the governing position adopted for this volume: it distinguishes an earlier Mahākavi Vidyāpati, treated as the pre-Jyotiriśvara poet of the Maithili Padāvalī tradition, from the later Vidyāpati Ṭhakkura associated with the Oiniwar-period courtly and learned world and with Sanskrit and Avahaṭṭa works such as Kīrtilatā, Kīrtipatākā, Puruṣaparīkṣā, Gorakṣavijaya and Likhanāvalī. Because most modern scholarship combines these corpora within a single fifteenth-century biography, the distinction used here must be argued methodologically rather than asserted as consensus. The task is therefore to keep composition, manuscript transmission, patronage, language, genre and later reception separate, and to ask where the evidence genuinely converges. Literary history often begins with the author-name printed on a modern title page and works backward. That method is hazardous for premodern South Asia, where texts circulated in manuscripts, anthologies, performance lineages and scribal copies long before modern critical editions. “Vidyāpati” can therefore function simultaneously as a historical personal name, an authorial signature, a prestige attribution, a lineage of reception and a later canonical umbrella. The central problem is not whether tradition is valuable; it is how to disaggregate the kinds of evidence that tradition carries. A lyric transmitted in a Nepalese anthology, a Sanskrit legal treatise with a courtly frame, and an Avahaṭṭa political narrative do not become coeval merely because later scholarship places them under one name.

social.title: Tirhuta/Mithilakshar and Scribal Culture
social.part: Part V — Language, Literature And Knowledge As Social History
social.summary: Tirhuta, also called Mithilakshar and historically “Maithili” script in some descriptions, belongs to the eastern Brahmi-derived family of writing systems. Yet the social history of the script cannot be reduced to an alphabet chart. Its significance lies in the manuscript worlds that connected Sanskrit and Maithili learning, household archives, teachers and pupils, legal and ritual texts, lyric anthologies, Nepalese repositories, correspondence and later movements of print and digital revival. This chapter therefore separates palaeographic ancestry from a fixed script identity, script from language, composition from surviving copy, and manuscript culture from modern claims about a single community. The aim is to reconstruct Tirhuta as a changing technology of knowledge and social memory. Writing systems change gradually. Later observers often attach a familiar name to every earlier regional hand that resembles it, but palaeography works more cautiously. Tirhuta belongs to an eastern line of Brahmi-derived scripts associated with Kuṭila and Gauḍī developments, and it is closely related to Bengali-Assamese, Newar and Odia traditions. The Unicode Standard describes these related scripts as differentiated branches rather than identical forms extending unchanged into antiquity. For social history this distinction matters: an early eastern inscription can illuminate ancestry without proving that contemporaries understood its hand as the same scribal system later called Tirhuta or Mithilakshar. The historical question is therefore when a recognisable regional convention became stable enough to support recurring scribal practices, not how far backward a modern name can be projected.

social.title: Oral Culture
social.part: Part V — Language, Literature And Knowledge As Social History
social.summary: Oral culture is not the unwritten residue left after “literature” has been removed. It is a social system of memory, performance, argument, pleasure and transmission in which words are inseparable from voice, occasion, audience, gesture and place. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, songs, tales, proverbs, ritual speech, narrative chants, joking, lament, praise and epic performance have carried historical experience across households and communities that were only unevenly represented in manuscripts and formal chronicles. Yet oral evidence requires chronological discipline. A song recorded in the nineteenth or twentieth century may contain older language or motifs, but its present form cannot simply be projected into the medieval period. This chapter therefore reconstructs oral culture through a hierarchy of dated witnesses, ethnography and performance analysis, while treating continuity as a question to be demonstrated rather than assumed. Oral culture preserves information differently from a charter, inscription or manuscript. Its archive exists in people, repertoires and repeated social occasions. A tale survives because someone knows when to tell it; a marriage song survives because a sequence of ritual acts calls it forth; a ballad survives because performers and audiences continue to value the hero, melody or social claim embodied in it. The result is both durable and flexible. Themes may remain stable while wording changes; episodes may migrate between genres; a performance may answer a new political situation with old narrative material. For social history this mobility is an advantage, because it gives access to values and conflicts often absent from official records. It is also a warning: oral memory is not a sound recording of the past. The historian must ask which layer of a performance is actually dated and which is an inference.

social.title: Angika and the Eastern Linguistic-Cultural Zone
social.part: Part V — Language, Literature And Knowledge As Social History
social.summary: Angika belongs to the eastern edge of the historical field studied in this volume, but the word itself cannot be allowed to do the work of history. Ancient Anga, medieval eastern vernaculars, colonial descriptions of Chhika-Chhiki, and the modern literary-linguistic identity called Angika are related objects of inquiry, not automatically identical ones. This chapter therefore studies an eastern linguistic-cultural zone centred on the Bhagalpur–Champa and Munger corridors and extending through graded contact toward Purnia, the Santal Parganas, Bengal and the wider Ganga valley. Its method is deliberately double: it takes present Angika identity seriously while refusing to project present labels unchanged into periods for which the evidence uses other names. Language maps are useful summaries, but they easily turn gradual transitions into hard borders. The eastern part of the Mithila–Anga field has never been organised by speech alone. Rivers, ferries, market towns, pilgrimage routes, marriage networks, military corridors, seasonal labour and administrative centres connected communities whose repertoires overlapped without being identical. The term “zone” therefore does not deny linguistic difference; it asks how difference was produced and maintained inside a field of repeated contact. Bhagalpur, Munger, the Kosi–Purnia corridor and the Santal Parganas occupy different positions in that field. A history of Angika must explain both internal coherence and permeability. It should be able to describe why speakers recognise a distinctive regional speech while also showing why its features intersect with Maithili, Magahi, Bengali, Santali and other neighbouring languages. This approach also prevents the modern political boundary of a district or state from becoming an imaginary medieval linguistic frontier.

social.title: Bajjika and Western Mithila
social.part: Part V — Language, Literature And Knowledge As Social History
social.summary: Bajjika occupies the western side of the linguistic-cultural field examined in this volume, especially the Muzaffarpur–Vaishali–Sitamarhi–Sheohar belt and its continuation into Nepal’s Madhesh. Yet its history cannot be written by beginning with a modern label and simply pushing that label backward. Ancient Vajji/Vṛji, medieval western Mithila, Grierson’s Western Maithili, twentieth-century Bajjika literary self-identification, and Nepal’s present census category are connected but not identical objects. This chapter therefore combines historical linguistics, sociolinguistics, census evidence, regional literary history and the social history of mobility. It takes Bajjika identity seriously while distinguishing between the date of a name, the age of a speech feature, the geography of a repertoire and the institutional moment at which a language becomes visible in print, education, statistics or digital media. The western Mithila plain is not a linguistic island. Muzaffarpur and Vaishali face Bhojpuri-speaking districts to the west, Magahi and Hindi-dominant administrative spaces to the south, central Maithili varieties to the east and north-east, and Nepal’s Madhesh across an international border that is recent compared with the older circulation of people. Speech features therefore travel through marriage, weekly markets, pilgrimage, labour migration, schooling and media. A contact-zone model makes it possible to describe a recognizable Bajjika core without turning every isogloss into a political boundary. It also explains why researchers report internal varieties influenced by Maithili, Bhojpuri or Magahi. The important historical question is not whether contact exists—it plainly does—but which features appear old, which diffuse more recently, and which become socially emblematic only after writers and language activists begin to name them as Bajjika.

social.title: Sanskrit Learning and Scholastic Institutions
social.part: Part V — Language, Literature And Knowledge As Social History
social.summary: Sanskrit learning is one of the strongest documented strands in the intellectual history of medieval Mithila, but its institutions have often been described with anachronistic vocabulary. This chapter reconstructs the learned world through teachers, pupils, manuscripts, commentaries, courts, debates and mobility. It gives special attention to Gaṅgeśa and Navya-Nyāya while keeping jurisprudence, Mīmāṃsā, grammar and other disciplines in view. It also separates dated evidence from later heritage memory, so that the historical importance of Mithila’s scholastic culture does not depend on calling it a modern-style university. The phrase “scholastic institution” can mislead if it evokes a modern university with a charter, permanent campus, salaried departments and centralized admissions. Sanskrit learning in medieval Mithila was institutionally real, but its durable units were usually different: teacher-households, circles of pupils, manuscript collections, lineages of commentary, courts that rewarded learning, assemblies of experts and reputations that drew students across regions. The historical task is therefore to identify recurring practices and relationships rather than to search for a single building called a university. A text that names a teacher, patron or place; a manuscript copied for study; a sequence of commentaries; and evidence of pupils travelling to a renowned master can together reveal an institution even when no campus archive survives. Conversely, later claims about a continuous “Mithila University” must be tested rather than repeated. This chapter uses “institution” in this distributed sense.

social.title: Architecture and Settlement
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: Architecture in Mithila, Vajji and Anga survives unevenly. Massive brick ramparts, stupas, monasteries, rock-cut shrines and temple fragments are visible; timber houses, thatch, fences, workshops and periodic markets are far less so. This chapter therefore joins architecture to settlement archaeology. It asks how water, rivers, routes, fortification, religious institutions, craft production and political authority organized built space, and it keeps excavated sequence separate from legendary or retrospective identification. The result is a social history of built landscapes rather than a catalogue of monuments. Architecture records labour, resources, political authority, religious practice and everyday habits in material form. Yet the surviving record of Mithila, Vajji and Anga is uneven. Monumental brickwork, fortifications and religious structures are more likely to survive than timber houses, thatched roofs, fences or temporary market sheds. A history based only on standing monuments would therefore exaggerate the architectural weight of elites and institutions. This chapter treats architecture together with settlement: where people lived, how water and routes shaped habitation, how defensive works reorganized space, how monasteries and temples concentrated resources, and how ordinary building materials disappeared through rebuilding and floodplain erosion. The central method is archaeological rather than typological. A plan, wall, mound, tank or sculptural fragment is interpreted first in its excavated or documented context. Later tradition may preserve valuable memory, but a legendary name does not automatically establish the original function or date of a structure.

social.title: Dress, Textiles and Ornament
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: Dress history in Mithila, Vajji and Anga survives through an unequal archive. Cloth normally decays, while stone beads, shell bangles, terracotta ornaments, production tools, sculpture and words endure. This chapter therefore reconstructs clothing and adornment by triangulating archaeology, art and text, with a chronology firewall against projecting later fashions or the modern reputation of Bhagalpur silk backward into periods for which continuity has not been demonstrated. Dress is not a decorative appendix to social history. Cloth, jewellery, hairstyles and bodily adornment connect production, gender, labour, status, ritual, climate and exchange. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, however, the archive is radically uneven: textiles themselves rarely survive in the humid alluvial environment, while beads, bangles, shell, terracotta and stone images survive far more readily. A historically responsible chapter must therefore resist reconstructing a complete costume from a single sculpture or a later ethnographic custom. The task is to combine archaeological small finds, images, texts and evidence for production while keeping the date and social setting of each source visible. Most garments were made from organic fibres that decay quickly unless preserved in exceptional conditions. Their absence from excavated deposits does not mean that textile production was unimportant; it means that the evidentiary burden shifts to tools, impressions, textual vocabulary and visual representation. Jewellery has the opposite bias. Stone beads, shell bangles, terracotta pendants and metal objects can survive for centuries, making adornment appear more archaeologically prominent than cloth. The resulting archive must be read as a preservation filter, not a direct inventory of what people valued or wore in proportion to surviving objects.
