social.title: Food History of Mithila, Vajji and Anga
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: A history of food in Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot begin by copying a modern recipe list backward into antiquity. Food is unusually vulnerable to historical distortion because cooked dishes disappear almost completely, while modern regional cuisines are vivid and familiar. The reliable sequence is the reverse: begin with charred plant remains, animal bones, fish and shell, grinding stones, hearths, ovens and vessels; then add dated texts, inscriptions and institutional records; only after that use later ethnography to test possible continuities. This chapter therefore distinguishes ingredients from dishes, production from consumption, and memory from dated evidence. A grain recovered from an archaeological layer proves cultivation or use more securely than it proves a named recipe; a medieval food-name proves vocabulary and social practice more securely than it proves an unchanged dish across centuries. The food history of the region was shaped by an alluvial landscape of monsoon rainfall, rivers, flood basins, ponds, wetlands and fertile but mobile soils. Such an environment favoured rice but never supported rice alone. Winter cultivation, pulses, oilseeds, livestock, fish, molluscs, fruits and collected plants broadened the subsistence base and reduced dependence on a single harvest. Floods could replenish soils and aquatic resources, yet they could also destroy standing crops, grain stores and transport routes. Food security therefore depended on seasonal diversity, storage, social exchange and access to different ecological niches. The contrast between north Bihar's flood-prone plains, the Ganga corridor and the eastern Anga zone helps explain why household diets combined field agriculture with riverine and wetland resources rather than forming a narrowly cereal economy.

social.title: Mithila Painting Before and Beyond the Modern Art Market
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: Mithila painting presents a paradox for the social historian. The practice is repeatedly described as old, yet its most durable and datable corpus is overwhelmingly modern because the older media were intentionally temporary. Floor diagrams were renewed, mud-plastered walls were resurfaced, pigments faded, houses were rebuilt, and floods, earthquakes and poverty repeatedly altered domestic architecture. The result is a severe survival bias. A responsible history therefore cannot begin with the modern paper painting and simply project its forms backward. It must distinguish surviving objects, dated photographs, textual or ritual evidence, later recollection and present practice, and then ask where those independent lines of evidence genuinely converge. Before the paper market, much of the documented painting tradition belonged to the house rather than to an autonomous object called a work of art. Images were made on earthen floors, plastered walls, thresholds, domestic shrines and the nuptial chamber. Their location mattered because the painted surface helped constitute a ritual setting. The same image moved to paper could preserve motifs and line habits while changing its social function: a wall participated in a wedding; a sheet could be stored, signed, priced, transported and exhibited. The historian must therefore treat surface, location and occasion as part of the work, not as detachable background. Aripan designs are among the clearest examples of why material survival cannot be equated with historical importance. Made on floors with rice paste and, in some practices, additional colour, they marked auspicious and ritually activated spaces for vows, festivals, household worship and life-cycle ceremonies. Their very purpose often required renewal rather than permanent conservation. Consequently, the absence of an old aripan object in a museum does not prove the absence of the practice, while a modern drawing of an aripan does not by itself establish the age of every motif. The strongest method combines dated documentation of practice with careful comparison of recurring design grammars.

social.title: Mithila Painting and the Twentieth-Century Cultural Economy
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: Mithila painting entered a new historical regime in the twentieth century. The domestic ritual practice discussed in Chapter 47 did not suddenly begin when administrators, craft officials, collectors or museums noticed it. What changed was the social life of the image. A painted wall or floor was tied to a house, ceremony and cycle of renewal; a sheet of paper could be counted, priced, signed, packed, retailed, exhibited, collected and archived. This chapter therefore studies cultural economy rather than origins. It asks how institutions, markets, biographies and new media changed who could paint, who could earn, what counted as a work, how artistic reputation was produced and how a regional women’s practice came to circulate in national and international art worlds. The Bihar–Nepal earthquake of 1934 is a crucial event in the modern archive because damaged houses exposed painted interior walls that were normally difficult for an outsider to see. W. G. Archer, then serving in the region, encountered the paintings during inspections connected with the disaster. The earthquake should not be narrated as the birth of Mithila painting. Its historical importance lies elsewhere: it disrupted domestic architecture and created an accidental window through which a colonial official could see and later document an art practice embedded in women’s interior spaces. A cultural economy begins partly with such acts of visibility, because documentation can detach a practice from its local context and present it to new audiences who possess different categories of value.

social.title: Music, Song and Performance
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: Music becomes historical evidence only when it is attached to a dateable setting: who performed, for whom, on what occasion, in what language, and through what medium. A song-text without a performance context is not the same thing as a sounded event; a living performance is not by itself proof that the same melody, instrumentation or social meaning existed centuries earlier. This chapter therefore treats music, song and performance as connected but separately testable histories across Mithila, Vajji and Anga. Buildings, manuscripts and metal objects may survive for centuries; sound disappears as it is made. Before recording technologies, historians must work through notation, literary description, iconography, surviving instruments, ritual prescriptions, named repertoires and later oral transmission. Each medium preserves something different. A manuscript can preserve words or musical signs but not a singer’s timbre; a sculpture can show an instrument but not the tune; an oral rendition can preserve a practice while also accumulating later changes. The Natya-sastra, Dattilam and later Sanskrit musicological traditions provide indispensable concepts for rhythm, melody, performance and aesthetic response, but they cannot be treated as direct descriptions of village practice in Mithila or Anga. Their value is comparative and conceptual. Regional history begins where a text, manuscript, inscription, named patron, repertoire or securely located performance connects those wider traditions to the eastern Gangetic world. A particularly important bridge appears around the early twelfth century in the work associated with King Nanyadeva. The Sarasvati-hrdayalankara or Bharata-bhasya tradition attributed to him preserves substantial musicological discussion, and D. R. Widdess has shown that the Panika song examples transmit melody and tala information of exceptional value for the history of early Indian music. This evidence demonstrates learned musical activity connected with the Karnata courtly sphere; it does not prove that all inhabitants of Mithila followed the same repertory or theory.

social.title: Theatre and Dramatic Cultures
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: The history of theatre cannot be written from playbooks alone. A dramatic text preserves possible speech, songs, roles and sequences, but performance also requires bodies, voice, movement, music, costume, a place, an audience and a social occasion. For Mithila, Vajji and Anga the archive is therefore uneven: some periods preserve manuscripts but no witnessed staging; others preserve living performance with uncertain antiquity; still others leave only literary references to actors or entertainment. This chapter uses a layered method. A play may establish a dramatic repertoire without proving exactly how it was staged. A modern performance may preserve an older narrative without being an unchanged medieval survival. The object of study is the changing institution of performance itself. Archaeology rarely preserves a temporary stage, painted backdrop or performer’s garment. Manuscripts may survive because they entered libraries, while popular scripts, memorized parts and inexpensive booklets disappear. Court records privilege patrons; literary histories privilege authors; ethnography may record only the late life of a tradition. The archive therefore systematically overrepresents durable and elite materials. A responsible history combines play texts, manuscript colophons, stage directions, courtly and religious contexts, references to performers, printed ephemera, and where available recorded performances. Absence of a surviving script is not proof that theatre did not occur, and possession of a script is not proof of a continuous troupe. The evidentiary asymmetry is itself part of the social history.

social.title: Fairs, Markets and Public Culture
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: A weekly haat, an annual mela and an everyday bazaar were not interchangeable institutions. Their calendars, catchment areas and social expectations differed. A haat concentrated ordinary exchange on one or two days and linked surrounding villages to itinerant traders, cultivators and petty retailers. A mela usually gathered a much larger and more heterogeneous public around a ritual date, shrine, river crossing, seasonal need or established custom. Permanent bazaars provided continuity between these periodic concentrations. The social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga therefore requires attention to time as well as place: the same field, ghat or roadside could be ordinary space for most of the year and become a dense temporary town when a fair opened. Exchange moved more than grain, cloth, cattle or utensils. Market days brought together people who lived in different villages, worked in different occupations and possessed different news. Prices, crop conditions, marriage prospects, legal disputes, employment, political rumours, pilgrimage routes and performances could circulate through the same gathering. Anand A. Yang’s study of Gangetic Bihar is especially valuable because it treats the bazaar as a social and political institution rather than as a neutral container for buying and selling. This chapter follows that insight while keeping the regional histories of Mithila, Vajji and Anga distinct. A market was simultaneously an economic node, a communication node and a public stage. Large fairs generated administrative reports, travel accounts, police arrangements, sanitary records, photographs and later tourism publicity. Small village gatherings often left only a name in a settlement report or census schedule. This imbalance can distort historical reconstruction. Yang’s reading of twentieth-century Bihar census material shows that the overwhelming majority of melas were small “fairlets” drawing mainly from nearby villages even though famous events such as Sonepur dominated public memory. The ordinary history of public culture therefore lies as much in modest periodic gatherings as in celebrated mega-events. Scale must be established from evidence rather than inferred from fame.

social.title: Mughal-Period Land, Revenue and Agrarian Society
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Mughal rule did not replace the agrarian society of Mithila, Vajji and Anga with a single uniform land system. It superimposed imperial fiscal claims, assignments and administrative categories upon village production, regional chieftaincies, hereditary local offices and ecologies shaped by the Ganga, Gandak, Kosi and their tributaries. The most useful contemporary source, Abu’l-Fazl’s A’in-i Akbari, gives unusually detailed fiscal statistics for the Bihar subah, including the sarkars of Tirhut, Hajipur and Munger. Yet those figures record assessed revenue and administrative knowledge; they do not by themselves tell us what every cultivator paid, what every zamindar retained, or how much was actually collected in a flood-prone year. This chapter therefore reconstructs Mughal agrarian society through a layered method: official statistics, regional revenue documents, the history of Bihar’s zamindars and chieftains, agrarian ecology, and later gazetteer summaries are used together but never treated as interchangeable archives. The Mughal state’s agrarian income depended on the crop produced by cultivators, but the path from field to treasury passed through multiple claims. Irfan Habib’s central warning remains essential: the Mughal land revenue was neither a modern property tax nor simply a landlord’s rent. It was a state claim upon agricultural produce, expressed through assessment, rates, measurement, crop estimates and cash equivalents. In regional society this claim interacted with the rights of zamindars, village headmen, hereditary record-keepers and cultivators. To study revenue is therefore to study power, labour and negotiation: who could demand, who could record, who could resist, who advanced cash, and who bore the risk when crops failed.

social.title: Trade between Bengal, Bihar, Nepal and the Gangetic World
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Trade connected the socio-economic worlds of Mithila, Vajji and Anga to regions far beyond their political boundaries. The Ganga formed the principal east–west trunk between the upper Gangetic plain and Bengal; Patna developed as a major inland entrepôt; Munger and Bhagalpur lay on the eastern river corridor; Hajipur and Tirhut fed northward routes toward Nepal; and Kathmandu connected plains commerce with Himalayan and Tibetan exchange. These links were already visible before European companies became major actors, then intensified and changed as English and Dutch merchants entered Bihar’s commodity markets. The evidence, however, is uneven. A late-sixteenth-century traveller, a seventeenth-century factory letter, a 1790s diplomatic mission and Buchanan-Hamilton’s early-nineteenth-century trade account cannot be collapsed into one timeless picture. This chapter therefore reconstructs circulation through securely dated layers: routes, transport, merchants, credit, commodities and market nodes are compared across sources while each observation remains tied to its own period. The commercial history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be reduced to a single Patna–Bengal route or to a modern India–Nepal border crossing. Early modern exchange worked through overlapping scales: weekly rural markets gathered produce; river landings concentrated bulky cargo; towns provided storage, credit and brokerage; long-distance merchants linked those towns to Bengal, the upper Gangetic plain and the Himalayan world. A commodity could therefore change carriers, forms and destinations several times before reaching a final consumer. The useful unit of analysis is the network—nodes, seasonal routes, intermediaries and transaction costs—not a straight line drawn between political centres.

social.title: East India Company Expansion and the Remaking of Agrarian Relations
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Between the military victories of the East India Company in the 1750s and 1760s and the Permanent Settlement of 1793 lay nearly three decades of experimentation. The decisive change was not that a wholly new agrarian order appeared overnight after Plassey or Buxar. Rather, a commercial corporation acquired political leverage, then fiscal sovereignty, and gradually inserted its own supervisors, councils, collectors, auctions, revenue farmers, courts and accounting practices into an older Mughal–Nawabi system of zamindars, amils, qanungos, patwaris and village producers. Bihar is especially revealing because the transition can be seen through Shitab Rai’s revenue administration, the Patna Revenue Council, early experiments in Tirhut, the Rajmahal–Bhagalpur supervisory system and the uneven fiscal geography of Monghyr. This chapter follows that transition from 1757 to the eve of the Permanent Settlement. It therefore stops short of treating the 1793 settlement itself in detail; that belongs to Chapter 55. The remaking of agrarian relations began before the Company directly collected land revenue. Plassey in 1757 enlarged Company influence at the Bengal court, but it did not transfer the countryside into a British administrative system. The Battle of Buxar in 1764 was more consequential for Bihar because Company forces defeated a coalition that included Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. Even then, military victory had to be converted into fiscal authority, administrative routines and enforceable claims over local intermediaries. The agrarian transition was therefore cumulative: war altered sovereignty; treaties redistributed rights; revenue institutions changed more slowly. Buxar linked Bihar’s political history directly to the making of Company rule. Mir Qasim had earlier shifted his capital to Monghyr and attempted to strengthen nawabi authority against Company interference. His defeat removed a major regional challenge. The settlement that followed brought the Company into a new relationship with the Mughal emperor and the Bengal nawab. From this point Bihar was not merely a corridor for Company trade or military movement. Its land revenue became part of the fiscal foundation of a territorial regime whose military and commercial ambitions increasingly depended on collections from the countryside.

54.29 The decennial settlement was an endpoint of experimentation, not yet the Permanent Settlement
54.30 Conclusion: Company rule remade agrarian relations through institutions before it fixed property law

social.title: Permanent Settlement and Landed Society
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 converted the experimental decennial settlement of Bengal and Bihar into a perpetual state demand upon designated zamindars, independent talukdars and other proprietors. Its importance lay not simply in fixing revenue, but in reworking the legal language of landed authority. A hereditary revenue-collecting right was increasingly treated as proprietary property, while punctual payment to the colonial state became the condition of security. Yet the settlement did not define every right below the zamindar. Raiyats, under-tenure holders, village officials, service tenures, rent-free grants and customary users continued to inhabit a layered agrarian field that subsequent regulations, courts and tenancy statutes tried to order. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga the effects were regionally uneven: Tirhut entered a large permanent settlement in 1793, Bhagalpur was only partially settled at that date, and Monghyr contained a mixture of estate forms and difficult fiscal geographies. This chapter therefore studies the Permanent Settlement as the beginning of a new landed society, not as a one-day replacement of all older agrarian relations. The decennial settlement of 1790–91 was initially framed as a ten-year arrangement. Cornwallis and his colleagues then chose to make the assessed demand perpetual in 1793. The change mattered because future agricultural expansion and rental growth would accrue chiefly below the state’s fixed demand. In return, the Company expected secure landed property and predictable revenue to encourage improvement. The settlement therefore joined fiscal calculation to a political theory of property. It was less an isolated regulation than the culmination of the experiments traced in Chapter 54. Regulation I of 1793 declared the public assessment on settled estates fixed in perpetuity. It did not freeze the actual produce of the land, the number of cultivators, the rent collected from each raiyat, or the internal structure of every estate. The distinction between public jama and estate income is fundamental. A permanently fixed state demand could coexist with changing cultivation, prices, rents and subordinate tenures. Much later agrarian conflict arose precisely within that widening space between fixed public revenue and variable private rental income.

social.title: Indigo and Commercial Agriculture
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Indigo was one of the clearest ways in which colonial commercial agriculture entered the agrarian society created under permanent settlement. The crop linked cultivators and labourers in Bihar to European capital, Calcutta agency houses, factory processing, long-distance transport and volatile international dye markets. Yet the system was not uniform. Indigo could be grown directly on factory-controlled land, by tenants under advance-and-contract arrangements, or by independent cultivators. North Bihar—especially Tirhut, Darbhanga, Muzaffarpur, Saran and Champaran—became the principal European indigo zone during the nineteenth century, while Bhagalpur and Monghyr also supported significant production. This chapter therefore treats indigo as both a crop and an agrarian institution: it altered land use, credit, labour, rents, contracts and the distribution of risk. It also traces the technological and market crisis created by synthetic indigo after 1897 and the distinct Champaran conflict that culminated in the 1917 inquiry and the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918. Indigofera plants produced a dye whose value depended on far more than acreage. The crop had to be cut at the correct stage, processed rapidly in vats, oxidized, settled, boiled or pressed and dried into cakes of marketable quality. The commodity therefore joined field cultivation to factory manufacture. A bad crop, delayed cutting, weak fermentation or falling London prices could affect the entire chain. For cultivators the relevant question was different: what land, labour and credit had to be diverted from food production in order to satisfy the factory. Indigo is best understood as a combined agricultural-industrial institution. European-supervised indigo manufacture expanded in eastern India from the late eighteenth century, drawing on export demand, Calcutta commercial finance and the Company state. Early concentration lay in Bengal, but Bihar became increasingly important during the nineteenth century. The chronology should not be simplified into a single founding date for the region. Factories appeared at different times, often through local leases, partnerships and estate connections. By the mid-nineteenth century North Bihar had become a major field for European planting enterprise.

social.title: Opium and Other Commodity Networks
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Opium turned Bihar into one of the most tightly regulated commodity landscapes of the British Empire. Yet the poppy was never the whole economy. Cultivators in Mithila, Vajji and Anga also produced grain, oilseeds, tobacco, sugarcane and indigo; specialist workers made and refined saltpetre; Bhagalpur sustained silk and tasar manufacture; lac and other forest-linked products moved through eastern markets. The historical problem is therefore not to isolate opium as an exotic drug crop, but to understand how a state monopoly operated inside a much broader field of private, licensed, illicit and subsistence exchange. This chapter follows the opium chain from advance to field, collection, Patna processing, Calcutta auction and Asian export, while comparing it with other commodity networks whose labour regimes, transport needs and degrees of state control were different. It also maintains a strict source hierarchy: cultivation records do not equal export statistics, factory output does not measure total local production, and late gazetteers must not be projected backward without period evidence. Opium joined agriculture to manufacturing, finance, transport and overseas commerce. A cultivator grew poppy, but the commodity recognized by the colonial state was the processed drug delivered, tested, mixed, packed and eventually sold through official channels. The difference matters because each stage redistributed control. The crop demanded irrigated and carefully prepared winter land; the agency system supplied advances and fixed delivery obligations; factory officers standardized quality; river transport moved chests eastward; and Calcutta auctions converted a Bihar-grown product into imperial revenue. The commodity chain therefore connected village households in the Gangetic plain to merchants and consumers far beyond India. It also created opportunities for leakage, bargaining and evasion at every link.

social.title: Famines, Scarcity and Food Security
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Scarcity has repeatedly exposed the relationship between ecology, markets, household resources and public authority in Mithila, Vajji and Anga. A failed monsoon or damaged rice crop could begin a crisis, but famine emerged only when households lost effective access to food: grain prices rose faster than wages, cattle and tools were sold, seed was eaten, credit contracted, employment failed, or transport could not move food from surplus to deficit areas. The same region therefore experienced radically different outcomes in 1770, 1873–74 and 1896–97. In 1769–70 severe drought interacted with Company revenue extraction, grain procurement, weak relief and epidemic disease to produce catastrophic mortality in Bihar. In 1873–74, by contrast, the colonial government imported enormous quantities of rice, created depots, organized transport and inspected villages on a scale unprecedented in the province; mortality was correspondingly much lower, though the operation was criticized as excessively expensive. The famine of 1896–97 showed a third pattern: formal famine codes and improved communications existed, yet distress was sharply uneven, with Darbhanga requiring very large relief operations while parts of north Monghyr escaped crop failure but still suffered high prices among the landless poor. This chapter therefore treats famine not as an event label but as a social process. It reconstructs scarcity through harvests, prices, wages, entitlements, migration, relief and mortality, and it keeps contemporary evidence separate from later administrative memory. The history of food security is the history of how these layers were connected—and of how public policy sometimes broke, and sometimes failed to break, the chain.

social.title: Colonial Surveys and the Invention of Social Categories
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Colonial surveys created an extraordinarily dense archive for the social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga, but the archive must be read as a history of classification as well as a description of society. From Buchanan-Hamilton’s early district inquiries to the censuses, Risley’s ethnography, Grierson’s linguistic survey and the gazetteers, officials progressively standardized names, boundaries and comparative tables. The central method of this chapter is chronological: a colonial category is evidence first for the date and administrative purpose in which it appears. It cannot be projected backward without independent period evidence. Colonial rule generated an expanding demand to describe the people it taxed, policed, recruited, litigated with and governed. The resulting surveys were never neutral inventories. Their headings reflected administrative problems: landholding, occupation, religion, language, “tribe,” “caste,” custom and rank. Yet it is equally misleading to treat every category as a pure colonial fabrication. Officials worked with locally supplied names, inherited textual vocabularies, previous revenue records and the testimony of intermediaries. The historical problem is therefore to reconstruct a process of translation. Social identities existed before the census, but the survey and census increasingly required them to be written into standardized boxes, compared across districts and made legible to provincial government. The documentary archive is invaluable precisely because it records this encounter between lived social description and bureaucratic classification.

social.title: Education under Colonialism
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Colonial education transformed the institutional ecology of Mithila, Vajji and Anga by linking schools, examinations and credentials to a growing public and professional labour market. The change was cumulative rather than substitutive. Sanskrit ṭols, vernacular schools, maktabs, madrasas and household learning persisted while government schools, aided institutions, colleges and university examinations expanded. This chapter traces that layered transition from the early nineteenth-century surveys to Patna University in 1917, with special attention to language, access, patronage, gender and the economic value of credentials. Education under colonialism did not begin with an empty landscape and did not proceed as a single replacement of “traditional” learning by English schools. Mithila, Vajji and Anga already contained Sanskrit scholarly institutions, elementary schools, maktabs, madrasas, household teaching and occupational transmission. The colonial period added new layers: government schools, inspection, grants-in-aid, prescribed curricula, public examinations, colleges and eventually a regional university. Older institutions adapted unevenly rather than disappearing at once. A socio-economic history therefore asks how access, language, credentials, patronage and employment changed. The decisive transformation was not simply the arrival of English; it was the growth of an educational bureaucracy that increasingly linked recognized schooling to examinations, certificates and salaried occupations.

social.title: Print Culture
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Print culture changed the social life of texts in Mithila, Vajji and Anga by making arguments, reports, literary works and linguistic claims reproducible across distance. It did not erase manuscript or oral transmission. Instead, presses, lithography, schools, postal systems, railways, journals and associations created a denser communication environment in which English, Hindi, Urdu, Maithili and Sanskrit occupied overlapping but unequal positions. This chapter follows that transformation from the nineteenth-century press regime to the early twentieth-century Maithili periodical world, with particular attention to script technology, multilingual readership, regulation, circulation and the making of regional publics. Print entered Mithila, Vajji and Anga through a layered ecology of presses, paper, type, lithography, editors, schools, postal routes, railways, booksellers and readers. It is therefore misleading to describe colonial print as a simple moment when manuscripts were replaced by books. The social effects of print depended on who could finance publication, which scripts could be set economically, where presses were located, how copies travelled, and which institutions taught people to read them. Calcutta remained a crucial publishing centre for much of eastern India, while Patna, Bhagalpur, Darbhanga and other towns gradually developed their own printing and journalistic capacities. Print expanded the reproducibility of texts and the speed with which arguments could circulate, but the new medium remained embedded in older practices of recitation, copying, commentary and collective reading. For this reason, the chapter treats print as an additional infrastructure of social communication rather than as a technological rupture.

social.title: Railways, Roads and Changing Markets
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Railways reorganized the economic geography of Mithila, Vajji and Anga without erasing rivers, roads, ferries or animal transport. South of the Ganga, the East Indian Railway reached major Anga towns in the early 1860s; north of the river, the Tirhut network expanded from famine-relief construction in the 1870s into a branching metre-gauge system. Stations and junctions changed market hierarchy, roads increasingly became railway feeders, and new links drew frontier trade toward railheads. At the same time, flood ecology, river crossings, gauge breaks and the continuing need for carts preserved substantial friction. This chapter reconstructs that layered transport economy and treats market integration as an uneven historical process rather than an automatic result of railway mileage. Colonial transport history in Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be reduced to a sequence in which railways arrived and older routes vanished. Before rail construction, the Ganga and its tributaries, ferries, seasonal roads, carts, pack animals and foot traffic already connected village production to market towns and longer-distance commerce. Railways entered this existing geography and altered the relative cost, speed and reliability of particular routes. They encouraged some towns to become junctions or collection centres, reduced the commercial advantage of certain older road and river markets, and made feeder roads more valuable. Yet much traffic still had to reach a station by cart, cross a river by ferry, or continue toward Nepal over roads and tracks. The historical question is therefore not whether rail replaced road and river, but how several transport systems were recombined into a new hierarchy of accessibility.

social.title: Labour Migration
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Labour migration became one of the most consequential connections between the agrarian households of Mithila, Vajji and Anga and the expanding colonial economy. Yet there was no single migrant stream. Seasonal workers, circular urban migrants, railway and workshop labourers, plantation recruits, women moving within family labour strategies, and indentured emigrants faced different destinations and different degrees of freedom. Railways lowered travel frictions, but recruitment networks and labour law often determined whether movement remained reversible. This chapter reconstructs those differentiated circuits while keeping census categories, household strategies and coercive labour regimes analytically distinct. Colonial labour migration from Mithila, Vajji and Anga took several forms that must be kept analytically separate. Some cultivators and labourers left for a few weeks or months during slack agricultural seasons; others worked repeatedly in Calcutta, Howrah or railway centres while maintaining a village household; some moved with families to plantation zones; and a much smaller share entered overseas indenture. Census tables tend to flatten these movements because they record birthplace or residence at a particular date, not the full sequence of departure, return and repetition. A history of labour migration therefore has to reconstruct circuits rather than assume that every person enumerated outside a home district had permanently left it. The key question is not simply how many moved, but what kind of labour relation, distance, recruitment mechanism and probability of return defined each movement.

social.title: Women and Colonial Modernity
social.part: Part Vii — Early Modern And Colonial Economic Transformations
social.summary: Colonial modernity altered women’s lives in Mithila, Vajji and Anga through schools, law, print, medicine, labour markets, migration and nationalist politics, but the changes were profoundly unequal. Female literacy remained low even as girls’ education became an explicit field of policy; statutes changed the legal treatment of widow remarriage, consent and child marriage without ensuring uniform social compliance; hospitals and trained female personnel expanded without displacing household medicine; and political mobilisation made women publicly visible while leaving the economic weight of unpaid labour poorly recorded. This chapter reconstructs those layered transformations while treating the silences of the colonial archive as part of the history itself. Women in Mithila, Vajji and Anga encountered colonial modernity not as a single transition from an old social order to a new one, but through overlapping institutions that moved at different speeds. Schools could expand while female literacy remained very low; statutes could alter legal possibilities while marriage practice changed slowly; hospitals and lady doctors could appear without displacing household medicine or dais; and nationalist mobilisation could draw women into public action without dissolving domestic obligations. The concept of modernity is therefore useful only when broken into specific processes—education, print, law, medicine, labour markets, transport, associational life and political participation. Each process was filtered through locality, class, caste, religious community, household wealth and age. The history is consequently one of selective access and negotiated change rather than a uniform story of either emancipation or decline.

social.title: The Historical India–Nepal Borderland Economy
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: The India–Nepal boundary across Mithila and the wider eastern Tarai/Madhesh did not create two self-contained economies. It cut across an older lowland–foothill–valley system in which cultivators, pastoralists, merchants, pilgrims, craftsmen, revenue farmers, carriers and state agents moved through linked markets and seasonal routes. From the late eighteenth century onward, Gorkha consolidation, Company expansion, the Anglo–Gorkha War, boundary demarcation, customs administration and railway construction altered the terms of movement without abolishing the economic continuities of the plains. This chapter therefore treats the border as an institution embedded in a corridor: politically real, fiscally consequential and increasingly surveyed, yet continually crossed by commodities, labour, credit, kinship and pilgrimage. The historical economy joining north Bihar to the Nepal Tarai and the Himalayan interior was older than the modern boundary. River systems, alluvial plains, forest belts and foothill passes produced a north–south gradient of exchange. Grain, livestock, cloth and manufactured goods moved toward the hills; forest products and highland commodities moved toward low-country markets. Political jurisdictions changed repeatedly, but the commercial logic of short-haul movement from village to hat, hat to customs point, and customs point to a long-distance route remained durable. The term borderland is therefore more accurate than frontier only if it does not imply political vagueness. States claimed revenue and sovereignty here, yet their lines intersected economic fields whose scale was set by ecology, transport cost and social networks as much as by jurisdiction.

social.title: Janakpur as Religious, Commercial and Urban Centre
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Janakpur’s historical importance cannot be reduced either to a sacred narrative or to a modern municipal chronology. The documented city emerged through the interaction of pilgrimage, temple institutions, ponds and ritual routes, cross-border exchange with north Bihar, transport infrastructure, administrative concentration and later urban growth. This chapter therefore treats Janakpur as a living urban system whose religious, commercial and civic functions repeatedly reinforced one another. It also separates epic and devotional identifications from claims that can be dated through administrative, archaeological, railway, census and modern urban evidence. Janakpur is identified in Hindu tradition with Mithila, King Janaka and Sita, and that identification has shaped pilgrimage, patronage and local memory for centuries. Yet an urban history cannot simply convert an epic setting into a continuously documented city. The strongest method is to distinguish several evidentiary layers: literary and devotional geography; archaeological or architectural remains; early modern and nineteenth-century pilgrimage institutions; twentieth-century transport and municipal records; and contemporary demographic and planning evidence. The city’s historical significance is not diminished by this distinction. On the contrary, it becomes possible to explain how sacred memory itself became a durable economic and spatial force. Temples, shrines, ritual paths and ponds formed a spatial grammar within which settlement and commerce could concentrate. A pilgrim did not visit an abstract “Janakpur”; movement occurred among particular shrines, bathing places, monastic establishments, markets and lodging points. Such repeated circulation gave specific sites economic value and encouraged services to cluster around them. The result was an urban form in which sacred geography and commercial geography overlapped without being identical. This is a central feature of Janakpur’s development: ritual destinations generated movement, movement supported exchange, and exchange helped sustain the physical institutions through which sacred identity was reproduced.

social.title: Land, Tenancy and Agrarian Society in the Nepal Tarai
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Agrarian society in the Nepal Tarai was created through the interaction of ecology, conquest, revenue policy, land reclamation, migration, tenancy and local intermediaries. The region cannot be described accurately by importing the Permanent Settlement model from British India or by treating terms such as raikar, birta, jagir and jimidari as interchangeable forms of landlord ownership. This chapter reconstructs the layered land regime of the Tarai, with particular attention to Saptari, Siraha, Dhanusha–Mahottari and the wider eastern plains, and follows its transformation from late-eighteenth-century revenue experiments through the land-reform legislation of the 1950s and 1960s. A single field could carry several distinct relationships at once: the state might claim land revenue; a grantee might receive that revenue under birta or another assignment; a village intermediary might collect dues; and an actual cultivator might hold occupancy, tenancy or customary claims. Colonial and later administrative vocabulary often tempts historians to collapse these layers into a simple opposition between landlord and peasant. Nepal’s records require greater precision. Tenure describes the legal or fiscal basis of a claim; taxation describes obligations to the state or assignee; cultivation describes who actually worked the soil. Agrarian class emerged from the interaction of all three, not from a label alone. The plains south of the Chure were highly productive but environmentally uneven. River migration, seasonal inundation, wetlands, sal forest and malaria affected where permanent cultivation could expand and how easily officials could measure holdings. Eastern districts such as Saptari and Mahottari contained old cultivated zones as well as forest, scrub and waste lands that states sought to bring under assessment. Reclamation was therefore both an ecological process and a fiscal project. A plot became economically valuable to the state only when settlement, labour, drainage and cropping could convert it into a dependable stream of revenue.

social.title: Forest Clearance, Malaria Control and Demographic Transformation
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: The demographic transformation of the Nepal Tarai after the 1950s was not the simple replacement of an empty jungle by settlers. The plains already contained towns, cultivated belts, forests, grazing grounds, pilgrimage routes and long-established Madhesi, Tharu and other communities. What changed rapidly was the relationship among disease ecology, forest access, state resettlement, spontaneous migration, roads, land law and agricultural expansion. This chapter reconstructs those linked processes, with particular attention to the eastern and central Tarai and to the Mithila/Madhesh districts, while using Chitwan and other Inner-Tarai projects only where they illuminate national policy rather than as substitutes for the regional history of Dhanusha, Mahottari, Sarlahi, Siraha and Saptari. Malaria control altered the cost and risk of permanent residence in lowland Nepal, but it did not by itself determine who migrated, where forest was cleared, or who gained land. Hill land pressure, state revenue goals, resettlement schemes, transport, cadastral administration, local labour demand, cross-border kinship and the availability of cultivable land all mattered. The analytical task is therefore to connect public health with political economy while refusing a monocausal narrative. In some districts disease control preceded rapid in-migration; in others dense cultivation and established Madhesi settlement already existed. The appropriate unit is a differentiated Tarai landscape rather than an imagined uniform frontier. The older stereotype of the Tarai as an uninhabited forest obscures substantial regional variation. Southern belts near the Indian boundary contained long-established villages, bazaars and paddy cultivation, while forest and grassland were more extensive toward the Chure and in malarial or poorly drained tracts. Revenue records discussed in Chapter 67 show that eighteenth- and nineteenth-century governments were already classifying, taxing and reclaiming land in Saptari and Mahottari. Forest was therefore not simply “waste.” It supplied timber, fuel, fodder, game, grazing, shifting access to fields and fiscal possibilities, and its clearance redistributed those resources.

social.title: Migration and Settlement
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Migration and settlement transformed the Nepal Tarai/Madhesh after the middle of the twentieth century, but neither process began in an empty landscape. The plains already contained long-established villages, market towns, pilgrimage centres, cultivated tracts, forests and grazing zones linked across the India–Nepal border. What changed after the 1950s was the scale, direction and institutional framing of movement. Malaria control reduced one environmental barrier; roads and markets lowered transport costs; land policy and resettlement programmes created new opportunities; and population pressure in the hills encouraged movement toward the lowlands. At the same time, cross-border marriage, labour and commerce continued older patterns that cannot be reduced to immigration in the modern political sense. Migration records movement from one place to another; settlement concerns the establishment of residence, cultivation, property claims and social institutions. A household could migrate temporarily without settling, settle after repeated seasonal movements, or maintain homes and fields on more than one side of a district or international boundary. Keeping these categories separate is essential because census, land and resettlement records capture different parts of the same social process. Older cultivated belts of Saptari, Siraha, Dhanusha, Mahottari and the border plains contradict any description of the region as a vacant frontier. Madhesi caste communities, Muslims, Tharus and other lowland populations formed villages, markets and agrarian relations before national development programmes. Forested and malarial zones existed beside settled landscapes rather than replacing them everywhere. Marriage, pilgrimage, livestock movement, seasonal labour, trade and cultivation connected Nepal’s plains with north Bihar across a politically bounded but socially permeable frontier. Such movement often followed kinship and market networks rather than administrative programmes. Birthplace statistics therefore need to be read alongside the long history of a borderland in which daily economic life crossed the international line.

social.title: Language, Education and Cultural Institutions in Nepal
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Language, education and cultural institutions in Nepal Mithila/Madhesh have never formed a single hierarchy. Maithili has long been a language of household life, ritual, literature, performance and cross-border communication, while Sanskrit, Nepali, Hindi, Urdu, Bhojpuri, Bajjika and English have occupied different institutional niches at different times. The modern state expanded schools, examinations, universities, academies and broadcasting, but it also attached unequal prestige and administrative power to languages. The historical problem is therefore not whether Maithili survived, but how institutions distributed literacy, credentials, public visibility and cultural authority among languages. This chapter treats language policy, schooling and cultural organisation together because each changed the social value of the others. The eastern and central Tarai/Madhesh were multilingual before mass schooling. Maithili dominated large parts of Saptari, Siraha, Dhanusha and Mahottari, but speech communities interacted with Bhojpuri, Bajjika, Urdu, Nepali, Sanskrit and Hindi through markets, courts, pilgrimage, marriage and religious instruction. A language could be dominant in the household and village while another carried administrative, scholastic or commercial prestige. The expansion of modern education therefore entered an already layered linguistic ecology rather than creating one from nothing. The 1952/54 census reported 918,211 persons under ‘Maithili and dialects’; the 1961 count was 1,130,402 and the 1971 count 1,327,242. Later censuses recorded 2.192 million Maithili mother-tongue speakers in 1991, 2.798 million in 2001, 3.093 million in 2011 and 3.222 million in 2021. These figures establish the large demographic base of Maithili, but they are not a simple time series of language shift. Census categories, dialect boundaries, enumerator practice and the treatment of Hindi, Bajjika and related speech changed over time.

social.title: Gender, Citizenship and Household Economy in Madhesh
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Gender, citizenship and household economy meet most visibly where formal rights encounter everyday dependence. In Nepal Mithila/Madhesh, women’s economic position has been shaped not only by wages and land but also by marriage, migration, unpaid care, civil-registration documents, inheritance practice, access to schooling and the ability to move between household, market and public office. The open India–Nepal border adds another layer because cross-border marriages and kinship networks can make citizenship rules unusually consequential for mothers and children. This chapter therefore treats citizenship as an economic institution as well as a legal status, while distinguishing constitutional rights, statutory pathways and their uneven implementation in households and local administrations. Most production and welfare in Madhesh pass through households before they appear in markets or state statistics. Cooking, care, fuel and water collection, livestock tending, crop processing, small trade, savings, remittances and decisions over schooling are organised through kinship and gender. A household can pool resources while distributing authority unequally. For that reason, rising household income does not automatically establish women’s control over assets, nor does female employment necessarily remove unpaid obligations. The historical unit of analysis must therefore include both market income and the allocation of work, property and decision-making inside the family. Women have long participated in transplanting, weeding, harvesting, fodder collection, livestock care, seed management, post-harvest processing and household food production. Yet the visibility of this work depends on statistical definition. Modern labour-force standards count work for pay or profit differently from production for a household’s own final use. A woman may therefore perform many hours of economically necessary farm work while being classified outside the labour force. This distinction is particularly important in rural Madhesh, where family farming and own-use production remain major components of livelihood.

social.title: Janakpur Art, Crafts and Cultural Economy
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: Janakpur’s cultural economy is not simply a market for paintings. It joins ritual practice, women’s domestic knowledge, portable art, craft production, pilgrimage, tourism, institutional development, public murals, training, galleries, collectors and digital circulation. The same motif can move from a wedding wall to handmade paper, from a household threshold to a textile, ceramic object or urban mural, and from a devotional setting to a tourist purchase. Such movement changes scale, materials, authorship and price, but it does not automatically sever the work from Mithila’s ritual and social worlds. This chapter therefore treats art and craft as economic activities embedded in living cultural institutions rather than as detached commodities. A cultural economy includes the labour that creates an object, the knowledge that makes it intelligible, the institutions that certify and circulate it, and the places and events that attract buyers. In Janakpur, painting is connected to festivals, marriage, pilgrimage, women’s organisations, local shops, hotels, museums, training programmes and public-space design. The economic value of Mithila art therefore depends on a network. A painting sold to a visitor carries not only pigment and paper but also stories about Janakpur, Sita, household ritual, women’s skill and regional identity. That symbolic value can generate income, but it also creates arguments about authenticity and ownership. Mithila painting in Nepal developed from practices that were not originally organised for sale. Women decorated mud walls, floors, thresholds and courtyards for weddings, festivals and auspicious household rites. Aripan floor designs, wall images and kohbar-associated forms were part of ritual preparation and social reproduction. They required time, materials and skill even when no money changed hands. Commercial art later drew from this reservoir of domestic expertise. The history of Janakpur painting must therefore begin with women’s unpaid cultural labour rather than with the first gallery exhibition.

social.title: Border Markets, Remittances and Informal Exchange
social.part: Part Viii — Nepal Mithila / Madhesh As A Social And Economic Region
social.summary: The India–Nepal border economy of Madhesh is neither wholly formal nor wholly informal. It is a layered system in which kinship travel, weekly markets, petty retail, commercial customs trade, labour mobility, remittance transfers, currency exchange and digital payments coexist. A person may cross the border legally without immigration formalities while the goods carried remain subject to customs rules. A household may receive a bank remittance from the Gulf, hand-carried earnings from India and commodities bought in a Bihar market during the same month. This chapter therefore separates movement of people, goods and money before asking how they interact. It also treats unrecorded exchange as an empirical category rather than automatically equating it with criminal trafficking. The Madhesh–Bihar border is lined not by one market but by overlapping market systems. Village haats, municipal bazaars, wholesale depots, railway stations, bus stands, customs yards and household shops connect producers and consumers on both sides. Their importance comes from repetition: the same families, carriers and traders meet across seasons, festivals and crop cycles. Market information therefore travels through social relations as well as posted prices. This continuity helps explain why border exchange can survive changes in tariff schedules, transport technology and administrative rules. The 1950 India–Nepal relationship permits unusually easy reciprocal movement and residence, but customs law still governs commercial goods. This distinction is essential. A farmer visiting relatives, a pilgrim travelling to Janakpur, a wage worker going to Bihar and a truck importing manufactured goods do not occupy the same legal category. Everyday speech often compresses these movements into the idea of an ‘open border’. Economic history must instead ask what is moving, in what quantity, under which documentation and through which institutional channel.

social.title: Independence, Land Reform and Agrarian Change in Bihar
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Independence did not reset Bihar’s countryside to a blank slate. The new constitutional state inherited the Permanent Settlement, great estates, occupancy raiyats, under-raiyats, sharecroppers, agricultural labourers, moneylending networks, fragmented plots and flood-prone ecologies formed over the colonial period. What changed after 1947 was the political legitimacy of that order and the institutional capacity to alter it. Bihar became one of the earliest laboratories of postcolonial land reform, but ‘land reform’ was never one measure. It included protection of homesteads, abolition of rent-collecting intermediaries, constitutional change, preparation of revenue records, voluntary Bhoodan transfers, consolidation of fragmented holdings and, eventually, statutory ceilings. These interventions reshaped the relation between state, landlord and cultivator without eliminating inequality. This chapter reconstructs that transition as an institutional history. Chapter 75 will examine the abolition of zamindari and its uneven consequences in greater depth; Chapters 76–83 will turn to production, river projects, credit, cooperatives and specialised regional economies. The transfer of political power in 1947 created an expectation that the social relationships underpinning colonial revenue extraction would also be transformed. Congress programmes before independence had repeatedly attacked intermediary landlordism and promised greater security to cultivators. Yet the state that inherited these promises also inherited the records, courts, administrative categories and property claims of the colonial regime. Agrarian reconstruction therefore began as a contest over how far political independence would alter legally entrenched interests in land. The central issue was not merely who owned a field in everyday speech, but how several layers of rights—proprietary, tenure-holding, raiyati, under-raiyati, mortgage, lease and service claims—would be translated into the law of the new republic.

social.title: Abolition of Zamindari and Its Uneven Consequences
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: The abolition of zamindari in Bihar was a genuine constitutional and agrarian rupture, but it was not a social revolution completed by a single statute. The Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 transferred intermediary interests to the State and ended the proprietary right of zamindars and tenure-holders to stand between the government and the raiyat. Yet the same law also defined property that outgoing intermediaries could retain, while tenancy, labour, credit, caste authority and political influence continued to operate below and around the abolished revenue hierarchy. The historical problem is therefore not whether zamindari was abolished—it was—but how far abolition redistributed effective control over rural resources. For Mithila, Vajji and Anga, the consequences were especially uneven because the same legal regime encountered different estate structures, ecological conditions, tenancy patterns and market connections. The vast Raj Darbhanga exemplified the bureaucratic great estate; elsewhere, village-scale landlords and tenure-holders exercised power through smaller but locally dense networks. Flood-prone north Bihar, riverine and market-oriented Anga, and the densely settled Tirhut–Vajji plain converted legal change into different combinations of direct state tenancy, retained landlord cultivation, concealed tenancy, landlessness and new forms of rural politics. This chapter treats abolition as both accomplishment and unfinished transition. Under the Permanent Settlement and the layered tenures that developed beneath it, revenue and rent passed through proprietors, tenure-holders and sub-tenure interests before reaching cultivators. The 1950 Act attacked that legal chain directly. Estates and tenures vested in the State, and the State acquired the superior interests that had permitted intermediaries to collect rents and exercise estate rights over fisheries, forests, ferries, hats, bazaars and related resources. This was more than a change of terminology: the State replaced the zamindar as the superior rent-receiving authority. But abolition did not erase every private right derived from land, because raiyati rights, under-raiyati interests and specified retained properties continued under other legal categories.

social.title: Agriculture after Independence
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: After independence, agriculture in Bihar changed through a layered sequence of land reform, irrigation, scientific crop improvement, groundwater development, credit expansion, mechanisation, road building and market integration. None of these transformations occurred evenly. The first decades remained dominated by monsoon risk and low yields; the Green Revolution raised wheat production more clearly than rice or maize; large river projects and tube wells extended irrigation but did not solve drainage and flood vulnerability; and small, fragmented holdings limited the income that even higher yields could generate. The history is therefore neither one of simple stagnation nor one of a uniform technological breakthrough. For Mithila, Vajji and Anga, the decisive variables were regional ecology and access. North Bihar’s Himalayan rivers produced both fertile alluvium and recurrent flood/waterlogging hazards. The Gandak–Ganga corridor supported intensive cultivation linked to growing urban markets. Anga’s Ganga-side districts combined foodgrains, horticulture and market connections with an important agricultural research centre at Sabour. This chapter follows production and technology across these settings while leaving the institutional history of Kosi and Gandak river-development projects to Chapter 77 and rural credit/cooperatives to Chapters 79–80. Agriculture entered independence carrying the weight of population pressure, small holdings, insecure tenancy, weak irrigation and limited non-farm employment. Land reform altered the legal structure of rural property, but it did not by itself supply water, improved seed, fertiliser, credit, storage or roads. In the alluvial districts of Mithila, Vajji and Anga, fertile soils coexisted with seasonal excess and scarcity of water. The post-1947 agricultural problem was therefore not simply to cultivate more land; it was to raise output from an already densely used countryside while reducing vulnerability to floods, drought, fragmented holdings and volatile markets.

social.title: Kosi, Gandak and Major River-Development Projects
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Post-independence river development in north Bihar was built around a difficult hydraulic fact: Mithila and Vajji possessed abundant water, yet the timing, sediment load and mobility of Himalayan rivers made that abundance dangerous as well as productive. The Kosi and Gandak projects therefore combined flood-control structures, diversion barrages, embankments, canals, roads, bridges, hydroelectric components and cross-border agreements with Nepal. They were not simply irrigation schemes, and they were not storage-dam projects in the usual sense. Their history is best read as an attempt to create a managed river landscape within an alluvial plain that continually changes channel, bed level and drainage relations. The projects produced real gains: protected tracts, new irrigation possibilities, transport links, power generation and a permanent hydraulic administration. They also produced second-generation problems - displacement, incomplete rehabilitation, waterlogging, canal inefficiency, siltation, embankment maintenance and the redistribution rather than elimination of flood risk. These contradictions are central to the socio-economic history of Mithila, Vajji and the adjoining Gangetic plain. Chapter 78 will examine floods themselves as social and economic events; the present chapter concentrates on the institutions and infrastructures created to manage rivers after independence. Independence inherited a long history of embankments, canals and flood inquiries, but the new state enlarged the scale and ambition of intervention. Large multipurpose projects promised to convert damaging monsoon flows into irrigation, power and planned development. In north Bihar this hydraulic vision was inseparable from national food policy, rural employment and the political expectation that scientific engineering could reduce chronic insecurity. The Kosi and Gandak projects were consequently presented not as isolated civil works but as development systems. Their construction required finance, land acquisition, labour, roads, rail access, cross-border diplomacy and administrative organisations capable of operating structures long after the ceremonial moment of inauguration.

social.title: Floods as Social and Economic History
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Floods in Mithila, Vajji and Anga are not merely episodes of excess water. They are recurring social and economic processes in which rainfall, river morphology, embankments, drainage, settlement location, landholding, caste, gender, transport, public administration and household assets interact. The same depth of inundation can fertilise one field, destroy another crop, isolate a school, erode a homestead, interrupt a market road or push a land-poor household into debt. A socio-economic history must therefore ask not only where water spread but who was exposed, what was lost, who could recover, and how repeated floods altered livelihoods and institutions over time. North Bihar’s flood history is also plural. Himalayan tributaries can rise early; Burhi Gandak and other systems may peak later; the Ganga can become a high master drain and slow the evacuation of local water; embankments may breach; drainage congestion may prolong inundation; and the Ganga corridor in Anga can experience high stages, erosion and backwater effects even when the northern tributaries behave differently. This chapter therefore treats major post-independence flood years as historically distinct events, while also examining the quieter annual accumulation of crop loss, debt, migration, interrupted schooling, public expenditure and adaptive knowledge. Hydrology determines where and how water moves, but disaster losses are socially distributed. A pucca house on raised ground, a thatched dwelling beside an embankment, a tenant’s standing paddy crop and a trader’s stock in a market town do not face identical risks. Land title, savings, livestock ownership, caste location, access to boats, roads, credit, health care and public relief shape what happens after inundation begins. This distinction helps explain why flood mortality, displacement and indebtedness can remain concentrated even when engineering works reduce average water levels in some protected tracts. Flood history must therefore combine river records with evidence on households, labour, markets and institutions.

social.title: Rural Credit, Indebtedness and Banking
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Rural credit after independence was one of the central institutions through which agrarian change was either enabled or constrained. A cultivator needed working capital before harvest but received income only after harvest; a landless household needed food, medicine or migration expenses without possessing conventional collateral; a dairy producer needed small recurring advances; and a flood-affected family often needed several kinds of credit at the same time. Credit therefore cannot be studied only as banking history. It is also a history of risk, landholding, caste, gender, markets, migration and the timing of household cash flow. Across Mithila, Vajji and Anga the long post-1947 transition was not a simple replacement of the moneylender by the bank. Cooperatives, commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks, Primary Agricultural Credit Societies, Self-Help Groups, microfinance institutions, traders, commission agents, employers, relatives and informal lenders coexisted and often financed the same household. The historical question is thus not whether formal credit expanded—it did—but who could use it, for what purpose, at what cost, with what documentation and repayment calendar, and what happened when crops, prices, health or floods disrupted repayment. Post-independence rural Bihar inherited longstanding relations of advance, mortgage, produce-linked lending and personal obligation. Colonial surveys had repeatedly recorded cultivators borrowing for cultivation as well as for food, ceremonies, litigation, rent and emergencies. Abolition of zamindari altered the legal structure of landed power, but it did not remove seasonal cash shortages. The basic agricultural asymmetry remained: expenditure on seed, labour, irrigation and consumption was required before sale proceeds arrived. Debt was therefore built into the annual rhythm of many rural households rather than being an exceptional sign of improvidence.

social.title: Cooperatives and Rural Institutions
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Cooperation after independence was not a single movement and not merely a branch of rural credit. It was a recurring institutional answer to a basic problem of small-scale production: cultivators, milk producers, fishers, artisans and rural women often operated individually but needed pooled access to finance, storage, inputs, water, procurement, processing, transport and markets. A cooperative promised to aggregate many small economic actors without converting them into wage workers under one private owner. Its ideal vocabulary was thrift, self-help, mutual aid and democratic membership; its practical history was shaped equally by state law, bureaucracy, elections, local hierarchy, working capital and the ability to deliver a service at the moment members actually needed it. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, this history acquired distinct regional forms. Primary Agricultural Credit Societies became visible not only through crop loans but through fertiliser, procurement, storage and public-service delivery. Dairy societies linked village producers with district milk unions and the Bihar State Milk Co-operative Federation. Fishermen’s societies became entangled with the legal settlement of jalkars. Water Users’ Associations represented a different, non-credit form of collective management. Since the 2000s, Self-Help Groups, Village Organisations, Cluster-Level Federations and Farmer Producer Organisations have widened the institutional repertoire beyond the classical cooperative society. This chapter therefore studies rural institutions as mechanisms for aggregation, bargaining and service delivery, while leaving the detailed commodity histories of silk, makhana, fish and dairy to Chapters 82–83.

social.title: Industrialisation and Its Limits
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Industrialisation after independence did not bypass Mithila, Vajji and Anga completely, but it arrived unevenly. Large public investments created striking nodes such as Barauni, railway engineering continued at Jamalpur, sugar factories tied cane-growing tracts to processing, and industrial estates appeared around Darbhanga, Hajipur, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur and other towns. Yet these nodes did not combine into a dense manufacturing belt. The central historical problem is therefore not an absence of industry, but the limited capacity of industrial activity to transform employment, settlement, supply chains and regional income on the scale seen in India’s more industrialised states. This chapter treats industry broadly enough to include large factories, agro-processing, power and fertiliser complexes, industrial estates and micro, small and medium enterprises, while keeping analytical distinctions clear. Construction is part of the secondary sector but is not the same as manufacturing; a refinery can be capital-intensive without employing a mass workforce; and thousands of tiny establishments can sustain livelihoods without generating the productivity effects of a thick factory ecosystem. These distinctions are essential for explaining both Bihar’s recurring industrial ambitions and their limits. At independence, undivided Bihar contained some of India’s most important mineral and heavy-industrial centres, but these were concentrated largely in the Chhotanagpur plateau and adjoining southern districts. The alluvial north and much of eastern Bihar remained primarily agrarian, with processing industries, railway workshops, tobacco, sugar, handloom and smaller urban enterprises rather than comparable concentrations of steel, coal and engineering. This internal geography mattered because later state averages could conceal two very different economies. For the regions considered in this volume, the relevant starting point was not an industrial blank slate, but a comparatively thin factory base attached to agriculture, transport and a few strategic public installations.

social.title: Bhagalpur Silk and Anga’s Textile Economy
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Bhagalpur silk is often presented as a single celebrated product, but historically it has been a dispersed textile economy: cocoon and yarn supply, reeling and spinning, dyeing, warping, household weaving, finishing, merchant finance, cooperative organisation and long-distance marketing. The centre of gravity lies in Bhagalpur and neighbouring Banka, within the wider Anga region, yet the value chain reaches into Jharkhand, other silk-producing states, metropolitan markets and export channels. This geography explains both the endurance of the craft and its vulnerability. A strong weaving tradition can survive even when local raw-silk production is modest, provided merchants, institutions and transport reconnect the stages of production. The chapter therefore treats ‘Bhagalpur silk’ not merely as a cultural label but as a socio-economic system. It follows the historical record from the early nineteenth-century survey of Francis Buchanan through cooperative and state support, the Weavers’ Service Centre, the rise of powerlooms, the Geographical Indication, the Bhagalpur–Banka Mega Handloom Cluster and contemporary design, testing and sericulture infrastructure. The central argument is that resilience has come from flexible household production and accumulated skill, while the recurrent limits have been raw-material dependence, working-capital asymmetry, uneven common facilities, imitation, volatile orders and weak bargaining at the producer end of the chain. Bhagalpur’s fame can obscure the wider geography that made its textiles possible. Weaving households were concentrated in neighbourhoods and villages across Bhagalpur town and district, while Banka contributed reeling, spinning and weaving tied to forest-based tussar ecology. Traders connected these clusters to Patna, Kolkata and national markets; yarn and cocoons could arrive from Jharkhand and other silk regions; and finished fabrics moved outward through wholesalers, exhibitions, exporters and later online retail. Such a network behaves differently from a factory. Capital equipment is distributed among households, production expands or contracts with orders, and the boundary between household, workshop and commercial enterprise is porous. This decentralisation reduced the fixed cost of survival but also shifted inventory and income risk toward weavers and small intermediaries.
