social.title: Makhana, Fish, Dairy and Specialised Regional Economies
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Makhana, fish and milk appear to belong to different sectors, yet in Mithila, Vajji and Anga they share a common economic logic. They are intensive in management rather than land alone, depend on fragile biological cycles, and derive value from infrastructure that links scattered households to markets. Makhana is rooted in ponds, chaurs and shallow-water fields; inland fisheries use many of the same aquatic landscapes; dairying converts fodder, crop residues and household labour into a perishable daily product. Each can provide income where conventional cereal farming is constrained by small holdings, floods, waterlogging or the need for year-round cash. Their histories therefore reveal how regional ecology became an economic asset rather than merely an obstacle. The post-independence transformation of these activities was institutional as much as technical. Makhana acquired a research centre, improved varieties, processing machinery and a Geographical Indication. Fisheries moved from local capture and pond use toward hatcheries, managed aquaculture, stocking, cold-chain support and large public programmes. Cooperative dairying linked village societies to milk unions, processing plants and the Sudha brand after COMFED was established in 1983. Around these three major systems sit other specialised economies—Shahi litchi in the Vajji–Muzaffarpur belt, Bhagalpuri Zardalu and Katarni in Anga, water chestnut and high-value horticulture in wetland districts. The central theme is diversification through place-specific knowledge, followed by a continuing struggle over processing, storage, collective organisation, ecological risk and producer bargaining power.

social.title: Education after Independence
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Education after independence changed the social geography of Mithila, Vajji and Anga more deeply than the simple multiplication of schools and colleges suggests. In 1947 the region inherited a sharply stratified system: old district schools, a limited college network, Sanskrit and traditional centres of learning, missionary or denominational institutions in some towns, and a vast rural population for whom distance, poverty, gender norms, caste hierarchy and the need for household labour could make sustained schooling difficult. The post-colonial state therefore faced two tasks at once: to extend formal institutions across a densely settled countryside and to turn nominal access into durable participation. The history is not a straight line from illiteracy to schooling. Every stage of expansion exposed a new bottleneck. More primary schools increased entry, but weak learning could block later progress. Secondary expansion made distance and adolescent mobility more important. College growth reduced the need to leave the region for a basic degree, yet specialised study and employment continued to pull students toward Patna, Delhi, Kolkata, Kathmandu and other centres. By the 2020s Bihar possessed a mass school system and one of India’s largest higher-education enrolments, while questions of teacher deployment, learning quality, college density, examination reliability and the value of credentials remained central. Across the Nepal border, Janakpurdham and other Madhesh centres participated in a parallel expansion after Nepal’s political opening of the 1950s, making education another institution through which the cultural region was connected but administratively divided.

social.title: Health and Public-Health Transformation
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Health after independence changed the social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga through a slow but profound transfer of risk from the household toward public institutions. In the middle of the twentieth century, a fever, obstructed labour, snakebite, kala-azar infection or childhood diarrhoea could still become a family catastrophe because diagnosis, transport, blood, trained personnel and medicines were distant or unaffordable. By the mid-2020s, the region possessed a layered network of sub-centres, primary and community facilities, ambulances, medical colleges, vaccination systems, disease-surveillance programmes and publicly financed health schemes. The transformation was real, but it was never uniform. Distance, flood, caste, gender, household income, staffing and the difference between a building and a functioning service continued to shape who received care in time. The history is therefore not simply one of more hospitals. It is the history of public-health capacity: surveillance, vaccination, maternal and child health, nutrition, vector control, clean water, health workers, emergency referral, medical education, insurance and the growing management of chronic disease. It also includes repeated moments when the system’s limits became visible—endemic kala-azar, the 2019 acute encephalitis crisis around Muzaffarpur, recurrent floods, COVID-19, and continuing shortages in specialist care. The region’s health transition must be read as an unfinished institutional achievement in which mortality fell substantially while preventable illness, malnutrition, anaemia and uneven quality remained major social facts.

social.title: Roads, Railways, Electricity and Communications
social.part: Part Ix — Post-1947 / Post-1950 Development
social.summary: Roads, railways, electricity and communications altered the social geography of Mithila, Vajji and Anga after independence by changing what distance meant. The region had always been densely settled and commercially active, but rivers, seasonal flooding, weak all-weather roads, fragmented rail gauges, limited electric supply and slow communication made movement costly and uncertain. A village might be physically close to a town yet effectively distant during the monsoon; a district might lie on a railway map yet remain poorly linked across the Ganga or Kosi; an electrified town could coexist with villages where lighting, irrigation pumping or radio communication remained intermittent. Post-1947 infrastructure history is therefore a history of reducing effective distance rather than merely adding kilometres of road, track, wire and fibre. The transformation occurred in overlapping waves. Major bridges created new north–south corridors; rural roads connected habitations to markets, schools and hospitals; gauge conversion and electrification reorganised rail mobility; household electrification turned electricity from an urban privilege into a mass utility; and telephony moved from scarce landlines to mobile and broadband networks. By the mid-2020s these systems had become interdependent. Roads carried maintenance crews and fibre; electricity powered mobile towers and data centres; phones coordinated buses, migration and emergency care; digital payments changed roadside commerce; and railway reservation became a networked service. Yet the old regional problem did not disappear. Flood damage, bridge congestion, weak maintenance, uneven feeder quality and the digital divide continued to determine whether formal connectivity became reliable everyday access.

social.title: Historical Formation of Caste Relations
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: Caste relations in Mithila, Vajji and Anga were neither an unchanged survival from an ancient textual order nor a purely modern political invention. They were historical institutions repeatedly remade through marriage rules, genealogy, settlement, landholding, tenancy, labour, religious service, literacy, state employment, colonial enumeration, law, education and electoral representation. The same caste name could therefore occupy different economic positions in different districts or even in neighbouring villages, while families within a single caste could diverge sharply in property, education and political influence. A history of caste must reconstruct these changing relations instead of treating ranked labels as sufficient explanation. This chapter provides that longue-durée framework for PART X. It does not replace the focused histories that follow: Dalit experience is treated in Chapter 88; Adivasi and forest-connected populations in Chapter 89; Muslims in Chapter 90; gendered household relations in Chapters 91–93; education and mobility in Chapter 94; reservation and new middle classes in Chapter 95; and rural elites and changing landed power in Chapter 96. Here the task is narrower but foundational: to show how caste became attached to kinship, work, land and state categories, how those attachments changed, and why modern democratic caste identities cannot simply be projected backward into medieval society.

social.title: Dalit Histories
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: Dalit history in Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be written as a footnote to the history of caste. It is a history of labour performed and appropriated, land possessed or denied, neighbourhoods segregated or opened, schools entered late and then used strategically, migration that loosened some village dependencies while creating new urban vulnerabilities, and public cultures through which communities named dignity in their own idioms. The constitutional category “Scheduled Caste” and the political-social term “Dalit” overlap but are not identical. The former is a legal list whose boundaries are defined by constitutional orders; the latter is a language of historical oppression, assertion and solidarity whose use has varied across communities and periods. This chapter therefore keeps legal classification and social self-description analytically distinct. The archive is uneven. Revenue records, censuses, district gazetteers and police or welfare files usually describe Dalit communities through the eyes of officials, landlords, reformers or administrators. They often reduce people to occupation, “custom” or deficit. Oral traditions, songs, village memories, association records, local political histories and post-independence ethnography reveal agency that such documents miss. The task is not to romanticise subaltern testimony or to reject official statistics; it is to read different archives against one another. That method is especially important in a region where Musahar, Ravidas/Chamar, Dusadh/Paswan, Dhobi/Rajak, Dom, Pasi, Chaupal, Nat, Rajwar and other Scheduled-Caste communities followed different demographic, occupational and political trajectories.

social.title: Adivasi and Forest-Connected Populations Where Regionally Relevant
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: Adivasi history enters a history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga unevenly. The plains core of Mithila and Vajji cannot be represented as a continuous forest-tribal zone, while the eastern and south-eastern borderlands of Anga have long been connected to Santal, Paharia and other Adivasi histories through settlement, labour, forest margins, colonial administration and the former Bhagalpur-Santal Parganas geography. Modern district boundaries further complicate the picture: communities, markets and kin networks cross Bihar-Jharkhand and India-Nepal borders that were drawn after many of the relevant social relations had formed. This chapter therefore uses three distinctions throughout. First, Scheduled Tribe is a constitutional and state-specific legal category, not a timeless ethnographic label. Second, forest-connected livelihood does not by itself establish Scheduled-Tribe identity; many non-ST households also depend on commons, grazing, fuelwood, bamboo, river margins and seasonal forest labour. Third, “Adivasi” is a political-historical vocabulary whose meaning can overlap with, but is not identical to, official schedules. The task is to recover the regionally relevant histories without projecting a single tribal frontier across all of Mithila, Vajji and Anga. The demographic and historical weight of Scheduled-Tribe communities varies sharply across the study area. In the central Mithila-Vajji plains, ST populations are generally small and dispersed. In the eastern districts and the Bihar-Jharkhand borderlands, however, Adivasi histories become much more visible. Bhagalpur and Banka are especially important because the nineteenth-century Bhagalpur district once extended into areas later separated as the Santal Parganas, while Purnia and Katihar formed part of a wider eastern frontier of migration, cultivation and labour. A regional history should therefore use a graded map of relevance: strong where settlement and institutions make Adivasi experience structurally important, and restrained where the evidence shows only small or recent populations.

social.title: Muslims of Mithila and Anga
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: The Muslim history of Mithila and Anga cannot be reduced to rulers, demographic percentages or moments of communal conflict. Muslim households entered the region’s social fabric through many routes: military and administrative service, scholarly and Sufi networks, agrarian settlement, artisanal production, trade, transport, migration and ordinary neighbourhood life. By the colonial period, Muslims were present across villages, qasbas and cities in sharply different class positions—from landholders and professionals to cultivators, tenants, weavers, petty traders and labourers. Their languages also varied. Local speech could be Maithili, Angika, Bajjika or other regional vernaculars, while Urdu carried literary, educational and public associations and Persian had earlier served administrative and scholarly worlds. This chapter therefore asks how Muslim social life changed rather than treating “the Muslims” as a single actor. It follows the interaction of religion with land, occupation, biradari, class, gender, education, language and political institutions. It also keeps India and Nepal analytically distinct: the open border connects families and markets, but citizenship, census categories, minority policy and language regimes belong to different states. Episodes of violence—including 1946 in Bihar and 1989 in Bhagalpur—must be confronted directly, yet they cannot be allowed to erase the much longer history of everyday interdependence and shared regional life. Islamic political power reached Bihar through the expansion of north Indian sultanates, while eastern India was also connected to Bengal, riverine commerce and itinerant scholarly and devotional networks. These processes did not transform Mithila or Anga at a single moment. Political authority, tribute, military stations, market towns and rural settlement changed at different speeds. Conversion likewise cannot be inferred from a ruler’s religion. Local Muslim populations were made over generations through settlement, marriage, occupational networks, patronage and religious institutions. A connected history therefore separates political incorporation from demographic and social change.

social.title: Gender and the Household Economy
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: A household is an economic institution before it is a statistical unit. It combines income, food, land, housing, care, credit, consumption, schooling, health expenditure, social obligations and protection against risk. Gender enters each of these domains through unequal claims on time, mobility, property, cash and authority. The relevant history is therefore not a story in which a self-contained ‘family’ slowly gives way to markets. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, households became progressively more entangled with wage migration, banks, ration systems, schools, health services, self-help groups, digital transfers and consumer markets while kinship continued to organise residence, obligation and legitimacy. This chapter analyses the household as a field of provisioning and bargaining. It does not duplicate Chapter 92, which measures women’s paid and unpaid labour in detail, or Chapter 93, which treats marriage, dowry, inheritance and family structure directly. Instead it asks who holds resources, who converts them into daily welfare, how shocks are distributed, how male migration changes managerial responsibility, and how public programmes alter the boundary between household and state. Survey indicators such as ‘female headship,’ joint ownership or participation in decisions are useful but incomplete: they record particular dimensions of authority and cannot by themselves tell us who controls assets, whose consumption is postponed, or who performs the work that keeps the household functioning.

social.title: Women’s Paid and Unpaid Labour
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: Women’s labour is one of the clearest cases in which economic reality exceeds the boundaries of ordinary employment statistics. A woman may transplant paddy, tend cattle, sort makhana, assist a family loom, cook for a work gang, collect water and fuel, care for children and an elderly parent, keep household accounts and participate in a self-help group—all within the same week. Some of those activities generate wages or sales. Some produce goods for household use. Some support a family enterprise without an individual payment. Others reproduce the labour force itself by feeding, cleaning, nursing and caring. A history that counts only the first category systematically understates women’s contribution. This chapter therefore treats paid and unpaid work as connected parts of one labour system. It does not repeat Chapter 91’s analysis of the household as an economic institution, nor Chapter 93’s forthcoming analysis of marriage, dowry, inheritance and family structure. Its narrower question is how women’s work has been organised, measured, rewarded and rendered visible across Mithila, Vajji and Anga, with comparison to Nepal-side Madhesh. The argument is not that all unpaid work is oppression or that all paid work produces autonomy. Rather, remuneration, time control, productivity, social protection, asset ownership and bargaining power must be examined together. Labour statistics require boundaries: who is counted as employed, what reference period is used, whether production is for the market or for own use, and whether assistance to a family enterprise qualifies as economic activity. Women’s activities often sit exactly at these boundaries. A man hired to thresh grain for cash is easily classified as a worker; a woman threshing the household’s own grain, feeding labourers and storing seed may appear partly as a producer and partly as a non-worker depending on the survey concept. The first task of women’s labour history is therefore conceptual: classification is evidence, but it is not the economy itself.

social.title: Marriage, Dowry, Inheritance and Changing Family Structures
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: Marriage is one of the institutions through which social hierarchy becomes household economy. It determines where people live, how labour is pooled, which kin are obligated to whom, how property moves across generations, and how status is displayed or contested. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, marriage has been reshaped by genealogy, caste and religious rules, landholding, education, migration, salaried employment, law, consumer markets and digital communication. None of these forces has replaced the others; they operate together. This chapter follows those changes without collapsing distinct institutions into one narrative. Dowry is separated from women’s own property and from Muslim mahr; statutory inheritance rights are separated from effective possession; civil marriage is separated from the social acceptance of partner choice; and residential household form is separated from the wider network of property and care. The result is a history of changing family relations rather than a catalogue of customs. Marriage in Mithila, Vajji and Anga has historically connected households rather than only individuals. It redistributes labour, residence, land expectations, ceremonial obligations, credit, prestige and care. A marriage can link villages and towns, create durable obligations between affinal kin, reorganise women’s access to natal and marital resources, and alter the labour available to a farm, shop or migrant household. The economic consequences therefore continue long after the wedding. At the same time, the institution is not uniform. Caste, class, religion, landholding, education, occupation and migration shape who marries whom, at what age, with what transfer of resources, and under what post-marital residence. A social history must consequently resist two reductions: marriage cannot be treated as a timeless “custom,” and it cannot be understood only through statute. Its history lies in the interaction between rules, bargaining, household assets, social reputation and individual preference.

social.title: Education and Social Mobility
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: Education changes social history when learning and credentials alter who can enter occupations, migrate, speak to the state, postpone marriage, claim professional authority or imagine a life outside inherited work. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, this process has been neither linear nor equal. The region contains old traditions of Sanskrit, Persian, Urdu and vernacular learning, nineteenth-century colleges, post-independence universities, mass government schooling, welfare hostels, scholarship systems and a contemporary digital education market. Each widened access for some groups while also creating new thresholds of language, examination, finance, information and geography. This chapter therefore asks not whether education expanded—that question was treated institutionally in Chapter 84—but how expansion was converted into mobility. The unit of analysis is the transition: from village to school, primary to secondary, secondary to college, degree to examination, credential to occupation, and one generation’s first educational foothold to the next generation’s accumulated advantage. Caste, gender, class, religion, locality, disability and migration shape every transition. Education can weaken inherited hierarchy, but it can also translate pre-existing resources into new forms of credentialled distinction. Schooling matters socially because it can convert time spent learning into literacy, certification, occupational eligibility and symbolic status. Yet the conversion is conditional. A child needs a school within reach, a household able to release labour time, teachers and materials that produce learning, progression through examinations, and a labour market that values the resulting credential. Families with land, salaried employment, educated relatives or urban residence can support each transition more easily than households dependent on seasonal labour. Education thus opens routes out of inherited occupations while simultaneously rewarding accumulated family resources. Social mobility is best understood as the changing probability that a child can cross these thresholds, not merely as the number of schools built.

social.title: Reservation, Affirmative Action and New Middle Classes
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: Reservation became one of the principal institutions through which the democratic state attempted to alter inherited inequalities in education, public employment and representation. In Bihar this history is unusually layered. Scheduled-Caste and Scheduled-Tribe safeguards intersected with backward-class commissions, the Karpoori Thakur formula, Mandal politics, a statutory division between Extremely Backward Classes and Backward Classes, women’s and other horizontal reservations, local-government quotas, welfare hostels, scholarships, examination support and, later, an Economically Weaker Sections quota. Across the border, Nepal developed a different but comparable inclusion system in which Madhesi representation became part of civil-service and federal-democratic reform. This chapter is not a legal digest and does not assume that a reserved seat automatically produces equality. Its historical question is how affirmative action changed pathways into education, bureaucracy, teaching, policing, technical employment, elected local office and professional life, and how these pathways helped create new salaried, credentialled and politically connected middle strata among communities previously weakly represented in state institutions. It also asks who remained outside these gains, why intra-category inequality became a recurring political question, and how the shrinking relative weight of secure public employment changed the meaning of reservation itself. The Constitution abolished untouchability and prohibited discrimination while also permitting special measures for historically disadvantaged groups. Article 16(4) allowed reservation in public employment for backward classes not adequately represented in state services; the First Amendment of 1951 inserted Article 15(4), enabling special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes as well as Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The resulting framework did not erase caste from public life. It moved caste into a new institutional language of backwardness, representation, equality and state responsibility. In Bihar, where access to education and administration had long been socially concentrated, these provisions created a constitutional route through which groups could demand a share in the modern state.

social.title: Rural Elites, Political Economy and Changing Landed Power
social.part: Part X — Caste, Class, Gender And Social Change
social.summary: Rural power in Mithila, Vajji and Anga has never been reducible to acreage alone. Before independence, large estates, subordinate tenures, rent collection, credit, caste standing and access to officials could be concentrated in the same hands. After independence the legal architecture changed radically: intermediary interests were abolished, Bhoodan sought voluntary redistribution, ceiling legislation authorised acquisition of surplus land, electoral democracy widened political competition, and later panchayat reservation opened local office to groups formerly excluded from formal authority. Yet power did not simply disappear with zamindari. It was converted. Families and groups that could combine land with schooling, political office, cooperative control, contracts, market brokerage, salaried employment, remittances and command over land records often remained influential even when holdings were fragmented. This chapter therefore studies rural elites as changing coalitions of resources rather than as a fixed caste or landlord category. It asks how older landed families adapted; how cultivating and backward-caste leaders rose; how labour migration altered dependence; why tiny operational holdings coexist with intense struggles over homestead and roadside land; how panchayats, PACS, procurement, welfare schemes and construction contracts created new forms of brokerage; and why the current digitisation and resurvey of land records may redistribute informational power without automatically settling social conflict. The Nepal-side Mithila comparison shows a related but distinct trajectory under the Lands Act of 1964 and subsequent federalisation.

social.title: The Longue Durée of Migration
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: Migration is not a late disturbance imposed on a formerly immobile society. Across Mithila, Vajji, Anga and the adjoining Nepal plains, mobility has repeatedly connected household survival, scholarship, pilgrimage, military and administrative service, trade, marriage, cultivation and wage labour. What changed over the longue durée was not the existence of movement but its scale, duration, destinations, transport technologies, labour regimes and relationship to household reproduction. The same village could generate a scholar travelling to a court, a bride moving through a marriage network, a boatman following a river market, a seasonal labourer entering a harvest circuit and, much later, a construction worker cycling between a Bihar village and a metropolitan worksite. These movements cannot be collapsed into one category, yet together they make migration a central social institution rather than an appendix to regional history. This opening chapter of PART XI therefore establishes the historical grammar of migration before later chapters examine particular destination systems: Kolkata, Delhi and Mumbai, Punjab and Haryana, the Nepal–India corridor, Gulf migration, remittances, urbanisation, informal economies and diaspora institutions. The argument is deliberately cautious. Ancient and medieval evidence often records routes, travellers, traders, monks, scholars and marriage alliances rather than statistically measurable migrant populations; colonial and modern censuses, by contrast, classify place of birth, last residence and reason for movement. A responsible longue-durée history must use each type of evidence for what it can actually show, without projecting the categories of the 2011 Census backwards into periods that organised mobility differently.

social.title: Calcutta/Kolkata and Mithila–Anga Migration
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: Calcutta was one of the first great external cities to become woven into the ordinary reproduction of households in Mithila, Vajji and Anga. The connection did not arise from one recruitment drive or one industry. It accumulated through river traffic, the East India Company capital, railways, jute mills, docks, warehouses, carts and rickshaws, construction, domestic and hotel service, petty trade, clerical work and later professional employment. A worker could be physically hundreds of kilometres from home while remaining economically and socially embedded in a village through remittances, return journeys, marriage obligations, land, debt and kinship. The result was a distinctive bi-local social formation. Calcutta could function as an urban labour market, a training ground, a political arena and a source of cash without necessarily becoming the migrant’s permanent home. This chapter reconstructs that layered corridor while avoiding two simplifications: not every north-Indian worker in Calcutta came from the present study districts, and not every migrant from Mithila or Anga entered the jute mills. The evidence is strongest when city labour histories, railway history, census migration tables, district gazetteers and oral-life histories are read together. For households in north and east Bihar, the importance of Calcutta lay not only in settlement but in repeatability. A city becomes part of a rural economy when routes are known, employers or contractors are identifiable, lodging can be arranged through prior migrants, and wages can be carried or remitted home. These conditions emerged unevenly from the nineteenth century onward. Some men stayed for years; others returned for harvests, marriages or illness; still others shifted between occupations within the metropolitan region. The analytical unit is therefore the corridor linking home and destination rather than the city alone. This perspective also explains why migration could remain socially conservative in some respects—supporting land, marriage and household obligations at home—while simultaneously exposing migrants to industrial discipline, urban politics, new skills and wider social networks.

social.title: Delhi, Mumbai and Post-Independence Mobility
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: After independence, migration from Mithila, Vajji and Anga ceased to be organised mainly around a small number of older eastern corridors. Calcutta/Kolkata remained important, but Delhi and Mumbai entered household migration strategies with growing force. The two metropolitan systems were not interchangeable. Delhi was closer by rail, located within the broad Hindi linguistic zone and increasingly surrounded by a National Capital Region of construction sites, workshops, warehouses and service jobs. Mumbai was farther away, more expensive to inhabit and embedded in a different linguistic and industrial history, yet its manufacturing, construction, transport, hospitality and informal-service economy created durable opportunities for migrants willing to bear higher entry and housing costs. The central historical change was therefore a widening of the mobility map. Households that had once depended on one destination could now compare wages, recruitment chains, travel time, housing, risk and the availability of relatives or co-villagers across several cities. This chapter follows that post-independence diversification without treating every migrant as a permanent settler or every movement as an escape from agriculture. Metropolitan work often remained part of a bi-local household economy in which earnings, care, land, debt, schooling and social obligations were distributed across source and destination. The following chapters will separately examine Punjab and Haryana, Nepal–India circulation, the Gulf, remittances, urbanisation and diaspora institutions.

social.title: Punjab, Haryana and Seasonal Agricultural Labour
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: The migration of agricultural labour from Bihar to Punjab and Haryana is one of the clearest examples of how India’s uneven regional development created a labour market across distant rural worlds. The corridor did not arise because rural people suddenly abandoned agriculture for the city. It grew because the Green Revolution intensified farming in north-western India at the same time that large parts of eastern India continued to contain small holdings, irregular employment and lower cash wages. Workers from Mithila, Vajji and Anga could therefore move from one agrarian economy to another, work during a narrow peak season, and return with earnings that mattered far beyond the number of days spent at the destination. The history is not a simple story of a fixed stream from “Bihar” to “Punjab.” Different districts entered at different times; workers moved through kin, village and contractor networks; some combined Punjab with Delhi, Rajasthan or other destinations; and the labour demand itself changed as combines, direct-seeded rice and mechanical transplanters spread. Haryana shared much of the rice-wheat ecology but had its own crop patterns, mechanisation levels and urban-industrial alternatives. Chapter 100 therefore treats seasonal agricultural migration as an evolving institution: a system made by crop calendars, wage differentials, railways, recruitment networks, class relations, state regulation, water stress, mechanisation and household strategies at both ends of the journey.

social.title: Nepal–India Circular Migration
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: The India–Nepal border is international in law but unusually permeable in everyday social life. In the Mithila–Madhesh and Anga-facing borderlands, households have long treated the line not only as a frontier of two states but also as a corridor linking labour markets, marriage fields, pilgrimages, schools, hospitals, bazaars and transport nodes. Chapter 101 therefore uses circular migration in a deliberately broad sense: repeated movement in which a person or household remains materially and socially connected to more than one locality, and in which return is built into the migration strategy even when individual spells become long. The 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship did not create these cross-border ties from nothing. It institutionalised an older geography shaped by the nineteenth-century boundary, shared languages, kinship and commercial routes. Article 7 is especially important because it committed the two governments, on a reciprocal basis, to grant nationals of the other country privileges concerning residence, ownership of property, participation in trade and commerce, movement and related matters. In practice the relationship has always been more complex than treaty text alone: national laws differ, documentation requirements vary by activity, and mobility becomes more regulated when it intersects with formal employment, banking, vehicles, customs or travel to third countries. The Sugauli settlement of 1816 fixed a political boundary across a landscape whose markets, pilgrimage routes, caste networks and marriage relations did not end at the new line. In the eastern and central Tarai, movement between today’s Nepal and Bihar continued through local fairs, seasonal farm work, cattle and grain trade, religious journeys and household visits. This historical background matters because later migration did not begin with an isolated economic ‘push’ from Nepal or a single ‘pull’ from India. It developed inside a borderland in which people already possessed route knowledge, linguistic competence and kin contacts on both sides. The resulting mobility could be extremely local—a few kilometres to a market or field—or extend from the border to Patna, Kolkata, Delhi and other Indian destinations. The political boundary therefore reorganised jurisdiction more decisively than it reorganised everyday social geography.

social.title: Gulf Migration
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: Gulf migration extended the mobility repertoire of Mithila, Vajji and Anga beyond the internal corridors described in Chapters 97–101. From the oil-boom decades onward, employment in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain offered a different combination of distance, earnings, risk and household strategy. The journey demanded passports, visas, contracts, recruitment payments and air travel rather than the railway ticket and village contact that often organised internal migration. Because the initial cost was higher and the legal distance greater, overseas work could generate larger cash remittances but also heavier debt, stronger dependence on intermediaries and sharper consequences when a contract failed. The history must be written with care because official data illuminate only part of the corridor. India’s emigration-clearance system records workers in categories that require clearance; it does not count every Indian employed in the Gulf. This distinction is crucial for Bihar. Ministry of External Affairs data show 89,127 emigration clearances for Bihar in 2025, the highest annual figure in the 2016–2025 series, but the number is not a census of all Bihari migrants abroad. District-level data likewise reveal striking differences inside the study region while capturing only the regulated ECR segment. The chapter therefore combines administrative evidence with a household-history approach and gives parallel attention to Nepal’s much more remittance-dependent overseas labour system.

social.title: Remittances and Household Transformation
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: Migration changes a household only when earnings are converted into transfers, decisions and assets. A remittance is therefore more than money crossing distance. It is the mechanism by which labour performed in Kolkata, Delhi, Mumbai, Punjab, the Nepal–India corridor or the Gulf enters the food budget, school fees, medical treatment, debt ledger, house, field, marriage account and savings decisions of a household in Mithila, Vajji, Anga or Madhesh. The transfer can be monthly or irregular, formal or hand-carried, small or transformative. Its meaning depends on who sends it, who receives it, which obligation is paid first and what would have happened without it. The evidence also demands caution. Bihar’s strongest nationally comparable household-remittance evidence still includes older NSS rounds, while village studies provide richer mechanisms but are not representative of an entire region. Nepal offers more recent nationally representative evidence through the Nepal Living Standards Survey 2022/23. These sources are not interchangeable. Used together, however, they show a common pattern: remittances often stabilise everyday consumption first, while education, health, debt repayment, housing, land, savings and small investment compete for the remainder. Household transformation is therefore incremental, uneven and deeply shaped by class, gender and migration cost. A migrant’s wage becomes historically significant at origin through the amount actually transferred and the claims organised around it. Households can treat migration as a portfolio strategy: one member earns elsewhere while others maintain land, children, elderly relatives and local social membership. Remittances allow this spatial division of labour to persist. They can smooth consumption in lean agricultural months, finance emergency care and reduce dependence on local moneylenders, but they can also become the income stream against which new debt or consumption is planned. The key unit of analysis is therefore not the migrant alone but the household balance sheet connecting destination earnings, transfer costs, origin expenditure and future obligations.

social.title: Urbanisation
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: Urbanisation in Mithila, Vajji and Anga is not adequately described by the growth of a few municipal populations. It is a transformation of the settlement system: villages acquire markets, schools, clinics, banks, transport stands and non-farm employment; district headquarters extend into peri-urban fringes; railway and highway corridors generate ribbon development; remittance-funded houses alter land use; and people commute daily between places that remain administratively ‘rural’ and places legally designated ‘urban’. The historical question is therefore how functions, densities, infrastructures and social relations become urban, not simply how many persons reside inside a municipal boundary. Measurement requires unusual caution in 2026. India’s last completed population census remains the 2011 Census; Census 2027 is under way in phases, but population enumeration for most of India is scheduled for February 2027. Accordingly, this chapter uses 2011 as the last nationally comparable Indian demographic baseline and treats later municipal notifications, infrastructure programmes and visible built-up expansion as evidence of institutional change rather than as substitutes for a new census urbanisation rate. Nepal provides a more recent 2021 census, but there too administrative municipality status and morphology-based urban classification produce very different pictures, especially in Madhesh. Urban growth can occur through natural increase, rural-to-urban migration, reclassification of settlements, expansion of municipal boundaries and the conversion of agricultural land at the urban edge. Conversely, many migrants from the study region move to Delhi, Kolkata or the Gulf without increasing the population of a local town. A regional history must therefore separate three processes: urban population growth, the spread of urban functions, and outward migration. Their interaction explains why a region can remain statistically weakly urbanised while its villages become deeply tied to urban labour, consumption, finance and communications.

social.title: Informal Economies and Street Commerce
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: The streets, station approaches, haats, bus stands, hospital gates, school corridors, neighbourhood crossings and peri-urban roads of Mithila, Vajji and Anga sustain a dense economy that conventional city histories often understate. Street vending is only its most visible layer. The wider informal economy includes own-account retail, food preparation, repair, transport services, loading, recycling, home-based production, petty contracting, domestic services and tiny workshops whose transactions may be legal and socially indispensable even when the enterprise is unincorporated, weakly registered or outside standard employment protections. Informality therefore describes an institutional condition, not a moral category. This chapter follows the historical movement from periodic markets and mobile petty trade to contemporary urban and peri-urban commerce. It treats public space, credit, transport, migration, household labour and municipal regulation as parts of one system. Current statistics are used cautiously: a self-employed worker is not necessarily a street vendor, an unincorporated enterprise is not necessarily unregistered, and informal employment can exist inside a formally registered enterprise. These distinctions are essential if the region’s everyday economy is to be reconstructed without collapsing different forms of work into a single residual category. An enterprise may be lawful yet small, unincorporated, family-run and only partly registered; a worker may hold an informal job inside a formal establishment; and a street vendor may possess a certificate while still lacking stable social protection. Conversely, an activity can violate a specific zoning, licensing or traffic rule without making the worker’s livelihood intrinsically criminal. Historical analysis should therefore separate legal status, registration, employment protection, tax treatment, premises and access to public space. The category “informal” is useful only when the institutional dimension being described is made explicit.

social.title: Diaspora Cultural Institutions
social.part: Part Xi — Migration, Urbanisation And Diaspora
social.summary: Migration does not automatically create a diaspora community. People may share an origin yet remain dispersed across workplaces, neighbourhoods, languages, classes and generations. A cultural institution is one of the mechanisms that converts this dispersion into a recurring public: an association, literary circle, festival committee, religious or welfare group, arts collective, publication, digital forum, student network or community centre that gives regular form to belonging. For migrants from Mithila, Vajji and Anga, and for Maithili-speaking populations moving within Nepal and across the India–Nepal border, such institutions have repeatedly carried language, ritual, literature, performance and mutual aid into places where these practices were no longer sustained by the density of the home locality. The history is therefore more than a list of organisations. Institutions alter culture while preserving it. A festival moved from village or town to Delhi, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Kathmandu, the Gulf or North America must be rescheduled around work calendars, rented venues and municipal rules; songs are shortened for stage programmes; food is cooked for large heterogeneous audiences; children may understand but not speak the ancestral language; and digital media may become more important than a permanent building. This chapter examines those transformations as part of the migration system traced in Chapters 97–105. A migrant population can remain socially fragmented for years. What turns common origin into collective life is repetition: the same families meet again for a festival, a literary evening, a condolence fund, a student welcome, a language class or a relief appeal. Repetition creates expectations; expectations create committees, membership lists, accounts, venues and calendars. At that point memory becomes institutional. This distinction matters historically because the existence of migrants in a city does not prove the existence of an organised diaspora. The historian must identify the mechanisms by which networks acquired names, rules, officers, publications, property, bank accounts, digital archives or recognised annual programmes.

social.title: Maithili Print and Literary Institutions
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Print did not create Maithili literature. It changed the material conditions under which literature could be copied, standardised, debated, sold, archived and made visible to readers who were not gathered in the same court, school, household or manuscript circle. That distinction is essential for a socio-cultural-economic history. The transition from manuscript to print was not a clean replacement of one technology by another, and the modern literary public was not produced by presses alone. Editors, patrons, subscription networks, literary associations, schools, universities, academies, prizes, libraries, bookshops, distributors and later digital platforms all helped determine which texts circulated, which spellings became normal, which genres acquired prestige and which writers entered the historical record. The modern Maithili field also developed across more than one political geography. Darbhanga, Madhubani and Patna were important, but so were Varanasi, Jaipur, Kolkata, Delhi and other cities in which mobile Maithils created print networks. Nepal supplied its own institutional centres in Janakpur, the Madhesh towns and Kathmandu. The result was a cross-border literary system in which a magazine, book, award, conference or digital archive could acquire meaning far beyond its place of publication. This chapter therefore studies print and literary institutions as social infrastructure: organisations and technologies that convert writing into a recurring public, while also producing exclusions, hierarchies and disputes over language, script, region and canon.

social.title: Angika Print and Literary Institutions
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Angika literary modernity cannot be reconstructed by starting from a list of organisations and projecting their categories backward. The speech forms now grouped under the name Angika long preceded the institutions that printed, classified and taught them. Modern print changed something different: it created repeatable editions, editorial norms, periodical rhythms, bibliographies, institutional offices and archives through which a regional literary field could recognise itself and argue about its boundaries. That field developed under unequal conditions. Angika has a vigorous corpus of poetry, drama, fiction, folklore, grammar, lexicography and criticism, yet its publishing market has generally been smaller and less securely institutionalised than those of major scheduled languages. Bhagalpur became the principal modern node, but Banka, Munger, the wider Anga region, the Santhal Pargana belt, Patna, metropolitan migrant centres and later the internet all contributed. The history is therefore best read as an ecology of editors, small presses, associations, universities, academies, newspapers, performers, collectors and digital volunteers rather than as a single institutional lineage. A rigorous history must distinguish linguistic antiquity, regional memory and modern publication. Oral songs, narrative cycles, ritual repertoires, proverbs and local speech obviously existed before modern Angika books and journals. At the same time, claims that a particular ancient or early-medieval text is straightforwardly 'Angika' require period-specific linguistic argument rather than geographical association with ancient Anga alone. Print history offers firmer chronological ground because editions, title pages, publishers, issue numbers and institutional records can often be dated. This chapter therefore begins with verifiable modern publishing and institutional evidence while treating older attributions as a separate philological problem.

social.title: Radio and Broadcasting
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Radio changed the scale and temporality of public culture in Mithila, Vajji and Anga. Print required a physical copy and a reader; broadcasting could carry a voice, song, agricultural advisory, drama, news bulletin or political speech across many households at once. Yet the existence of a transmitter did not create a single regional public. Reception depended on signal strength, electricity or batteries, receiver ownership, listening time, language choice, gendered control of household space and the station’s editorial decisions. Radio therefore belongs to social and economic history as much as to media history: it reorganised cultural labour, created new professions, altered the circulation of music and speech, and made the state audibly present in everyday life. The regional story is also transborder and technologically layered. Akashvani stations at Patna, Bhagalpur and Darbhanga formed different nodes in the Indian public-service system, while Radio Nepal and the later explosion of FM stations created another broadcasting ecology across Madhesh and Kathmandu. Maithili, Angika, Bajjika, Hindi, Nepali, Urdu, Sanskrit, Santhali and other languages shared frequencies and institutional space rather than occupying sealed territories. Medium wave, FM, cassette recording, satellite distribution, mobile streaming and on-demand audio did not simply replace one another. They accumulated. This chapter therefore reconstructs broadcasting as an institutional chain linking language politics, public service, cultural performance, labour, technology, listening practices and preservation. A printed page can travel slowly and be reread; radio’s distinctive power is that many separated listeners can hear the same scheduled event at approximately the same time. This simultaneity mattered for morning news, weather, agricultural advice, devotional music, festival coverage and emergency communication. It also created ritualised listening habits around programme schedules. In a region where mobility, flood disruption and uneven literacy shaped access to information, the spoken broadcast could cross some barriers that print could not. But simultaneity should not be confused with equality. Reception varied by distance from the transmitter, quality of the set, atmospheric conditions and whether a household could control the time and place of listening.

social.title: Cinema, Video and Recorded Performance
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Cinema and recorded performance transformed regional culture in a different way from radio. Broadcasting organised a schedule around a transmitter; moving images and recordings created objects that could be replayed, copied, sold, carried across borders and watched outside the moment of performance. For Mithila, Vajji and Anga, the history therefore cannot be reduced to a list of feature films. It includes cinema halls, itinerant screenings, film songs, studio recordings, cassettes, VHS, VCD and DVD circulation, filmed theatre and dance, wedding and ritual video, television-derived video, documentary practice, festival circuits, mobile-phone viewing, YouTube channels and digital archives. These media altered performance itself because artists increasingly performed for cameras as well as for physically present audiences. The region also exposes a recurring paradox of small-language media. Maithili possesses a long literary and performance tradition and a transborder speech community, yet its feature-film sector has remained intermittent; Angika film production has been still more weakly institutionalised. At the same time, audio-visual culture in both language zones is abundant when one counts songs, stage recordings, devotional video, comedy, interviews, documentaries and online performance. The historical problem is therefore not cultural scarcity but the uneven conversion of cultural production into a stable industrial system of finance, distribution, exhibition, rights management and preservation. This chapter reconstructs that wider moving-image economy and treats preservation failure as part of the history itself.

social.title: Newspapers and Public Debate
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Newspapers created a distinctive arena of public life because they turned events, arguments and institutional claims into serial, datable objects that could circulate beyond a meeting, court, market or village. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, however, the newspaper cannot be separated neatly from the literary magazine. Early Maithili periodicals carried essays, letters, language debates, social reform, institutional proceedings and current affairs beside poetry and fiction. Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, Nepali and English newspapers also shaped the region’s public sphere, often reaching far larger readerships than Maithili or Angika publications. The history of newspapers is therefore multilingual and institutional: it concerns printers, patrons, editors, correspondents, distributors, advertisers, readers, associations and archives as much as individual articles. This chapter treats the press neither as a transparent record of society nor as a simple vehicle of modernisation. Newspapers select; their readerships are socially uneven; advertising and patronage affect survival; editors establish thresholds of relevance; and political or social movements attempt to make themselves visible through print. Yet precisely because newspapers are selective, they provide unusually rich evidence for the history of public argument. Editorials, correspondence columns, reports, subscription appeals, obituaries, advertisements, election news and corrections reveal what institutions considered debatable and which groups could gain a printed voice. The task is to reconstruct both the debate and the conditions under which that debate entered print. Every issue is the result of decisions about what counts as news, which language to use, whose statement is credible, how much space an item deserves and whether it should appear as report, editorial, advertisement or letter. These categories matter historically. A flood report written from a district headquarters is different from a village letter describing relief failure; an association resolution is different from an editor’s endorsement of it. Researchers should therefore record genre, placement and authorship rather than extracting sentences as free-standing facts. The newspaper becomes most valuable when read simultaneously as evidence about an event and evidence about the institution that framed the event.

social.title: Sahitya Akademi, Academies and Institutional Canon Formation
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Literary institutions do more than honour books after they have been written. They create recurring procedures through which manuscripts become editions, editions become eligible books, books become award candidates, authors become representatives of a language, and selected works enter libraries, syllabi, translation circuits and public memory. In that sense an academy is not merely a building or a committee. It is a mechanism for allocating attention. The effect can be constructive: preservation, publication, translation, grants, seminars and recognition can sustain a language whose commercial book market is limited. But the same mechanism is necessarily selective. Every list of awardees, prescribed texts, invited speakers or funded publications also leaves other writers, genres, regions and forms outside the frame. For Mithila, Vajji, Anga and Madhesh, canon formation therefore has to be studied institutionally rather than treated as a self-evident ranking of literary merit. Sahitya Akademi, the Bihar Maithili Academy, universities, examining bodies, Nepal Academy, literary associations, journals, publishers and digital archives operate at different scales and under different rules. Their decisions overlap but are not identical. Maithili is especially revealing because Sahitya Akademi began giving its annual award in the language in 1966, long before Maithili entered the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India in 2004. Literary recognition, constitutional recognition and administrative support thus followed different chronologies. This chapter reconstructs those chronologies while asking a larger question: how does institutional recognition turn a changing literary field into a teachable, prizeable and apparently stable canon?

social.title: Women Writers and Alternative Literary Publics
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Women’s writing cannot be reconstructed by beginning with prize lists and then working backward. In Mithila, Vajji, Anga and Madhesh, women participated in literary culture through a much wider range of forms: household storytelling, songs attached to marriage and ritual, letters, diaries, memoir, school and association writing, periodicals, fiction, translation, performance, painting-linked narrative, radio and recorded speech, and now digital publication. Some of these forms were signed and published; others circulated collectively or survived only because someone later recorded them. A social history of literary modernity must therefore ask not only which women became authors in the formal sense, but which channels allowed women’s words, narratives and interpretations to acquire an audience. The phrase ‘alternative literary publics’ is used here for spaces of circulation that coexist with, precede, challenge or bypass the most prestigious institutions of literature. They include women-only storytelling settings, little magazines, local associations, children’s literature, translation networks, public readings, diaspora groups and digital archives. These are not automatically emancipatory spaces, and ‘women writers’ are not a single social bloc: caste, class, religion, education, rural or urban location, language repertoire and national citizenship all shape access. The task is to reconstruct changing infrastructures of voice without reducing women either to victims of exclusion or to symbolic exceptions whose visibility is mistaken for equality.

social.title: Videha and Digital Literary Culture
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Videha is useful to social and cultural history not simply because it publishes Maithili literature online, but because its development exposes the infrastructures required to make a small-language literary public durable on the web. A digital journal must repeatedly solve problems that print can hide inside established institutions: how writers submit work, how issues acquire dates and sequence, how old material remains findable, how scripts render across devices, how audio and images are preserved, how readers learn that a new issue exists, how mobile users navigate, how disabled readers gain access, and how a publication survives changes in hosting, browsers and platforms. The history of Videha is therefore also a history of digital maintenance, editorial labour and vernacular technological adaptation. This chapter treats Videha as a case study rather than as a self-validating success narrative. Many claims about firsts, totals and institutional milestones originate in Videha’s own pages, announcements and retrospectives; they are valuable primary sources for institutional self-understanding but should be independently corroborated when priority matters. The strongest evidence lies where different traces converge: dated issue pages, serial announcements, archived copies, bibliographic records, repository histories and surviving tools. This source-critical approach also clarifies an apparent chronological ambiguity. The present site identifies Videha as ‘Since 2000’; a retrospective describes the venture beginning in 2000, an extant web presence from 5 July 2004, and a numbered fortnightly issue sequence beginning on 1 January 2008. These dates describe different phases of one born-digital institution rather than requiring a single artificial founding date.

social.title: Digital Archives and Cultural Preservation
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: Digital preservation changes the scale at which the social and cultural history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga can be reconstructed. Manuscripts dispersed among families, institutional records, fragile newspapers, cassette recordings, photographs, field notes, performance video and born-digital literary material can now be copied and connected without physically gathering every original in one repository. But the possibility of copying also creates a dangerous illusion: a scan on a website is not automatically an archive, and a file on a hard disk is not automatically preserved. This chapter therefore treats digital preservation as an institutional process joining conservation, selection, description, technical integrity, rights, access and long-term stewardship. It uses official archival initiatives in India and Nepal as comparative evidence while keeping the regional problem in view: the materials needed for Mithila–Vajji–Anga history are scattered across public institutions, private collections, religious establishments, periodicals, performance communities and transborder networks. The durable objective is not merely to digitise more objects, but to make their provenance, relationships and future intelligibility survive changes of software, storage and institutions. Digitisation creates a digital representation of an analogue object; preservation keeps a trustworthy representation usable across time. A manuscript photographed once may become easier to consult immediately, yet the photographs can still be lost through disk failure, account closure, corrupted files, obsolete formats or missing metadata. Preservation therefore begins where one-time scanning ends. The National Mission for Manuscripts has long joined documentation and conservation to digitisation, while the National Archives of India’s mass-digitisation programme explicitly couples online access with preservation of physical and digitised records. The distinction is essential for regional archives because copying without stewardship can multiply files while leaving cultural evidence just as vulnerable.

social.title: Unicode, Tirhuta and Technological Recognition
social.part: Part Xii — Cultural Modernity And Mass Media
social.summary: The technological history of Maithili cannot be reduced to the arrival of computers or the spread of mobile phones. For a language with a historic script, the decisive question is whether text can be represented as text rather than merely displayed as pictures of letters. Tirhuta, also called Mithilakshara and Maithili script, illustrates the difference. Before standard encoding, users could design attractive fonts and produce print or PDF pages, yet the underlying data often depended on private mappings to Latin, Devanagari or other code positions. Such material could look correct on one machine while remaining unsearchable, unexchangeable and fragile. Unicode recognition changed the conditions of possibility by assigning stable identities to Tirhuta characters, but it did not automatically create fonts, keyboards, literacy, software support or archives. This chapter therefore treats Unicode encoding as one stage in a longer chain of technological recognition. The official Unicode block for Tirhuta occupies U+11480–U+114DF, and the script entered the Unicode Standard in Version 7.0 in 2014. The mature encoding proposal prepared by Anshuman Pandey documented both the script’s historical independence and contemporary digital use, including periodical production in Tirhuta and the limitations of legacy encodings. The proposal itself is a valuable historical document because it records a moment when a regional writing tradition had already entered desktop publishing but had not yet obtained interoperable plain-text representation. The history after encoding is equally important: fonts, shaping engines, keyboards, web standards, converters, teaching and preservation determine whether encoded characters become a living digital medium.

social.title: Demographic Structure and Population Change
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: PART XIII begins with demography because the contemporary economy of Mithila, Vajji and Anga is built on population structure: the number of people, their age distribution, household organisation, sex composition, education, mobility and settlement pattern. High population density can intensify pressure on agricultural land and public services, but it can also create deep labour markets, dense commercial networks and large consumer demand. A young population may offer a demographic dividend only when education, health and productive employment expand at comparable speed. Migration may remove workers from local labour markets while simultaneously sustaining households through remittances. Demography therefore belongs inside economic history rather than in a statistical appendix. The central methodological difficulty is geographical. Modern censuses enumerate states, provinces, districts, sub-districts, municipalities, villages and households; they do not enumerate a single administrative unit called ‘Mithila–Vajji–Anga’. The historical-cultural regions overlap present-day Bihar and Nepal and have changed in meaning and boundary over time. This chapter consequently works with layered evidence rather than pretending that a fixed modern boundary can be projected backwards. For India, the last completed population census remains Census 2011 while Census 2027 is under way with a reference date of 1 March 2027. For Nepal, the 2021 census provides a more recent complete enumeration. Surveys such as NFHS add fertility, health and household indicators, but they are samples, not substitutes for a census.

social.title: Agriculture in the Twenty-First Century
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Agriculture remains the largest spatial system of the contemporary economy of Mithila, Vajji and Anga even where its share of measured income has fallen. Fields, orchards, ponds, wetlands, livestock, irrigation channels, farm roads, wholesale markets and seasonal labour networks organize rural life and connect villages to towns. The twenty-first-century agricultural question is therefore not whether the region is becoming ‘less agricultural’ in a simple sense, but how farming is being recomposed under small holdings, migration, mechanisation, rising input costs, changing diets, expanding roads and markets, and recurrent climate shocks. A household may cultivate rice and wheat, lease additional land, sell milk, send a member to Delhi or the Gulf, hire a combine, and market vegetables through a trader. Such a household is simultaneously agricultural, migrant, service-using and market-dependent. The regional frame requires the same caution established in Chapter 117. Mithila, Vajji and Anga are historical-cultural regions rather than current statistical units. Agriculture must be reconstructed from district, block, crop, irrigation, livestock and market evidence rather than from a fabricated single regional total. Bihar’s official agricultural statistics provide the main Indian baseline; Nepal’s agricultural statistics are needed for the Madhesh side of the transborder economy. The Fourth Agriculture Roadmap of Bihar, launched for 2023–28, places sustainability, soil health, water conservation, climate resilience, organic inputs, horticulture and allied activities within a single policy framework. This chapter uses that framework critically: policy targets show intended direction, while farm structure and risk determine what is feasible on the ground.

social.title: Land Fragmentation and Rural Livelihoods
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Land fragmentation is one of the central structural facts of the contemporary rural economy of Mithila, Vajji and Anga. Yet the phrase is often used too loosely. A household may own very little land but hold it in one compact parcel; another may operate a somewhat larger area scattered across several plots. These conditions create different costs and opportunities. This chapter therefore separates four concepts: ownership, operational holding, parcel fragmentation and livelihood dependence on land. Only after those distinctions are made can the relationship between land and poverty, migration, mechanisation, tenancy, women’s rights, land records and rural enterprise be analysed clearly. The Indian side of the region must be read against Bihar’s unusually small farm structure. The Agriculture Census 2015–16 recorded 91.21 percent of operational holdings in Bihar below one hectare and another 5.75 percent between one and two hectares; the average operated area was 0.39 hectare. These are dated structural baselines, not 2026 measurements, because the next agricultural census does not yet provide an equally complete public state-level replacement. They nonetheless show why rural livelihoods cannot be understood through crop income alone. The land base is typically too small to support a household without livestock, wage work, migration, public employment, self-employment or transfers. On the Nepal side, the National Sample Census of Agriculture 2021/22 provides a more recent direct measure of parcel fragmentation. Madhesh Province reported 738,340 holdings divided into 2,174,798 parcels, an average of 2.9 parcels per holding; Saptari averaged 3.3 parcels, and Siraha and Dhanusha 3.4 each. The cross-border comparison is valuable because it demonstrates that fragmentation is not simply an artefact of one state’s land administration. It is produced by long-term inheritance, demographic pressure, land markets, settlement history and the social value of retaining claims to land across the Gangetic–Terai plain.

social.title: Migration-dependent Economies
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Migration-dependent economies are economies in which household reproduction, local consumption, labour markets and investment are materially shaped by earnings generated outside the place of origin. This is more specific than saying that a region has many migrants. In large parts of Mithila, Vajji and Anga, migration has become a recurring institution linking villages and small towns to distant labour markets while families, land claims and social obligations remain anchored at home. The result is not simple depopulation. It is a multi-local economy in which labour circulates, money and information return, and household decisions are made across two or more places. The evidence must be handled historically. Bihar’s 2019–20 Economic Survey described the state as labour-surplus and noted long-standing migration to other Indian states and foreign countries. Earlier NSS and longitudinal village surveys recorded extensive out-migration and remittance receipt, but their numerical estimates belong to their own survey years and should not be presented as current 2026 rates. More recent administrative systems such as e-Shram and One Nation One Ration Card improve visibility and portability for mobile workers, but they are not direct substitutes for a migration census. On the Nepal side, the 2021 population census and the 2022/23 Living Standards Survey provide newer benchmarks for absence abroad and remittance dependence in Madhesh Province. This chapter therefore focuses on the economic architecture of mobility: why workers leave, how corridors are organized, who remains behind, how destination wages influence origin labour markets, how skills and enterprises circulate, and how risks are distributed. Chapter 121 will examine remittance use, consumption and housing in greater detail. Keeping the two questions separate prevents a common analytical error: treating every consequence of migration as a consequence of remittance spending alone.

social.title: Remittances, Consumption and Housing
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 120 examined migration as a labour-market system. This chapter turns to what happens after earnings move back toward the household. Remittances are neither a single-purpose transfer nor a transparent measure of prosperity. A payment received from Delhi, Punjab, Gujarat, Maharashtra, the Gulf or another destination may be used in the same month for grain, school fees, medicine, a loan instalment and bricks. The analytical task is therefore to reconstruct allocation over time rather than force every rupee into a rigid consumption-versus-investment category. The evidence for Mithila, Vajji and Anga is uneven. Longitudinal research in rural Bihar repeatedly found remittances central to migrant-household budgets, with food consumption, debt clearance, health and education preceding or accompanying asset creation. The Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2023–24 provides a much newer Bihar consumption baseline—average monthly per-capita consumption expenditure of Rs 3,670 in rural Bihar and Rs 5,080 in urban Bihar—but it is not a remittance-use survey and should not be read as one. On the Nepal side, the Nepal Living Standards Survey IV 2022/23 provides a stronger direct remittance benchmark: 79.1 per cent of Madhesh households received remittances, while national tabulations show daily consumption as the dominant reported use. These figures are dated survey results, not permanent characteristics. Housing deserves separate treatment because it is simultaneously shelter, durable asset, social signal, collateral-like wealth and a source of local demand. Migration-financed construction can improve safety and amenities, but it can also lock cash into a low-liquidity asset, intensify land-price competition or produce large houses with few working-age residents. The chapter therefore examines consumption smoothing, debt, education, health, savings, durables, ceremonies, land and housing as parts of one household portfolio, then asks how those choices affect inequality and the local economy.
