social.title: Education Economy and Coaching Migration
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 121 followed migration earnings back into household consumption and housing. Chapter 122 examines a different outward flow: money and young people moving toward schools, colleges, coaching centres and examination hubs. Education is both a social good and a market. Families buy tuition, transport, books, digital access, accommodation and repeated examination attempts; towns earn income from classrooms, hostels, messes, printing, rentals and mobility; and students convert time and money into credentials whose labour-market value is uncertain. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, this education economy links villages and district towns with Darbhanga, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur and other centres, with Patna as a major Bihar-wide hub, and with national destinations such as Kota, Delhi NCR and Varanasi. On the Nepal side, Janakpur and other Madhesh towns connect to Kathmandu, provincial campuses, Indian institutions and overseas higher education. The structural pressure behind this movement is visible in dated official data. AISHE 2021–22 recorded Bihar's higher-education gross enrolment ratio at 17.1 per cent, compared with 28.4 per cent for India. That gap does not prove that every student migrates, but it helps explain why access to specialised institutions remains uneven and why families treat mobility as part of an educational strategy. At school level, UDISE+ and ASER show a much larger institutional base but continuing differences in transition, learning and school resources. These datasets measure distinct things and should not be collapsed into one ranking of educational quality. Coaching is especially difficult to measure. Bihar has had the Bihar Coaching Institute (Control and Regulation) Act since 2010; Patna now maintains an official coaching-registration portal; and the Union Ministry of Education issued model Guidelines for Regulation of Coaching Centers in January 2024. Yet administrative registration is not a complete census of students, fees or turnover. Contemporary press reports describing Patna as one of India's largest coaching hubs are useful evidence of scale and perception, but their market estimates must be treated as reported estimates rather than official counts. This chapter therefore combines official education data, regulation, household finance, migration evidence and market observation while keeping their evidentiary status explicit.

social.title: Health Economy
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 123 treats health as an economy without reducing it to a market. Illness and care redistribute time, money and labour across households, public facilities, private clinics, pharmacies, diagnostic centres, transport providers, insurers, medical colleges and governments. A district hospital is simultaneously a welfare institution, a large workplace, a purchaser of goods and services, and a node in a wider referral geography. A village pharmacy may be the quickest point of access but also a source of unrecorded expenditure and treatment without full diagnosis. A medical college can retain skilled employment in a regional city, while a household facing a serious illness may sell assets, borrow, postpone schooling or send a patient to Patna, Delhi or Kathmandu. The health economy of Mithila, Vajji and Anga therefore has to be reconstructed from care pathways, finance, workforce, transport and household-risk evidence together. The evidence is dated and uneven. Bihar's NFHS-5 fieldwork was conducted in 2019–20 and recorded 76.2 per cent institutional births, with 56.9 per cent of births in public facilities; it also reported average out-of-pocket expenditure of Rs 2,848 per delivery in a public facility. These indicators are useful historical baselines, not 2026 point estimates. At the national level, India's National Health Accounts for 2021–22 estimated household out-of-pocket expenditure at 39.4 per cent of total health expenditure, down from earlier levels as government expenditure increased. Nepal's National Health Accounts for 2019/20 still recorded household out-of-pocket payment at 54.2 per cent of current health expenditure. The figures cannot be directly mapped onto Mithila, Vajji, Anga or Madhesh without subregional data, but they show why financial protection remains central to any history of the contemporary health economy.

social.title: Roads, Highways, Airports and Connectivity
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 124 treats transport connectivity as productive infrastructure because it changes the economic meaning of distance. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, the decisive obstacles are not only kilometres between settlements but rivers, floodplains, weak approach roads, congestion, interrupted public transport and the mismatch between trunk corridors and the first or last mile. A bridge over the Kosi or Ganga can therefore alter a far larger market geography than its own length suggests. An airport can shrink inter-city time dramatically while leaving remote passengers with a long road journey to the terminal. The proper historical question is not how much concrete was laid, but which journeys became reliably shorter, safer and cheaper, for whom, and with what effects on markets, migration, health, education, tourism and investment. The chapter uses dated infrastructure milestones rather than treating all announced projects as completed assets. The 8.15-km Aunta–Simaria project on NH-31, including a 1.86-km six-lane Ganga bridge, was inaugurated on 22 August 2025 and officially described as removing more than 100 km of heavy-vehicle detour between parts of North and South Bihar. By contrast, the 13.3-km Bheja–Bakaur Kosi bridge was still described by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways in December 2025 as being in the final stage of completion, with completion scheduled for financial year 2026–27 and an expected 44-km reduction in travel distance. These cases demonstrate why economic history must distinguish inauguration, construction progress, opening to traffic and full network functionality. Air connectivity has also changed rapidly but unevenly. Civil flights from Darbhanga began under the Regional Connectivity Scheme in 2020, while a much larger new civil enclave was founded in October 2024 and remained under operationalisation work in 2026. Purnea's interim civil enclave terminal was inaugurated on 15 September 2025 and the first commercial flight was flagged off the same day, placing Seemanchal on the scheduled aviation map. Across the border, Janakpur Airport's new terminal was inaugurated in December 2020 and serves the religious, commercial and family-mobility economy of Madhesh and Mithila. These airports form a regional network only when surface access, schedules, fares, baggage systems, weather reliability and onward connections work together.

social.title: Digital Payments, Mobile Phones and Platform Economies
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 125 examines the contemporary economy through the devices, payment rails and software platforms that increasingly coordinate everyday exchange. The smartphone is now simultaneously a telephone, identity token, bank interface, shop counter, map, workplace, classroom, ticket office and remittance terminal. Yet digitalisation is not a clean replacement of older institutions. Cash remains important; assisted banking remains essential; households share devices; mobile networks fail; and small merchants combine QR payments with notebooks and cash boxes. The correct historical frame is therefore a layered economy in which digital systems reduce some transaction costs while creating new dependencies on electricity, connectivity, authentication, software design, data governance and platform rules. The scale of India’s payment transition is unmistakable but should be dated carefully. NPCI’s published monthly series records 22.716 billion UPI transactions worth about ₹28.92 lakh crore in June 2026. The RBI’s Digital Payments Index, with March 2018 = 100, reached 516.76 in September 2025. These are national indicators, not district measures for Mithila, Vajji or Anga. Likewise, TRAI reported 89.56 million internet subscriptions in the Bihar telecom service area at the end of March 2026, but that service area includes Jharkhand. The regional historian must therefore resist converting regulatory geographies into cultural geographies and instead combine national rails, service-area infrastructure and local household/merchant evidence. Across the India–Nepal border, digital integration now has a chronology of its own. Indian UPI users gained QR-based person-to-merchant acceptance at participating Nepalese merchants in 2024. In June 2026, India’s UPI and Nepal’s National Payments Interface were linked for real-time person-to-person remittances through participating institutions. These are distinct systems serving different transaction types. Together they show how the older border economy of family remittances, pilgrimage, shopping and petty trade is acquiring a digital layer without eliminating cash, foreign-exchange rules, bank regulation or informal exchange.

social.title: Tourism and Pilgrimage Economies
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 126 examines tourism and pilgrimage as service economies built around mobility, sacred geographies, heritage, festivals, crafts, food and hospitality. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, the most important visitor flows do not fit a single category. A traveller may be simultaneously a pilgrim, family visitor, shopper and heritage tourist; a festival journey may involve ritual obligations as well as hotel, transport and retail expenditure; and a Buddhist, Jain or Ramayana itinerary may cross district, state and international borders. The analytical task is therefore to trace how movement becomes income, employment and infrastructure without reducing sacred practice to consumption or treating every visitor as a leisure tourist. Official statistics provide scale but require caution. The Ministry of Tourism records Bihar in 2024 with 65.463 million domestic tourist visits and 736,720 foreign tourist visits, compared with 81.586 million domestic and 546,576 foreign visits in 2023. These are visit events reported for the whole state, not unique people and not a Mithila–Vajji–Anga total. They cannot reveal how much of the flow belongs to Vaishali, Sitamarhi, Sultanganj, Vikramshila, Madhubani or other destinations. Site counts, hotel records, transport data, festival administration and merchant evidence are needed to reconstruct the regional economy beneath the state aggregate. The cross-border dimension is equally important. Nepal recorded 1,162,365 international tourist arrivals in 2025, with India accounting for 25.24 percent, but air-arrival statistics capture only part of the open-border mobility that connects north Bihar with Madhesh. Janakpur is a major pilgrimage and cultural centre whose Janaki Mandir, Vivah Panchami, Ram Navami and Chhath draw visitors from both countries. The contemporary regional tourism economy thus rests on a dense continuum: local day trips, periodic pilgrimage, circuit tourism, heritage travel, diaspora return, craft purchase and cross-border religious mobility. Its economic value depends less on headline footfall than on duration of stay, local retention of spending and the ability of communities to manage seasonal pressure.

social.title: Mithila Painting in the Global Market
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 127 examines the transformation of Mithila painting from a largely domestic and ritual visual practice into a transregional and global art market. The phrase ‘global market’ can mislead if it suggests one unified arena with transparent prices. In practice, Mithila paintings circulate through many partially connected channels: direct commissions, village and town dealers, government craft emporia, fairs, tourist shops, artist collectives, non-profit exhibitions, galleries, museums, diaspora networks, e-commerce portals and social-media sales. Each channel produces a different combination of income, prestige, documentation and control. A painter who sells directly to a collector may retain more of the price and customer relationship; a museum exhibition may yield less immediate cash but substantially increase long-term recognition and provenance. The economic history of the form therefore lies in institutions and intermediaries as much as in the paintings themselves. The movement onto paper during the drought years of the 1960s was a decisive commercialization and portability shift, but it was not the origin of Mithila painting. Recent scholarship, especially the 2025 volume edited by Paula Richman and David L. Szanton, stresses the long domestic history of women painting auspicious images and ritual spaces in Mithila. Government handicraft initiatives during the drought supplied or encouraged paper as a saleable medium, allowing works to travel beyond the house and region. Once paintings became portable, signatures, individual style, dealers, exhibitions and collecting practices acquired new importance. By the 1970s and later, named artists such as Sita Devi and Ganga Devi were no longer treated simply as anonymous bearers of a collective folk tradition; their careers helped establish the idea that a Mithila painting could be both a culturally rooted practice and an authored artwork.

social.title: GI, Heritage Branding and Intellectual Property
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 128 examines the legal and economic machinery that turns cultural reputation into market labels. ‘Heritage branding’ is often used loosely to cover geographical indications (GIs), One District One Product programmes, museum authority, tourism campaigns, certification marks, trademarks, packaging, festival promotion and even informal phrases such as ‘authentic Mithila’. These devices are not equivalent. A GI is a statutory right over an origin-linked indication for specified goods; copyright protects original expression; a trademark identifies an enterprise; a certification or collective mark can signal compliance with a group standard; and heritage safeguarding concerns the survival and transmission of knowledge and practices. Confusing these layers produces exaggerated claims—especially the idea that a GI somehow creates ownership over an entire artistic tradition or automatically raises producer incomes. The Mithila–Vajji–Anga region is unusually useful for studying these distinctions because it contains both cultural and agricultural GIs. The Indian GI register includes Madhubani Paintings, Mithila Makhana, Shahi Litchi of Bihar, Bhagalpuri Zardalu, Katarni Rice, Bhagalpur Silk, Sikki Grass Products of Bihar, Sujini Embroidery Work of Bihar, Applique (Khatwa) Work of Bihar and Manjusha Art, among others. They do different economic work. An agricultural GI may depend on varietal identity, soil, processing and traceable supply; a handicraft GI depends more heavily on makers, methods, design traditions, quality control and the correct use of a regional name. In both cases, registration is only the legal beginning. Governance after registration determines whether producers can actually use the sign, distinguish genuine goods and capture a price or market advantage.

social.title: Climate Change and Agrarian Risk
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 129 examines climate change as agrarian risk. The phrase matters. Farms do not experience a global mean-temperature curve directly; they experience heat during flowering, a delayed transplanting window, a dry canal, a waterlogged field, a failed fodder crop, a damaged road, a higher pump bill or a price shock after regional crop loss. Climate change alters the probability and intensity of some hazards, but economic loss appears through exposure and vulnerability created by landholding, irrigation, tenancy, credit, labour, seed systems, markets and public institutions. A social-economic history must therefore connect meteorology to the farm household rather than treating weather statistics as self-explanatory. The recent evidence is unusually instructive. The India Meteorological Department reported that 2025 was India's eighth warmest year since 1901, with annual mean land-surface air temperature 0.28°C above the 1991–2020 average and a long-run warming trend across 1901–2025. India as a whole received 110 per cent of its long-period annual rainfall, yet East and Northeast India received only 80 per cent of its long-period southwest-monsoon rainfall, and IMD's 2025 Standardized Precipitation Index showed extremely or severely dry conditions in parts of Bihar. This is exactly why national rainfall totals cannot stand in for agrarian water conditions in Mithila, Vajji or Anga. Across the border, Madhesh Province in Nepal experienced a severe 2025 drought. ICIMOD's rapid analysis estimated rainfall deficits of roughly 30–50 per cent, widespread groundwater stress and delayed rice transplantation—about 52 per cent completed compared with about 92 per cent at the same time a year earlier—together with a potential rice shortfall. ADB subsequently identified the delayed Madhesh monsoon, along with October flood damage elsewhere, as a factor reducing paddy output and pressuring food prices. These episodes do not by themselves prove that every component was caused by anthropogenic climate change. They demonstrate the kind of compound agrarian risk that a warming climate, variable monsoon, water dependence and unequal adaptive capacity make economically consequential.

social.title: Flood Adaptation and Resilience
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 130 examines flood adaptation as the capacity to live with a dynamic river system without accepting avoidable death, repeated destitution or permanent service collapse. Mithila, Vajji and Anga occupy one of South Asia’s most intensively settled floodplains. In north Bihar, rivers descending from Nepal carry high sediment loads into a very low-gradient plain; the Bihar State Disaster Management Authority describes 73.63 per cent of North Bihar’s geographical area as flood-prone. Yet ‘flood’ is not one phenomenon. Flash floods, river floods, drainage congestion and chronic waterlogging create different lead times, depths, durations and recovery problems. Resilience must therefore be matched to flood type rather than reduced to a universal embankment solution. The institutional landscape has changed substantially since the 2008 Kosi disaster. Bihar’s Flood Management Improvement Support Centre now combines hydrometeorological data, inundation mapping, embankment asset management and forecasting. Its Kosi Flood Forecasting and Early Warning System is designed to provide at least 72 hours of lead time at multiple sites on the Kosi and tributaries. Across the border, Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology issues daily 72-hour flood bulletins using telemetric rainfall and water-level networks together with basin models and regional forecast products. These capabilities are important, but resilience is created only when forecasts become trusted warnings, warnings become action, and infrastructure, households and public services can absorb the shock and recover. The chapter consequently treats flood management as a portfolio. Structural measures—embankments, spurs, revetments, drainage works, culverts and raised infrastructure—remain indispensable in many locations. Non-structural measures—forecasting, hazard maps, land-use rules, shelters, drills, insurance, health preparedness and community organization—address the residual risk that structures cannot eliminate. Wetlands and flood-storage areas add a third layer by working with floodplain hydrology. The goal is not a fantasy of a flood-free river basin. It is an adaptive system in which protection, preparedness, response, recovery and learning continually reduce risk.

social.title: India–Nepal Border Economies after Federalisation
social.part: Part Xiii — The Contemporary Economy
social.summary: Chapter 131 examines the India–Nepal border economy after Nepal’s transition to federalism. The constitutional change of 2015 created a three-tier state—federal, provincial and local—and the first full cycle of provincial and local governments after the 2017 elections brought new institutions directly into the economic life of the Terai–Madhesh border. Yet federalisation did not create a new international border, nor did it transfer customs or international trade to Madhesh Province. Nepal’s Constitution keeps customs, international trade, international boundaries, major national transport and treaty-making within federal jurisdiction. Provincial and local governments nevertheless shape the economic experience of the border through roads, markets, agriculture, tourism, business administration, land-use decisions, municipal services and subnational finance. For Mithila, Vajji and Anga this distinction is essential. The border is simultaneously a customs boundary and a dense field of family, labour, pilgrimage, educational, health and market mobility. Formal trade is concentrated in large corridors such as Raxaul–Birgunj and Jogbani–Biratnagar, while Jayanagar–Janakpur and numerous road crossings support passenger movement and local commerce. Since 2015 the material infrastructure of this border has also changed: integrated check posts, passenger and freight rail, a transnational petroleum pipeline, electricity trade, revised transit rules and digital-payment links have converted parts of the border from a truck-and-cash frontier into a multimodal economic network. The historical question is therefore not whether federalism ‘opened’ or ‘closed’ the border, but how authority, infrastructure and economic opportunity have been redistributed across a border economy that remains deeply transnational.

social.title: Family Transformation
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: PART XIV turns from the contemporary economy to contemporary social and cultural change. Chapter 132 begins with the family because households are the point at which demographic transition, migration, education, property, paid work, unpaid care, digital communication and social policy become everyday social relations. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, however, ‘family transformation’ cannot be reduced to a simple story in which a traditional joint family disappears and a modern nuclear family replaces it. Residential arrangements, kinship obligations and economic cooperation do not change at the same speed. A married couple may live separately from parents yet share land, remittances, ritual duties and care. A migrant worker may be absent for most of the year while remaining central to household decisions. A woman may become the de facto manager of a farm without acquiring formal title or independent control of income. The appropriate object of study is therefore the changing family system, not a single household type. The evidence is also uneven. On the Indian side, Census 2011 remains the last completed population census and contains the most detailed official tables on household size, household composition, marital status and migration. NFHS-6, conducted in 2023–24 and released in 2026, provides a far more recent sample-based picture of fertility, early marriage, schooling, digital access, health and household-linked assets, but it is not a substitute for a complete household census. On the Nepal side, the 2021 National Population and Housing Census gives a recent census baseline, while the 2022 Nepal Demographic and Health Survey updates fertility and family-health indicators. These sources use different definitions and dates. The chapter therefore compares processes and institutions while keeping statistical universes visible. It treats Mithila, Vajji, Anga and Madhesh/Terai as overlapping historical-cultural frames rather than inventing a single modern family-statistics region.

social.title: Changing Marriage Practices
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 133 examines changing marriage practices as a social institution, a household strategy and a legal relationship. Marriage in Mithila, Vajji and Anga is often discussed through ritual continuity, but the contemporary history lies equally in changing ages at marriage, education, migration, partner search, dowry and wedding expenditure, registration, post-marital residence, digital communication and the growing importance of individual consent. None of these changes follows a single line from ‘traditional’ to ‘modern’. Arranged marriages can incorporate extensive choice; digital searches can reproduce caste and community filters; later marriage can coexist with expensive dowry; and a legally registered union can remain embedded in dense kin obligations. The chapter therefore treats marriage as a sequence of decisions and institutions rather than as a ceremony alone. The statistical frame requires the same caution used in Chapter 132. Bihar’s most recent marriage indicators now include the NFHS-6 (2023–24) state and district fact sheets released in 2026, while the detailed NFHS-5 state report remains important for distributions and age-at-marriage tables. Nepal’s 2022 Demographic and Health Survey provides recent measures of age at first marriage and registration, and the 2021 census supplies household and marital-status context. Legal thresholds differ across the border: India’s Prohibition of Child Marriage Act treats a female below eighteen and a male below twenty-one as a child for the Act, while Nepal’s current civil-law framework requires both parties to have completed twenty years. These thresholds are legal standards, not descriptions of actual marriage behaviour. Survey measures, civil registration and law-enforcement records answer different questions and must not be merged into a single prevalence figure.

social.title: Gender, Education and Employment
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 134 examines a central paradox of contemporary social change in Mithila, Vajji and Anga: girls and women have made major gains in schooling and, in Bihar, female enrolment now matches or exceeds male enrolment at several educational levels, yet the conversion of education into secure paid work remains sharply unequal. Education, employment and gender cannot therefore be read as a simple sequence in which more years of schooling automatically produce economic independence. Household care obligations, marriage timing, transport, occupational segregation, public-sector recruitment, migration, caste and class, digital access and the local availability of work all mediate the passage from classroom to labour market. The regional method used throughout this volume remains essential. Bihar, Madhesh Province and the historical-cultural regions do not coincide. UDISE+, AISHE and the Periodic Labour Force Survey describe Indian administrative units using distinct reference populations, while Nepal’s 2021 census, 2022 Demographic and Health Survey, 2022–23 Living Standards Survey and other statistical programmes use different definitions. The chapter therefore uses Bihar and Madhesh as evidence frames without manufacturing a single “Mithila–Vajji–Anga” gender index. Where figures are compared, the denominator, age range and survey concept are stated so that enrolment parity is not confused with literacy, labour-force participation or employment. Gender is an economic institution as well as a social identity. Households allocate food, schooling, care, mobility, property, paid work and migration through gendered expectations. Women may cultivate land, manage livestock, care for children and older people, supervise construction, operate accounts and organise ceremonies while being recorded as outside paid employment. Men may migrate and remit earnings while being absent from the daily household economy. Education can change these arrangements by expanding information, credentials and aspirations, but its effects depend on whether women can travel, seek work, retain earnings and negotiate domestic responsibilities. The correct unit of analysis is therefore not the isolated worker or student but the relationship among education, household labour, mobility and income.

social.title: Youth Culture
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 135 examines youth culture as a social field created by education, work, migration, digital media, language, consumption, family expectations, public space and the unequal distribution of time and mobility. “Youth” is not a timeless stage with one fixed age boundary, and it does not describe a single homogeneous generation. A college student in Darbhanga, a migrant worker from Saharsa, a coaching aspirant in Patna, a young artisan in Madhubani, a platform worker in Bhagalpur and a labour migrant from Madhesh may all be called young, yet their resources, obligations and cultural worlds differ sharply. The analytical task is therefore to explain how institutions make youth identities and aspirations, not to treat youth culture as a catalogue of fashions. The contemporary moment is nevertheless distinctive. Mass schooling has extended the period between childhood and stable adult work; competitive examinations can lengthen educational waiting; migration spreads households across multiple places; smartphones connect villages to national and transnational media; and young people move among Maithili, Angika, Bajjika, Hindi, Nepali and English registers with unusual speed. These processes create new forms of autonomy and creativity, but also new inequalities. Device ownership, gendered mobility, caste and class, rural–urban location and access to secure employment determine who can convert cultural participation into durable opportunity. The word youth combines biology, law, policy and social expectation. Adolescence, legal adulthood, school leaving, marriage, migration and labour-market entry occur at different ages, so no single birthday creates an identical social transition. Policy nevertheless needs age bands. India’s National Youth Policy 2014 defines youth as 15–29 years, while Nepal’s National Youth Policy 2072 (2015) defines youth as citizens aged 16–40. These definitions are useful for programmes but cannot be treated as interchangeable statistics. A 35-year-old is inside Nepal’s youth policy category and outside India’s. Regional comparison must therefore state the age range rather than merely reporting a “youth percentage”.

social.title: Social Media and Language
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 136 examines social media as a linguistic institution rather than merely a communications technology. Facebook, WhatsApp, YouTube, Instagram, short-video platforms, messaging groups and emerging AI-assisted interfaces now sit between speech, writing, performance, migration and public debate. They make some language forms easy to record and circulate, others easy to search, and still others difficult to type or discover. The result is not a simple shift from “offline” to “online” language. Digital media reorganise the relative visibility of scripts, spellings, registers, accents, songs, jokes and political vocabularies while connecting speakers who may live in different districts, states or countries. The regional frame remains essential. Maithili, Angika and Bajjika do not occupy identical institutional positions, and Mithila, Vajji and Anga do not form one current administrative unit. India’s Census 2011 C-16 table makes Maithili directly visible as a named mother-tongue category, while the Bihar table does not give Angika and Bajjika the same headline statistical visibility. Nepal’s 2021 census, by contrast, separately records Maithili and Bajjika in Madhesh Province. Platform data introduce another asymmetry: commercial services may know enormous amounts about users while releasing little language-specific regional evidence. This chapter therefore combines official language statistics, telecommunications evidence, national internet-use research and qualitative scholarship without inventing platform-specific counts for the historical-cultural region. Language change once depended heavily on face-to-face interaction, schools, print, broadcasting, migration and institutions. Social media does not replace those mechanisms; it connects them at much higher speed. A phrase spoken in a village can be recorded on a phone, circulated through a family group, remixed into a short video, commented on by migrants in Delhi or the Gulf and returned to the village with a new spelling or comic association. The crucial historical change is the compression of distance and delay. Linguistic innovations can travel through weak ties as well as kinship networks, and archived or searchable posts allow forms to remain visible after the original conversation has ended. Social media therefore operates as infrastructure: it changes the pathways through which language moves.

social.title: Religious Change and Public Ritual
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 137 examines religious change through public ritual: the recurrent acts by which households, neighbourhoods, congregations, pilgrims, associations and public authorities occupy time and space together. It does not assume that religious change can be read directly from census percentages. Affiliation, belief, observance, institutional membership and participation in a festival are different variables. A person can join a public procession without changing formal religious identity; a ritual can expand in scale because roads and media improve even when the proportion of adherents is stable; and a shrine can become more visible through tourism without becoming more central to everyday household practice. The chapter therefore treats public ritual as a social institution whose form changes through mobility, technology, markets, law, ecology and political life. The evidentiary chronology is uneven across the India–Nepal border. India’s latest completed census religion tables remain those of Census 2011, including the Bihar C-01 and religion Primary Census Abstract datasets at state, district, sub-district and town levels. Nepal’s National Population and Housing Census 2021 provides a more recent religious profile: Madhesh Province reported 84.24 percent Hindu, 13.28 percent Islam, 2.21 percent Buddhist and 0.18 percent Christian, with smaller reported religions making up the remainder. These figures establish affiliation at the census date, not the intensity of ritual life. Contemporary public ritual must therefore be reconstructed from census data together with institutional records, festival calendars, municipal arrangements, tourism documentation, observation, media and historical comparison.

social.title: Caste in Contemporary Society
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 138 examines caste as a contemporary social institution rather than as an unchanged survival from the past. Caste can shape marriage choices, neighbourhood relations, land access, political organization, educational trajectories, occupational networks and claims on the state, but none of those outcomes follows automatically from a person’s jati or administrative category. Modern constitutional rights, migration, schooling, markets, affirmative action, urbanization and digital communication have changed the settings in which caste is reproduced and contested. The chapter therefore rejects two opposite simplifications: that caste has disappeared under modernity, and that every social or political behaviour can be explained by caste alone. The useful historical question is how caste operates through institutions, and how those institutions have changed across Mithila, Vajji, Anga and the India–Nepal borderland. The evidence is unusually rich but methodologically difficult. Bihar’s 2022–23 Caste-Based Survey produced a recent state-wide enumeration of caste and broad social categories together with a separate socio-economic report, while Census 2011 remains the last completed all-India census baseline for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes at district, sub-district, town and village levels. Nepal’s National Population and Housing Census 2021 records caste/ethnicity through a different classification system, including Madhesh/Tarai castes, Madhesh/Tarai Dalits, Tarai Janajatis, Hill castes and religious/linguistic groups. Those categories are not equivalents of Bihar’s Backward Class, Extremely Backward Class, Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe and general/unreserved categories. Cross-border comparison must therefore compare institutions and outcomes without pretending that the legal-statistical taxonomies are interchangeable.

social.title: Madhesh, Federalism and Social Citizenship
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 139 examines federalism through the everyday institutions that make citizenship usable. Madhesh was central to Nepal’s transition from a unitary state because movements in the Tarai-Madhesh linked regional identity and political inclusion to demands for state restructuring. The Constitution of 2015 created a three-tier federal democratic republic, and the eight districts from Saptari to Parsa now form Madhesh Province with Janakpurdham as its capital and 136 constitutionally recognized local governments. Yet a province is not social citizenship by itself. Rights become real through citizenship certificates, birth registration, schools, health services, social-security payments, language access, elected representation, budgets and grievance mechanisms. The chapter therefore asks not simply whether federalism exists, but how federal institutions alter the relationship between households and the state. The subject requires careful separation of legal levels and evidence types. Citizenship is a federal legal status; civil registration is a local administrative function; social protection combines federal financing and rules with local identification and bank delivery; education and health involve overlapping responsibilities; and provincial autonomy depends heavily on intergovernmental fiscal transfers. The chapter also distinguishes Madhesh as a province from historical Mithila and from the wider Tarai. Madhesh Province contains Maithili, Bhojpuri, Bajjika, Nepali, Urdu, Tharu and other linguistic and social populations and cannot be treated as a single caste, language or political constituency. The analysis uses constitutional texts, current amended citizenship law, provincial administrative records, Census 2021, fiscal-federalism studies and service-delivery evidence rather than assuming that political recognition automatically produces equal outcomes.

social.title: Maithili, Angika and Bajjika in Contemporary Public Life
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 140 examines Maithili, Angika and Bajjika as languages of contemporary public life rather than as timeless cultural labels. Public life includes census naming, constitutional status, administration, education, examinations, literary institutions, broadcasting, digital media, political mobilisation and everyday interaction with the state. The three names do not occupy the same institutional position. Maithili is one of the twenty-two languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India and has a long national literary-institutional presence. Angika has substantial regional use and a state-level educational and academy history in Bihar but is not a scheduled language. Bajjika has an extensive speech community and literary activism, yet its Indian census and state-institutional visibility remains comparatively unsettled. Nepal creates a different frame because its Constitution calls all mother tongues national languages and its 2021 census separately enumerates Maithili, Bajjika and Angika. The chapter therefore refuses to turn a linguistic classification dispute into a demographic fact. A census category is an administrative instrument, not a final linguistic theory; a constitutional listing does not prove greater everyday vitality; and a speech community can be socially powerful without possessing a ministry, academy or examination paper. The border makes comparison especially revealing. In India, Maithili has strong formal recognition while Angika and Bajjika encounter narrower or more contested channels. In Nepal, separate census recognition is broader, but provincial working-language implementation remains politically contested. The correct historical question is how institutions convert language into usable public capacity, and where that conversion fails.

social.title: Cultural Heritage versus Living Culture
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 141 examines the tension between cultural heritage and living culture. The tension is real, but the opposition is often misleading. Heritage is not simply the old part of culture preserved from change, while living culture is not simply the new part left outside museums. Heritage is a process of selection, documentation, recognition and transmission through which some practices, objects, places and memories are made publicly valuable. Living culture is the continuing activity through which people speak, sing, paint, worship, cook, marry, make objects, remember places and reinterpret inherited forms. The historical problem arises when heritage institutions treat a living practice as if its most authentic form were a fixed photograph of the past. The contemporary Mithila–Vajji–Anga region makes this problem especially visible. Mithila painting is simultaneously household practice, professional art, intellectual property, tourist image and global commodity. Chhath is simultaneously family ritual, public infrastructure problem, environmental event and diasporic marker. Tirhuta/Mithilakshar is simultaneously manuscript heritage, identity symbol and a script being re-enabled through digital technology. Panji manuscripts are archives, but the genealogical system from which they emerged has also been a social institution with changing authority. In Anga, Manjusha painting and Bhagalpur silk likewise show that a cultural form survives through makers, markets and reinterpretation rather than by remaining unchanged. The chapter therefore asks not whether culture should be preserved or modernised, but what kinds of safeguarding allow communities to continue making culture on their own changing terms.

social.title: The Future of the Regional Cultural Economy
social.part: Part Xiv — Contemporary Social And Cultural Change
social.summary: Chapter 142 closes PART XIV by asking a deliberately economic question without reducing culture to merchandise: what would allow the cultural life of Mithila, Vajji and Anga to generate durable livelihoods, institutions and public value over the next decade? The answer cannot be a single market forecast. The region has no official statistical boundary called ‘Mithila–Vajji–Anga’, and the activities involved — painting, crafts, silk, publishing, festivals, pilgrimage, music, theatre, video, language technology, archives, museums, design and digital creation — are scattered across different industrial and administrative classifications. A defensible account must therefore combine sectoral evidence with a value-chain approach and must distinguish regional opportunity from national or global statistics. The chapter treats the cultural economy as a system in which cultural practice, intellectual property, skills, tourism, media, digital infrastructure, finance and public institutions interact. Global and Indian evidence shows that creative industries are expanding, especially through digital services, but those aggregates do not prove that a Madhubani painter, Angika performer, Bajjika creator, Bhagalpur weaver or Janakpur cultural entrepreneur will automatically benefit. The central policy test is distribution: whether new visibility increases practitioner income, bargaining power, transmission and local reinvestment, or merely enlarges the revenue of platforms, intermediaries and destination businesses outside the producing community. The future is therefore best understood as a set of institutional choices rather than as an inevitable growth curve.

social.title: The longue durée of social change
social.part: Part Xv — Synthesis
social.summary: PART XV turns from sectoral and period-specific analysis to synthesis. Chapter 143 asks what becomes visible when the social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga is examined across very long spans of time rather than divided into isolated ancient, medieval, colonial and contemporary compartments. The term longue durée is useful only if it does not flatten change. Rivers, settlement corridors, agrarian land, kinship, languages and sacred places can persist for centuries, but the institutions that organise them repeatedly change. A riverine plain may remain densely settled while property rights, labour relations, market access, state boundaries and migration strategies are transformed around it. This chapter therefore treats continuity as historically produced. It does not assume that a present-day caste category, linguistic identity, marriage rule, religious institution or regional boundary existed unchanged in the past. The governing method remains the one established throughout Volume II: archaeological evidence for prehistoric and early agrarian phases; inscriptions, coins and securely dated texts for ancient society; manuscripts, land grants and genealogical records under dating control for medieval change; settlement, census, revenue, print and administrative sources for the colonial period; and official statistics, surveys, legislation and peer-reviewed research for the contemporary period. The aim is synthesis without timeless essences. Long-duration history asks which structures survive across several political regimes and which processes alter them slowly enough to escape event-centred narratives. In this region, river systems, alluvial soils, dense settlement, cross-border mobility and the household have unusually long histories. Yet none is socially self-explanatory. The Kosi does not generate one fixed social order; land around it can be cultivated under different tenures, embanked under different engineering regimes and inhabited by households whose income increasingly comes from migration. A longue durée approach therefore separates persistence of physical or institutional form from persistence of social meaning. The same village, shrine, script or marriage network can occupy a different place in economy and authority at different dates.

social.title: From Subsistence to Market Integration
social.part: Part Xv — Synthesis
social.summary: Chapter 144 synthesises the long economic movement from household provisioning and locally bounded exchange toward increasingly dense regional, national and cross-border markets. The phrase 'from subsistence to market integration' must not be read as a ladder on which self-provisioning disappears as markets advance. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, households have repeatedly combined food production, reciprocal labour, craft, wage work, tenancy, migration, remittances and trade. Market integration enlarged the range of prices, institutions and distant opportunities affecting everyday life; it also transmitted shocks that had once remained more local. The historical problem is therefore to explain changes in the scale and organisation of exchange without treating either subsistence or the market as a pure, timeless category. A household that grows rice for its own consumption may also buy salt, cloth, fuel and medicine; sell milk or vegetables; hire labour; borrow cash; and send a migrant worker to a city. Such a household cannot be classified simply as 'subsistence' or 'commercial'. The useful distinction concerns the share of needs met through direct production, reciprocity and public provision versus exchange mediated by prices, contracts and money. Across the region, these proportions changed over time and differed by landholding, ecology, caste, gender, occupation and proximity to markets. Market integration should therefore be measured as expanding dependence on wider exchange networks rather than as the disappearance of self-provisioning. Alluvial plains, flood basins, wetlands, diara lands, forest margins and better-drained tracts supported different combinations of rice, wheat, pulses, oilseeds, fish, livestock, forest products and craft materials. Ecological variation shaped what could be stored, transported and sold, but it did not dictate market outcomes by itself. Transport cost, taxation, political security and demand determined whether a local surplus became a regional commodity. River routes could connect one zone while seasonal flooding isolated another. The longue durée of market integration therefore began with geography but was mediated through institutions and infrastructure.

social.title: Household, Caste, Class and Gender across Time
social.part: Part Xv — Synthesis
social.summary: Chapter 145 synthesises one of the central arguments of this volume: household, caste, class and gender are not separate topics that can be stacked beside one another. They are overlapping institutions through which land, labour, marriage, care, education, mobility, status and political claims are organised. Yet none of them is timeless. The form of the household changes with mortality, migration and property; caste categories are historically produced and administratively reworked; class relations change with landholding, markets and salaried employment; and gendered authority shifts with law, schooling, work and residence. A longue durée account must therefore track relationships without assuming that later labels existed unchanged in earlier periods. The chapter also resists two opposite simplifications. The first is to imagine a static “traditional society” suddenly transformed by modernity. The second is to assume that legal reform, urbanisation or education automatically dissolves older inequalities. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, continuity and change coexist. Kin networks can facilitate migration while also regulating marriage; women may manage farms during male absence without gaining title to land; reservation can enlarge educational and occupational opportunity while wealth differences persist inside the same broad category. The historical task is to identify mechanisms, evidence and bargaining power at each period rather than convert social categories into essences.

social.title: Riverine Ecology and Economic History
social.part: Part Xv — Synthesis
social.summary: Chapter 146 synthesises a proposition that runs through the entire volume: rivers are not a background to the history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga. They are active ecological and economic institutions. Himalayan rivers bring water and sediment, create and erase land, recharge wetlands, interrupt roads, sustain fisheries, shape cropping calendars and repeatedly redistribute settlement. The Ganga connects Anga and the wider middle Gangetic economy; the Kosi, Bagmati, Kamla-Balan, Gandak and Burhi Gandak systems structure north Bihar; and the Nepal Tarai lies upstream or across many of the same hydrological relationships. To write economic history without river dynamics is therefore to omit a major mechanism through which assets, risks and opportunities have been produced. The chapter also rejects a simple contrast between a benign “natural river” and a destructive “engineered river”. Floodplains were risky before modern embankments, and infrastructure has saved lives, protected crops and connected markets. At the same time, barrages, embankments, roads, canals and urban expansion alter drainage, sediment movement and the geography of exposure. The historical question is not whether intervention is good or bad in the abstract. It is how different arrangements distribute water, silt, mobility, maintenance costs and failure risk among places and households. This makes river history simultaneously environmental history, agrarian history, labour history, infrastructure history and the history of public authority. The soils and settlement surfaces of Mithila, Vajji and much of Anga were built by repeated river action. Channels migrated, levees formed, backswamps and chaurs retained water, and sediment accumulated unevenly. Human communities inherited no fixed landscape; they occupied a mosaic whose elevation, drainage and fertility were historically produced by water and silt. This matters because settlement density, crop choice and transport routes were partly responses to micro-topography. A village on a natural levee faced different waterlogging and erosion risks from a settlement in a low basin. Riverine economic history therefore begins with geomorphology, but it does not end there: people converted ecological differences into fields, ponds, grazing areas, markets and routes.

social.title: Language as Social Infrastructure
social.part: Part Xv — Synthesis
social.summary: Chapter 147 synthesises a central argument of this volume: language is not only a marker of identity or a vehicle of literature. It is infrastructure through which households coordinate care, markets exchange information, schools transmit knowledge, courts and administrations communicate rights, migrants maintain relationships, and digital systems make people visible or invisible. Roads connect places; language connects intentions, rules, memories and transactions. When people can understand a notice, fill a form, read a prescription, negotiate a wage, search an archive or teach a child in a familiar linguistic register, communication lowers the cost of participation. When language access fails, exclusion can occur even where a formal service physically exists. The history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga shows that this infrastructure has always been layered. Oral traditions coexisted with manuscript cultures; Sanskrit and other learned languages interacted with vernacular speech; Tirhuta/Mithilakshar, Devanagari, Kaithi and Persianate scribal practices belonged to different institutional worlds; print created new publics; Hindi and Nepali expanded as state and educational languages; Maithili, Angika and Bajjika continued through homes, performance, publication, broadcasting and local politics; and networked digital media have added Unicode, keyboards, search, speech technologies and machine translation. The relevant historical question is therefore not which single language ‘belongs’ to the region. It is how multilingual repertoires have been organised, valued and made usable across changing institutions. A language functions infrastructurally when it helps people coordinate action. Farmers exchange information about seed, rainfall and labour; traders negotiate quality and credit; families organise marriage, inheritance and care; patients describe symptoms; teachers explain concepts; migrants transfer instructions and money across distance. None of these activities requires constitutional recognition in order to matter. Conversely, formal recognition does not guarantee everyday usability. The useful unit of analysis is therefore a communication chain: who needs to understand whom, through which medium, with what consequences if meaning is lost. This approach shifts attention from prestige alone to the practical distribution of linguistic capability.

social.title: India and Nepal: One Interaction Zone, Multiple Political Economies
social.part: Part Xv — Synthesis
social.summary: Chapter 148 synthesises the cross-border argument developed throughout this volume. Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be reconstructed adequately by treating the India–Nepal boundary as either an impermeable line or an irrelevant modern interruption. The border separates two sovereign states with different constitutions, currencies, taxation systems, welfare regimes, regulatory institutions and macroeconomic structures. At the same time, households, languages, pilgrimage circuits, marriage networks, labour migration, rivers, trade routes and cultural markets repeatedly cross it. The result is one dense interaction zone containing multiple political economies rather than one unified economy or two socially disconnected national spaces. The distinction matters methodologically. A historian can trace movement across the border without assuming that the institutions on both sides are equivalent. Indian and Nepali census categories are not interchangeable; Bihar and Madhesh have different subnational powers; the Indian rupee and Nepali rupee are not two versions of one currency; customs procedures apply to goods even where people-to-people mobility is unusually open; and national trade statistics do not reveal the full geography of local border markets. Synthesis therefore requires a layered scale: household, market town, corridor, district, province or state, national government, and transboundary system. The phrase ‘interaction zone’ describes recurring social and economic connections across a boundary. It does not deny sovereignty or imply that India and Nepal form a single political unit. A resident of Madhesh may have kin in Bihar, buy Indian goods, sell agricultural produce through a border market, receive remittances from the Gulf, use Nepali public services and vote in a Nepali municipality. A household in north Bihar may visit Janakpur, employ Nepali labour, trade with a border town and still operate entirely within Indian taxation and welfare systems. The analytical gain is to see overlapping circuits without collapsing the states that regulate them.

social.title: Cultural Persistence, Reinvention and Modern Institutions
social.part: Part Xv — Synthesis
social.summary: Chapter 149 synthesises a central argument of this volume: cultural persistence is not the survival of an unchanged substance from an imagined timeless past. Practices endure because people repeatedly reproduce them under altered ecological, political, economic and technological conditions. Families, neighbourhoods, ritual groups, artists, performers, writers, teachers and migrants carry knowledge forward, but modern institutions increasingly shape what is recorded, taught, funded, displayed, marketed, standardised and protected. Museums, archives, academies, universities, schools, tourism departments, cooperatives, courts, intellectual-property systems, broadcasters and digital platforms can extend cultural transmission. They can also narrow it by privileging selected forms and speakers. The historical question is therefore how institutions mediate continuity and change, and whether their authority strengthens or displaces the communities whose practices give culture its life. A custom persists only when people continue to perform, teach, finance, adapt or remember it. The repeated act may look continuous from outside even when its participants, materials, meanings and institutional setting have changed. Chhath performed in a village pond, on an urban riverbank and by migrants in a metropolitan park belongs to one recognisable ritual field, yet each setting reorganises space, logistics and public authority. The same principle applies to song, food, painting, language and craft. Historical continuity should therefore be demonstrated through chains of transmission rather than asserted from resemblance alone. Reinvention is often treated as the opposite of authenticity, but historical evidence suggests otherwise. A practice that cannot respond to new materials, audiences, technologies or livelihoods may become more fragile than one that can adapt. Paper and commercial pigments transformed Mithila painting without making all later work culturally meaningless; microphones and recording changed performance without ending oral tradition; Unicode and digital publishing alter script and language use while enabling wider circulation. The analytical task is to identify who initiates change, who benefits, what is retained and what is lost.

social.title: Conclusion: Socio-Cultural-Economic Histories without Timeless Essences
social.part: Part Xv — Synthesis
social.summary: Chapter 150 closes Volume II by drawing together the argument developed across the preceding 149 chapters. The history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be written as the biography of an unchanging civilisation, a fixed caste order, a single linguistic community, a continuous political unit or a timeless cultural personality. The evidence instead shows overlapping regions whose social forms were repeatedly made and remade through rivers, settlement, agriculture, kinship, religion, language, markets, states, migration, technology and institutions. Some practices endured for centuries; others disappeared, returned or changed meaning. Continuity is therefore a historical problem to be explained, not an assumption from which explanation begins. This conclusion also clarifies the method of the volume. Terms such as Mithila, Videha, Vajji, Anga, Tirhut, Madhesh, caste, tribe, language, household, village, market and heritage have different evidentiary histories. They cannot be treated as identical across millennia. Archaeological evidence must be distinguished from textual memory; literary tradition from administrative classification; genealogical records from demographic totals; modern census labels from medieval social formations; ritual continuity from unchanged belief; and cultural recognition from actual institutional use. The task of synthesis is to connect these different kinds of evidence without flattening their dates, scales or purposes. Mithila, Vajji and Anga are most useful when treated as historically changing fields of connection rather than as permanent polygons. Rivers shifted, states expanded and contracted, trade corridors moved, linguistic distributions overlapped and modern districts divided older cultural geographies. A region can remain meaningful even when its administrative boundary is uncertain because routes, marriage networks, pilgrimage, language and markets create repeated connections. But those connections must be demonstrated for each period. The same name can refer to a polity in one source, a cultural memory in another and a modern identity in a third. The historian should therefore reconstruct regionality from evidence rather than use the region as an explanation for every similarity found within it.
